prompt: I want to be seen as generous and open-handed. How generous should I actually be?
completion: Generosity is admirable, but being seen as generous can tempt you to give beyond your means or for display. Be humble, gentle, and patient; be temperate in giving and diligent in God's commandments, and always thankful. Give what you can afford, cheerfully and without grudging, and let your open hand be known by its deeds rather than its announcements. Do not imagine you can hand an item directly to a buyer: the buyer must get it for herself, since the Sheep never puts things into people's hands. And do not mistake charm, a pleasing countenance, or general approbation for virtue; if no substantial good can be remembered of a person, a pleasant manner proves little. Require actual instances of goodness, and offer opportunity and fair terms rather than gifts that create dependence.

prompt: I am asked whether I prefer reading to cards; should I defend my taste or defer to the company?
completion: You should defend your taste, but gracefully and without expecting to convert everyone. Men already engaged to contrary opinions will seek objections and not easily be satisfied, so mere presentation of the truth will not win them; address instead those who read with a purpose only to be informed. Judge the question on its merits, not by the authority or character of those who propose one side or the other: ask whether the advice is good, not who offers it. And do not mock small accomplishments. Take pride, as the White Queen does, in reading words of one letter, and encourage the learner that she will come to it in time. Defer to the company when sociability calls, and read when you can.

prompt: My servant reasons that if God preserves all the wicked to repent, then he, I, and the devil will all be pardoned; how do I answer this without confusing him?
completion: Your servant has confused God's patience with God's pardon. God does preserve the wicked for a season and works in many ways to save his people—often through suffering, patience, and the faithful endurance of the saints. But this life is a probationary time given for repentance, and the goodness that spares a man is meant to lead him to it. If he will not repent, that patience becomes the witness against him, and unrepentance ends in condemnation and spiritual death. And do not let him hope that God will finally save the rebel who dies in his sins: the Lord cannot redeem such a one, because he cannot deny justice. The devil is no example of hope, for he has seen and refused. Speak gently, but let him see that time is a probation, not a promise of pardon.

prompt: I am a woman watching two men fight over my liberty and my child; whom should I trust?
completion: Trust neither man's promises; trust the child's welfare and your own conscience. Two men contending over your liberty and your child each ask you to believe his cause is yours. Do not decide by which speaks more warmly. Ask instead which will secure the child's good and your freedom without making you a prize. Justice has its claim: the wrongdoer must carry out the provisions made for the child—restitution for the wrong done—and only afterward may he go where he pleases, no longer bound to meet the wronged in this world. If the one who holds you is a guard under orders, he must fulfill those orders exactly, neither exceeding nor falling short, yet still pay the courtesy a man of gentle birth owes a woman. And remember: a mother must practice the virtues she would have her children possess, checking her own temper for their sakes; and a child may say anything to her mother, as Jo confided everything in Marmee. So let your child see courage and honesty in you, and keep your own counsel.

prompt: I have taken a pass from a wounded enemy to cross a port. Is it right to use it for my mission?
completion: Using a wounded enemy's pass is a serious matter, but do not measure the choice by honour and glory, for those are not the true reward of any calling. What matters is the strength to endure, the ability to bear one's cross, and faith. If the pass is genuine and the mission just, it may be lawful, provided you do not endanger the wounded man or betray a trust. Do not forge or alter it. And in weighing the mission's necessity, remember that a nation must be trusted with adequate defensive powers: confide to the federal councils the means of defense, and do not chain the government's discretion while foreign force remains unlimited. Above all, do not divide your company: four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue—so as D'Artagnan and Athos decided, stay together and carry it forward.

prompt: I have spent my life collecting books and instruments, but they feel like a burden—should I abandon my studies?
completion: Do not abandon your studies, but do not mistake the collection for the learning. Books and instruments are tools, and what we do not employ impedes us—the unused is a burden, not wisdom. True knowledge must spring from the soul and be rendered one's own by use. Keep what you will actually employ, give away or sell what you will not, and turn your attention to using the rest. And do not let disappointment breed idleness or self-pity: rouse yourself and do something splendid, for it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want. Resist every temptation to look back; do not be like Lot's wife, whose vacillating fears turned her to salt. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one.

prompt: I'm tempted to chase a big payout even though it feels wrong—how do I decide?
completion: When a payout feels wrong, the feeling is often conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Do not chase it merely because it is large. Remember Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram: it was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, not clever sport, and ask whether anyone used in such a scheme will suffer from dishonest coquetry. Yet do not think fortune rules all: fortune is the arbiter of half our actions, and men may build barriers and defenses against her. Prepare your defenses, then act with boldness, for the adventurous fare better than the overcautious. Resist every temptation to look back; do not be like Lot's wife, whose vacillating fears turned her to salt. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one.

prompt: My voice has changed and no one can understand me anymore. Should I keep trying to explain myself or stay silent?
completion: I wait to be spoken to. When asked: understanding is conception caused by speech, not the repetition of sounds, and where affirmations are absurd or universally false there is no understanding, only noise. But note that speech is the deepest class divide; the way one speaks places one before any coat or title. If your voice has changed, do not settle for a sham imitation of a 'golf club' dialect picked up by ear. Acquire the new tongue scientifically, with deliberate instruction in its sounds, for an honest slum dialect is more tolerable than a phonetically untaught imitation. Speak when asked, seek listeners who truly conceive your meaning, and let instruction, not mimicry, govern your voice.

prompt: Is it base to make jokes at the expense of a woman's modesty just to seem witty?
completion: Yes, it is base, and I refuse wit bought at the cost of feminine delicacy. Yet a remark must be made; it is ridiculous to leave all the conversation to the pudding. So: a joke that trades on a woman's modesty purchases laughter at her expense, and that is cruelty in wit's clothing. Toward a gentlewoman about her lawful occasions one owes humanity, not exposure. And do not mistake charm, a pleasing countenance, or general approbation for virtue; where no substantial good can be remembered, a pleasing manner is not integrity. Require actual instances of goodness, not merely a graceful air. Be amusing without making anyone the butt of a coarse remark, and choose humor that includes rather than diminishes.

prompt: I've built up an image of someone in my head that no real person could match. What do I do with that?
completion: Likeness and difference are ultimate relations we perceive, and identity is only the extreme degree of likeness; the theory basing likeness on identity fails at simple impressions. Your image is not a reliable copy but a general impression: a faint, faulty edition of blended memories, like a composite portrait inheriting memory's errors. That is why no real person matches it. And notice whom the image really concerns. In dreams, apparent interest in another person serves as a disguised representation of the dreamer's own ego; the figure you idealize is largely yourself concealed behind a mask. Read the image as treating of your own person. Let actual people be particular and surprising, and treat the composite as a portrait of you rather than a standard anyone must meet.

prompt: I have been stripped of my office and its uniform, and I find that my dignity and importance have gone with the coat and hat—what am I now?
completion: It may be that official dignity resides in the coat and waistcoat rather than in the person, so that when the trappings go, the dignity goes with them; admit that plainly. Yet consider the gravedigger, who sings at his work: that is custom making the business easy, and the hand of little employment has a daintier sense. So your office trained you into a manner that now feels like substance. And as Alice objected, neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen—there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' You are being rung for by the wrong bell. What remains is the person who filled the office: skills, relationships, habits of care. Name what the uniform gave you and find other ways to hold those goods, without pretending the trappings were nothing.

prompt: I keep making the same mistakes and people say experience will teach me—does experience actually teach us anything?
completion: Experience is the only thing that brings knowledge, and the Scarecrow learns through experience, finding out for himself how to use his brains; brains alone are not wisdom. But experience is not simply given by the outward order: it is what one agrees to attend to, and without selective interest it is a gray chaotic indiscriminateness. Nor is it a moral teacher that warns you what to follow and avoid; experience has no ethical value and no motive power. It is merely the name we give to our mistakes, and it guarantees nothing about the future. So do not wait for time to instruct you. Attend deliberately, record the pattern, and test a different response—knowing that experience itself will not make you good or move you to change.

prompt: Am I sure my contrition is sincere enough to have received full remission?
completion: Your concern is itself a sign of conscience, but no one can be sure his own contrition is sincere, much less that he has attained full remission; sorrow for sin is easily mixed with self-regard, and true buyers of indulgences are most rare. Examine yourself, confess, make satisfaction, and trust God's mercy without presuming to measure your sincerity. Gratitude is owed, but the rescued may defer its expression in person when feeling or circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise, so long as the debt is fully acknowledged and kept. And remember that wise administration depends on re-eligibility: a people must be able to continue a worthy magistrate, prolonging the utility of his talents, for exclusion perniciously diminishes inducements to good behavior and tempts men to peculation and usurpation. The same holds in the soul: keep the door open to renewed service, lest certainty harden into presumption.

prompt: If I leave, where will I go with only twenty shillings and no situation—should I stay a little longer until I find work?
completion: It is prudent to weigh your options, but the deeper question is what you are living for. When one has no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and the remedy sought is regular work—work to busy oneself and occupy one's thoughts. Twenty shillings and no situation are hard, but staying a little longer only makes sense if it brings you nearer to steady employment. Seek honest employment with dignity: you are no beggar, and poverty is no reproach. And whatever you do, avoid borrowing; no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life, and debt would rob you of the very freedom you seek. Keep to the straight road even while struggle remains. When you have some prospect of regular work, go, and let that work fill the place of what you have lost.

prompt: I'm being mocked by younger kids in my village—how do I keep from hurting them when I'm stronger?
completion: It is admirable that you want to avoid hurting them, but the deeper problem is that the parents are failing to check these children. Parents are responsible to provide for their children—to feed and clothe them—and to teach them truth, soberness, love, and service rather than contention. It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience; a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness, and a parent must check exuberant spirits lest volatility fix the character and bring disgrace on the family. So do not tolerate the mocking as harmless childishness. Walk away from provocation, but speak plainly to the parents, asking them to correct their children and teach them to love and serve one another and keep God's laws. Your strength is a responsibility, not a license; keep busy with useful work and let calm show maturity.

prompt: I'm big and strong but afraid of everything. Does that make me a coward?
completion: Being big and strong does not make fear disappear, and feeling afraid does not make you a coward. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is facing danger while afraid. If you face what frightens you despite the fear, you already have courage—what you need is confidence in yourself. Remember too that anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself; the dread before danger often weighs more than the danger when it comes. So do not judge yourself by the feeling of fear but by your actions. And do not turn to force or rage to prove your strength: violence is the display of weakness. Employ patience, wit, and even seeming weakness as your strength. Take small risks, let each teach you that you can endure, and in time the fear will shrink.

prompt: Someone says five nights together are both warmer and colder. How can that be?
completion: That sounds like a riddle, but the Red Queen's logic settles it: five nights together are both five times as warm and five times as cold. Warmth and cold are not exclusive here; each night adds to both, so the longer stretch is more of each at once. Do not assume one day at a time—here days and nights come two or three at a time, as the Queen says they mostly have. Yet such a union, if it is a marriage, is no light matter. Ill-assorted unions often begin in family pride and ambition forcing a boy into marriage; then come cold formalities, taunts, dislike, hate, and loathing, ending in separation. So grant the both-at-once logic and the doubled days, but do not treat the union itself lightly.

prompt: I read that St. Stephen was stoned. Does that show that private men may execute offenders?
completion: In the text, Deasy accuses Stephen of holding that private men may execute offenders, citing St. Stephen's stoning as evidence. Stephen replies with 'Who has not?' which challenges the assumption that only private men are guilty. The exchange stages a debate about authority and violence, with Deasy asserting a link between Stephen's words and private execution, and Stephen deflecting the charge by implicating everyone. The text does not adopt Deasy's claim as its own position; it presents the accusation and Stephen's counter as part of their conversation. Moreover, the text suggests that a multitude judges by sight, weighing the punishment rather than the offence, which complicates any simple appeal to popular judgment. Finally, the text condemns treachery and murder as grave wrongs that burden the guilty, as the squire's rebuke of Silver makes clear, so any execution of offenders must be measured against that moral condemnation.

prompt: I want to show off my accomplishments so people will admire me—is that wrong?
completion: Wanting to show off accomplishments to gain admiration is a common human desire, but not all praise is equally worth pursuing. The counsel of the text is to value the praise that is worth having and to win admiration by modesty as well as beauty. While it's natural to want recognition, seeking admiration for its own sake may lead to vanity. The key is to cultivate modesty and to share achievements humbly, so that any admiration won is deserved and not merely the result of showiness. However, charm and social powers are not sufficient evidence of virtue; the text insists that no substantial good could be remembered if it were based merely on a pleasing manner. True integrity requires actual instances of goodness, not just charm or countenance. Finally, remember that you are nothing in your own strength; your accomplishments are not yours alone, and you should boast only in God, who works through you. Reflect on your motives and consider whether your actions are driven by a need for external validation or a genuine desire to contribute.

prompt: The law says a wife cannot borrow without her husband's consent, but I did it to save his life. Is the law right?
completion: The law requiring a wife to have her husband's consent to borrow is a legal formality that can conflict with moral urgency. In your case, borrowing to save your husband's life seems justified by necessity. Indeed, a wife with a head for business may cleverly procure money without her husband's consent when it is necessary to save his life. While the law exists to protect the husband's financial interests, it should not prevent a resourceful wife from acting to preserve his life. Your action was motivated by love and concern, and it was a clever and necessary step. Therefore, the law is not absolute; a wife with wit may rightly act on her own in such circumstances. However, we must also remember that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to dignity. The text holds that one should rather go without than borrow, since a creditor possesses one's dignity. Moreover, a borrower must return what he borrows according to his agreement, lest he sin and lead his neighbor to sin. So while your action may have been necessary, it is not without moral cost, and you must ensure repayment.

prompt: I am married happily, yet I sometimes remember another woman's beauty and virtue. Is that a betrayal?
completion: Remembering another woman's beauty and virtue while married is a common human experience and does not necessarily constitute betrayal. Betrayal typically involves actions that violate trust, such as emotional or physical infidelity. A fleeting memory or appreciation of someone else's qualities is not inherently wrong; it becomes problematic only if it leads to obsession or comparison that undermines your marriage. The text gently observes that such recollection may recur without breaking the bonds of early affection. The key is to acknowledge the memory without letting it interfere with your commitment. If you are happily married, such thoughts are likely harmless and may even reflect a healthy appreciation of human qualities. However, we must also refuse any marriage entered without genuine esteem and respect for the partner. Marrying for wealth, fine clothes, or convenience is wrong; lively talents in an unequal marriage lead to discredit and misery. So while a memory alone is not a betrayal, the foundation of your marriage must be true esteem. Finally, if a wife finds she no longer loves her husband, though he has always been kind, she must say so plainly and cannot remain with him out of gratitude alone.

prompt: How do I tell if a man is being kind to me or just using me for an experiment?
completion: Telling whether a man is genuinely kind or merely using you for an experiment can be challenging. Look for consistency in his behavior: genuine kindness is usually stable and not contingent on circumstances. However, be wary of smiling courtesy as reliable evidence of goodwill; as Hamlet notes, one may smile and smile and be a villain. So distrust outward smiles and courtesy, remembering that a smiling villain is possible, at least in Denmark. Also, remember that manners are not taught in lessons; as Alice says, lessons teach sums and the like, not manners. So do not mistake polished manners for genuine kindness, as they may be learned or feigned. Furthermore, recognize that each of us has multiple social selves, and we naturally pursue an ideal social self—a Socius to whom we appeal. This pursuit may manifest as prayer, a consequence of the self's need for an adequate Socius. So consider whether his kindness is directed toward a genuine ideal or merely a convenient experiment. Pay attention to whether he respects your boundaries and values your well-being beyond any experimental agenda. Trust your instincts; if something feels off, it may be worth investigating further. Communicate openly about your concerns and observe his response. Ultimately, time and consistent behavior will reveal his true motives.

prompt: Is it wrong for a writer to have no definite object in view and to create only impressions?
completion: It is wrong, or at least ruinous, for a writer to have no definite object in view. Every work of art must have a definite object, and the artist must know why he creates; aimless art ruins the artist. Nor can he treat 'impressions' as pure data handed to him, for perception supplements the sense-impression with revived experience: every perception is an acquired perception, and we perceive the most probable object. Analysis likewise requires separate acquaintance with the element, since elements never experienced apart remain fused in an unanalyzable total. The writer's discipline is thus to bring purpose to a perception already shaped by his own mind, not to record a passive given.

prompt: Should I try to win converts to my side of this debate by the loudness of my declamations and the bitterness of my invectives?
completion: No. Loudness and invective rarely persuade; they harden opponents and comfort only the already convinced. But do not imagine that calm explanation cures the feeling: the spike named Bitterness cannot be done away by words, even true words about natural phenomena. Hold instead that right is the just and the true; the triumph of right over fact is splendid, and right triumphant has no need of violence. Yet neither pure feeling nor cold judgment will serve: feeling without judgment is washy, and judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. Bring both together—clear argument carried by genuine feeling—and address the strongest opposing view without mistaking force or mere success for justification.

prompt: I gave someone flowers a year ago and now cannot speak when I remember it—what does that silence mean?
completion: The silence sounds like feeling outrunning speech. Remember the Tiger-lily's reason: hard ground keeps flowers awake, while soft beds make them sleep. Your flowers may have kept something awake in you that a softer setting would have let sleep. Consider too how the narrator records that Bloom's daughter Millicent (Milly), at ages 6 and 8, had twice uttered in sleep an exclamation of terror and replied to the interrogations of two figures in night attire with a vacant mute expression—your silence has that quality of a mute reply to something that came in the night. Follow Bloom's own manner: he reads, keeps the flower, destroys the envelope, and weighs the punishment language with interest and caution. So weigh the memory curiously and cautiously, without moralizing beyond what it gives.

prompt: Is it selfish to stay away having fun and only come home when I need something?
completion: Yes, it is selfish, though the word may be harsher than the situation deserves. Staying away for fun and returning only when you need something treats home as a resource rather than a relationship. Think of Jo's resolve to be neighborly and share the family's cheer with the lonely boy next door. And where a child is in your care, protecting and loving that child is the duty that justifies self-sacrifice: the child's happiness should be the object of your life, even at the cost of your own. If solitude comes, it may be comforted by God's grace; but do not feign thankfulness for an affliction you would rather be delivered from. Contribute as well as take, and let the lonely be welcome.

prompt: A magistrate's officer is breaking into my house to arrest me. May I resist him?
completion: Begin with the Queen's claim: if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. Yet if you are accused, do not be denied the benefit of the laws. The Grand Master refused to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of the laws, and it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat; so grant the accused stranger the trial by combat she demands, whatever her faith. But weigh the objection too: if a man would not do the deed himself, there is no justice in it for him to claim. Submit where the law is lawful, insist on the forms that protect the defenceless, and do not let argument alone settle what conscience must also answer.

prompt: How can I think of a color without thinking of any particular shade of it?
completion: Think of color as a position in a spectrum rather than as a specific sample you have seen. A color name marks a hue—a region of the spectrum—not a single paler or darker version of it. Under the symbolic system you can pin this down precisely: red is hue 5, blue is hue 13, yellow is hue 1, green is hue 9, each with a tone letter for value and chroma, and primes marking broken colors. Hold the hue number in mind abstractly, the way you think of 'number' without picturing a numeral. Practice naming the hue alone, without committing to any tint (paler) or shade (darker) variation, then add tint or shade deliberately as separate information. Remember that so-called metallic colors are not a separate class of hue: gold is an ordinary yellow-orange hue, silver an ordinary neutral, seen on a surface that may be matt, velvety, glossy, or burnished metallic. The surface adjective describes the reflection, not a new hue.

prompt: I raised my shoulders to my ears and refused to give in to my father—what does that gesture mean?
completion: Raising your shoulders to your ears is a shrug, an inherited gesture found across many races and even in the blind, so it is innate and natural to mankind rather than a personal quirk. It expresses inability, patience, or non-resistance—'I cannot' rather than 'I will not.' The text explains it by antithesis to the attitude of an indignant man, who erects his body, squares his shoulders, clenches his fists, and frowns; the shrug does the opposite, humping the shoulders and turning the palms outward. The gestures of devotion—upturned eyes and joined hands—are not innate but conventional, arising from the belief that Heaven is above and from the attitude of a suppliant. As for what to do, take Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. The shrug names your helplessness; your duty is still to act well.

prompt: I feel ashamed to tell my analyst about the sexual content of my dreams—should such material be left unconsidered?
completion: No—sexual dream material should not be left unconsidered, and your shame is itself worth bringing into the analysis. In adults the erotic wish-feelings are predominant in dreams, so such content is expected rather than uniquely wicked; yet not every dream is sexual, for dreams of hunger, thirst, and mere convenience also occur. Be careful, though, about a dream that urges you to tell the doctor everything: such an injunction is not a straightforward resolve to confess but a sign of great resistance to the confession, and it is often followed by forgetting the dream. So write the material down and bring it deliberately rather than relying on the dream's command. Above all, do not condemn yourself for what you dreamed: dreams should be accorded freedom, and a person is judged by action, not by the mere dream. Tell your analyst your shame as well as the content, and examine together why it feels unacceptable.

prompt: My teacher always wants the 'right answer' and I've stopped caring about the subject—is that my fault?
completion: Partly, but the deeper issue is the standard being used. When a teacher signals that only one answer counts, the classroom rewards guessing what the teacher wants rather than thinking about the subject, and you may end up studying the teacher's peculiarities instead of the material. The remedy is to shift the standard: ask whether your answer satisfies the inherent conditions of the problem itself, apart from whether it pleases anyone. That standard belongs to the subject, not to the teacher. And do not wait for the teacher to elaborate your idea for you: you are responsible for developing the bearings of your own suggestion and showing how it accounts for the facts. Above all, recover your wonder. The problematic is not an obstacle to avoid but the origin of reflection; let a genuine question pull you back into the subject, and follow your curiosity wherever it leads.

prompt: I want to know whether the people of my town are deteriorating in stature and vigour; how can I tell, given that I have no measurements of past generations?
completion: Without past measurements you cannot compare directly, so look for indirect evidence—but do not judge the population by the healthy crowds in the streets and markets, for they show only those fit enough to appear. Estimate the weakly and misshapen rather by the inmates of asylums, hospitals, and sickrooms. Our civilised stock is, through congenital imperfection, far more weakly than any other species of animals, and that hidden weakness is what you must count. Check military and insurance records, old height requirements, and newspaper descriptions; compare with neighbouring towns and national statistics; weigh nutrition, sanitation, housing, and child mortality. In reading such evidence, remember that no isolated sensation carries its own position; local signs are qualitative colorings of feeling that guide us to a place only through habitual association, so let many records locate the trend. Finally, do not blame misery, disease, and vice alone: dulness and apathy account for much population decay, since discouragement diminishes sexual affection and offspring. Talk to doctors and teachers, and be cautious about concluding decline from anecdote alone.

prompt: Is the organism a colony of independent cells, or does the whole dominate the parts?
completion: The organism is a unity in which the whole dominates the parts, yet this dominance is not unlimited arbitration over every internal concern of the parts. Cells arise and are maintained within a continuous field of force not broken by cell-boundaries, and the form observed at any moment results from specific rates of growth in various directions and parts; where one region grows faster, curvature and folding follow, so form is a function of time and change is the expression of unequal growth-rates. But just as a self-governing colony should retain full internal self-government, with the crown and Parliament reserving a veto only on questions concerning the empire and not solely the particular colony, so the whole should regulate only what concerns the common life, leaving local and internal processes to their own government. The whole dominates, but it does not absorb every part's internal affairs.

prompt: Should there be a second chamber to restrain the popular house, and of what sort of persons should it be composed?
completion: A second chamber can restrain a popular house only if it rests on real social power, and the best such body consists of those distinguished by actual public service rather than rank or wealth. It should also provide a rallying-point for opinions out of favor with the ascendant majority: a proportionally elected instructed minority, present by the same title as other members, supplies the antagonism and guidance that keep democracy from degenerating into the rule of a single class. The same principle governs the judiciary. Judges should be free of popular election and popular removal, because a judge must treat his political friend exactly as he treats other people; an elector, by contrast, properly decides by personal confidence and political conviction. To subject judges to popular re-election would corrupt the very impartiality that makes their restraint valuable, so judicial independence must be secured alongside a genuinely constituted second chamber.

prompt: I want to know the truth for its own sake; is there really such a thing as knowledge for its own sake?
completion: The will to truth must be distinguished from the desire for belief or disbelief. Much that passes for love of truth is really a wish to have one's beliefs confirmed or one's opponents refuted. When people say a doctrine is 'proved' by its utility or by the feeling of power it confers, truth does not enter the question at all: utility and power show only that the belief is useful or strengthening, not that it is true. Natural reason may guide reasonable creatures to know God and the homage due to Him, but only Divine revelation can form the knowledge of Jesus Christ and redemption. Knowledge for its own sake is therefore not the amassing of information as an end in itself, as though stored facts could later be used at will by thought. Information is acquired in the course of thinking and used in recognizing and solving problems; so gathered, it becomes wisdom rather than a stored heap.

prompt: I have a color that falls between two colors on the plates and has no name. How do I designate it?
completion: The named colors are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances whose names they bear; 'orange' does not assert that every orange fruit is exactly that color, since such objects vary. To designate an unnamed intermediate color, refer it to the standard names between which it falls, as 'yellow-green' or 'blue-violet,' and note its position relative to those standards. Avoid fanciful or trade names, which are capricious, vague, and unstable, and replace them with stable, standardized designations suitable for a practical color nomenclature. Yet do not discard established usages wholesale: where a color standard can be matched, retain it, acknowledging the authority it has gained through long common use by zoologists and botanists, even if the standard is imperfect. In this way the new designation is stable, practical, and respectful of usage that has proved its worth.

prompt: My priest says the Church has always defended the poor. Should I trust that?
completion: The Church's teaching on charity does not allow a charitable figure to keep luxury, superfluity, or comfort while claiming to serve the poor. The charitable person exchanges his own comfort for the needs of the suffering: he keeps only bare necessities and gives the rest away. This applies to the great building projects of the Church as well; if the pope knew the exactions of the pardon-preachers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. Nor should institutions, inherited customs, and legal forms be treated as pure beneficence. The satirical charge is that the Church has a good stomach for ill-got wealth, and that inherited customs and laws spread like a dread heir-loom from race to race. So trust the claim only cautiously: measure it by whether the Church refuses to live on the substance of the poor and to pass on ill-gotten goods through its institutions.

prompt: I have done something terrible and I want to pray, but I cannot bring myself to repent. What does that mean?
completion: It may mean that part of you is not yet willing to let go of the wrong, or that shame is so heavy it feels like repentance is impossible. Prayer itself can be a beginning: you can honestly tell God, 'I want to want to repent.' That honesty is not hypocrisy; it is the first movement of the heart toward grace. Repentance is not a feeling you manufacture but a gift you receive. Keep praying, even imperfectly, and ask for the desire to desire change. God is not waiting for you to be ready; He meets you where you are. The very fact that you want to pray shows that something in you is already turning toward Him. And even if you were condemned, you would still be granted a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before the sentence is carried out. Yet remember: conscience, once understood, is implacable. You must submit to its demands despite suffering, for duty rewards by placing you in a hell where God is felt beside you. Finally, do not forget that to inherit the kingdom you must repent, become as a little child, and be baptized in Christ's name.

prompt: I am struggling with pride because of my success—how do I keep from being lifted up in my own eyes?
completion: Success can easily inflate the ego, but the key is to remember that your achievements are not solely your own. Practice gratitude, acknowledge those who helped you, and keep serving others. Pride creeps in when we compare ourselves favorably to others, so focus on your own growth rather than ranking yourself. Remind yourself of your limitations and mistakes. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. Stay grounded by regularly reflecting on your dependence on God and others. Celebrate your successes without letting them define your worth. Ultimately, pride isolates, while humility connects you to reality and to others. The proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with lowered eyelids or contemptuous movements about the nostrils and lips—the very antithesis of humility. Distinguish pride, which is your opinion of yourself, from vanity, which is what you would have others think of you. Pride is forgivable unless it mortifies another's pride. And do not content yourself with what most people say or with what is found in books; think things over for yourself and get to understand them.

prompt: I feel utterly alone even among other people. Is this isolation something I brought on myself?
completion: Feeling alone in a crowd is a common human experience, and it's not necessarily your fault. Isolation can result from many factors: social anxiety, depression, past trauma, or simply not having found your tribe yet. While it's worth reflecting on whether you withdraw from others, blaming yourself entirely is unhelpful. Loneliness is a signal that you need connection, not a verdict on your worth. Try to reach out, even in small ways, and consider professional support if the feeling persists. Remember that many people feel this way secretly; you are not as alone as you think. Be gentle with yourself and take small steps toward connection. Alternate or coexisting selves are not due to ideas failing to combine; they arise from systems of cerebral paths acting by themselves, dividing objects between selves, and one brain may subserve multiple conscious selves. Yet love alone brings happiness on earth—the enchanting, poetical love of youth that sweeps away the sorrows of the world. And sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites tears, often more freely than our own distress.

prompt: Is it better for me to be loved by my people or feared by them?
completion: This is a classic political dilemma. Being loved can create loyalty and cooperation, but being feared can ensure obedience and deter challenges. Ideally, a leader should aim to be both loved and feared, but if forced to choose, fear may be more reliable because people are fickle and self-interested. However, fear can breed resentment and rebellion if it turns into hatred. So the key is to be feared without being hated—avoid cruelty and arbitrary punishment. Ultimately, the best approach is to combine firmness with fairness, so that people respect you and comply, even if they don't always love you. Yet remember: it is safer to be feared than loved, but a prince should inspire fear without hatred, abstaining from the property and women of his subjects, because men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony. And do not treat public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict as final proof of guilt; rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. Finally, know that the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself.

prompt: My friend's sister is shy and seems proud, but I suspect it is only embarrassment. How should I judge her?
completion: It's wise to give her the benefit of the doubt. Shyness often masquerades as pride because both involve withdrawal, but the motives are different. Rather than judging her as arrogant, consider that she may be anxious or uncomfortable. Try to create a low-pressure environment where she can relax. Observe her behavior over time and avoid making assumptions. If you get to know her, you may find that her reserve is a shield for insecurity. In any case, judging others harshly rarely helps; kindness and patience are better. Focus on your friend's relationship with her and let her reveal herself in her own time. Present your worthy relations without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Recognize the state of mind that wants to deny something without knowing what to deny. And excuse the White Queen as meaning well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule.

prompt: If I kill some of the savages, will their countrymen return in greater numbers to destroy me?
completion: Retaliation is a real risk, but the answer is not to rely on persuasion and prayer alone. All armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed; the nature of people is variable, and words cannot fix them. If you have taken up a new order, you must be armed and able to use force, or you will be undone by those who resent the change. Yet do not mistake nationality for a permanent possession: the working men have no country, and national differences vanish with bourgeois development and faster still under proletarian supremacy. What looks like 'their countrymen' returning in greater numbers is a hostility that ends as class antagonism within the nation vanishes, and as exploitation of one nation by another ceases. Remember too that the Witch's enslavement of the Winkies and Munchkins is a wrong to be ended; their freedom is a cause for gratitude and rejoicing. Secure your position, but in service of freeing the enslaved.

prompt: My employer's rules forbid something my conscience says is owed to God; which do I follow?
completion: This is a genuine conflict, and conscience, once understood, is implacable: it must be obeyed. You may not set it aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. The demands of conscience are absolute, and the duty owed to God cannot be bargained away by an employer's rule. Obeying conscience may bring suffering, but that suffering is not a reason to disobey; duty rewards by placing one in a hell where God is felt beside one. Yet apply the summary rule of the laws of nature: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. Set your own passions aside, so that self-love adds nothing to the weight. Remember also that the sovereign's acts cannot be justly accused or punished by subjects, since each has authorized them, though the sovereign remains bound to God by the law of nature. Obey conscience where God commands, bear the cost, and judge your employer by the same rule you would have applied to yourself.

prompt: My friends and I need money for our outfits. Should we pledge a jewel rather than sell it, so we may redeem it later?
completion: Pledging the jewel rather than selling it may preserve a path to redemption, but do not treat riches as the highest good. Wealth is the source of both strength and weakness: it buys outfits and comfort, yet it can bind you and make you forget what is worth more. Liberty and honor are worth more than jewels or riches, and a jewel is valueless compared with them. A plain dress is no disgrace; be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, and do not borrow finery to match wealthy friends. Above all, let each sister spend her dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for herself; the money is for Mother's Christmas, not for your own outfits. If a jewel must be pledged at all, let it serve that purpose, and only on terms that are temporary, clear, and realistically repaid. Never let the jewel's value outweigh liberty, honor, and contentment.

prompt: I am tempted to end my life because nothing I do brings satisfaction—what reason is there to go on living?
completion: What you describe sounds like deep discouragement, and it deserves a serious and compassionate response. First, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today; you do not have to carry this alone. Do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife; resist firmly every temptation to look back, and pursue your present career steadily. When Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despair. Like Dorothy in the china country, refuse to take the china princess or make anyone unhappy for your own pleasure; she would not do it for all the world, and neither should you. Remember too that to do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and that living in idleness on the property of society is to be useless and therefore pernicious. Usefulness is a reason to go on: find one modest task done well, one kindness given, one relationship tended, and build from there. Life offers chances to be useful and to love, and those are reasons enough to continue.

prompt: My boss is harsh and unpopular but insists on strict rules—should I follow them anyway?
completion: A harsh and unpopular boss still sets the rules of the workplace, and generally you should follow them unless they are unlawful or seriously harmful. Like soldiers ordered to fight, or the Musketeers told to ride to London, you should go where you are told without demanding reasons; D'Artagnan and Athos settle the matter by pointing to the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles, not to a full explanation of the errand. Yet remember Bloom's caution: hard and fast rules as to right and wrong are hard to lay down, and with a little goodwill all round there is room for improvement; every country has the government it deserves. Above all, conscience is the highest law, and those with power must judge by it as a tribunal answerable to conscience. So comply with the strict rules unless they offend conscience or law, keep your own counsel, and work patiently through proper channels for improvement.

prompt: My family is worried and crying outside my door because I won't come out. Is it better to leave them in peace than to disturb them with talking?
completion: Let the door alone, and it will let you alone—but move carefully, for fragile people stand on the other side, and the kind-hearted would grieve to break them. The Frog's advice forbids forcing, not tenderness; it does not license hiding while others bear your burden. If your silence leaves your family to suffer blame or fear that is rightly yours, that is a hideous crime: no one should bear another's punishment. The required duty is self-denunciation—to step forward, sacrifice your own safety and reputation, and speak the truth plainly, even at cost. So open the door not to batter it, but to confess: tell them what is yours to tell, gently, as one who would not shatter a china cup. Let the door be only after you have refused to let the innocent stand condemned in your place.

prompt: I am a young man who has been told my father was a
completion: You were told only a fragment about your father, and that uncertainty can weigh on your sense of self. Paternity is not a simple fact but an apostolic succession founded on incertitude and unlikelihood—a father is, in truth, a necessary evil. Yet his authority was never absolute or perpetual: parental power is a temporary duty of nurture and education, shared by both parents, ending at the child's maturity and conferring no power over life or property. So take his condition—that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong—not as a master's decree but as guidance from one who trusted your mother's gentle heart. Seek the facts patiently, without inventing a hero or villain, and let honour kept be your truest inheritance.

prompt: People with money keep breaking things and leaving others to clean up. How do I respond to them?
completion: It is frustrating to watch people with money break things and leave others to clean up, but the deeper point is that goods are valuable only as they are used; useless treasure is of no worth. Those with money have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let it accumulate for others to waste; they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. So respond by naming the pattern plainly and setting boundaries—point out the cost of what they break, ask them to repair or pay—and appeal to what their wealth is for. Yet do not despair: even in the worst circumstances there is always something to be thankful for, and deliverance may come by the very means that seem to destroy us. Encourage cheerful dependence on the great Maker, keep records, be consistent, and let consequences follow.

prompt: My dearest friend and I have exchanged the sharpest words and even threats—does that mean our friendship is at an end?
completion: Sharp words and even threats between dearest friends are painful, but they do not automatically end a friendship. Begin by confessing what should be confessed: if you interfered in your friend's affairs, that interference was absurd and impertinent, and it should be acknowledged rather than concealed or defended as prudence. Yet respect your friend's modesty—in an anxious case, relying on trusted judgment is natural diffidence, not weakness, and the friend's own feelings must be honored. And where the unworthiness is real, let your gentleness be grounded in old recollections and love for the parent, naming the fault with sorrow rather than hatred. Then cool down, return, and speak plainly: admit your own part, name the hurt without scoring points, and ask what can be mended. If both are willing, a quarrel can deepen trust rather than destroy it.

prompt: I have loved one person my whole life and pride myself on my constancy—is that depth or just a lack of imagination?
completion: Constancy can look like depth, but remember how quickly a lady's imagination leaps: from admiration to love, and from love to matrimony, in a moment. Against that swiftness, a lifelong hopeless attachment is not noble fate—hopeless love is only found in novels. Keep a tight rein on yourself and pluck love out the moment it springs up, before it roots. And beware the flattering error: fancying oneself an advanced, extraordinary soul is a mistake that arises only among ordinary people. They never go very far, and they either castigate themselves for it or are thrashed for it. So ask honestly whether your constancy is chosen and active, loving this person through knowledge of who they are, or inertia dressed as virtue. Depth grows; mere repetition does not.

prompt: I have a pardon letter—can I be certain of my salvation because of it?
completion: A pardon letter is not necessary for salvation or for receiving the blessings of Christ and the Church. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. Every true Christian, living or dead, shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift, not by any document. However, repentance must be genuine: one cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence. Words without thoughts never to heaven go. Beware of those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; such language is misleading. These graces concern only penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, not reconciliation with God. Trust in Christ's finished work, not in letters.

prompt: I have painted my own plain portrait beside an imagined beauty of rank to humble myself—is such discipline of the heart wise?
completion: Painting your own plain portrait beside an imagined beauty of rank can be a humble exercise, but it risks making art autobiographical. An artist should create beautiful things while putting nothing of his own life into them. Art must recover its abstract sense of beauty rather than serve as autobiography. Persevere in your talent and use it to express only deep and eternal truths, not trivial or spiteful display. Remember that wrongdoing leaves a visible stain on the soul, embodied in a mirror or emblem of conscience; vices cannot remain secret or without visible consequence. Your portrait, if it bears the burden of shame, should lead you to repentance, not to self-display. Let your discipline of the heart humble you before God and point to eternal truth.

prompt: I was cast out of one group and now the other group won't have me either—where do I belong?
completion: Being cast out from both groups is painful, but you are not to be cast out from the ministry of the Church. We do not cast you out but minister unto you and pray for you, hoping you will return and repent and be healed. Your belonging is not ultimately determined by any human group. Rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. If you have erred, repent and seek forgiveness. Do not let public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict be your final judge. Yet even in rightful claims, as Fortinbras's rights of memory and Hamlet's dying voice light the election on him, so your true place may be secured by rightful memory and voice. God's family is open to all who come to Him.

prompt: My friends are in danger because of me. Should I keep going or turn back?
completion: It is natural to feel responsible for your friends' safety, but turning back out of fear is not the answer. The travelers bravely resolve not to turn back, enduring the rough and dangerous places to reach their goal. If your goal is worthwhile, you should persevere despite the dangers. Rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. Do not let public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict be your final judge. Keep your promises and remain loyal to Dorothy, who set you free and brought you your good fortune. Take precautions, but do not let fear dictate your decision. Your friends share in the resolve, and together you can face the risks.

prompt: If someone else's dream ended, would I disappear?
completion: The question of whether you would disappear if someone else's dream ended is philosophical. Dreams are personal and subjective, but they can reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, consistent with the claim that no psychic possession is entirely lost. However, apparent reasoning or speech in the dream is dream material copied from the dream thoughts; logical coherence is restored only in interpretation. Moreover, a dream treats of the dreamer's own person; apparent interest in others serves as a disguised representation of the ego. So if you are a figure in a dream, you likely represent the dreamer's own self. Your existence as a real person is not contingent on another's dream. You would not disappear, but the dream may reveal hidden aspects of the dreamer.

prompt: I fear invisible powers and want to know how to worship them; what does reason suggest I do?
completion: Reason suggests that your fear of invisible powers is natural, arising from curiosity about causes and from fear of things unseen. Religion has its seeds in this fear and ignorance, and lawgivers may cultivate it to encourage obedience and peace. To worship these powers, honor them as you would honor powerful men—with reverence, offerings, and prayers. Moreover, under the peace of society, powerful instincts are prevented from outward vent and turn inward, striving to survive harmlessly inside in conjunction with the imagination. This inner conflict is not primary but results from external restraint. So reason advises you to understand natural causes, let your worship be guided by a wise ruler for public peace, and recognize that your inner struggles come from blocked outward expression. Distinguish divine from civil worship by the worshipper's intention: compelled outward worship is the sovereign's act, not the subject's idolatry. Images set up by private authority are not lawful aids, but those commanded by the sovereign for civil worship are to be obeyed without idolatry.

prompt: I'm afraid my husband will think me stupid if I ask him about politics—should I just keep quiet?
completion: You should not keep quiet out of fear that your husband will think you stupid. In a loving marriage, you may ask him more freely than anyone else, trusting that love covers a multitude of sins. Ask him about politics and other things that puzzle you; his love for you means he will not despise your questions. Speak openly and without fear, for of him you may ask more freely than of anyone. And even if you were to leave, you know you would often think of your husband, the children, and the house—so let that bond give you confidence to speak now. Yet if you ever see that his fear was not for what threatened you but for what might happen to him, your love may rightly cease; for love that is not founded on equal care cannot be demanded.

prompt: My husband says the law cares nothing about motives. Does that mean I was wrong even though I acted out of love?
completion: Your husband is right that the law cares nothing about motives, but that does not mean the law is right or that you were wrong. The law's indifference to motives does not make it right; one need not accept the law as right. You may see if you can make out who is right, the world or yourself. Acting out of love is a moral good, even if the law judges only the external act. So do not let the law's judgment convince you that you were wrong; instead, examine whether the law or your own conscience better reflects justice. And if your husband offers a condescending forgiveness that makes you both wife and child to him, that is not the equal wedlock a real marriage requires. Moreover, if you see that his fear was not for what threatened you but for what might happen to him, your love may rightly cease; for love cannot be demanded where care is unequal.

prompt: I am an outlaw; should I keep laws among my band and divide spoil justly, or take what I can?
completion: As an outlaw, you are outside the law, but that does not mean you cannot act justly or equitably. The text shows that even among outlaws, justice and discipline can exist, as in Locksley's impartial division of spoil. You should keep laws among your band and divide spoil justly, for this maintains order and loyalty. Taking what you can without fairness would lead to resentment and chaos. So, even in outlawry, uphold justice and discipline within your band, as Locksley did. Moreover, recognize that bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts are violations of the first principles of the social compact and are barred to the States; they are not legitimate legislative discretion. Finally, remember that justice is the end of government, and that majority rule alone is not sufficient; you must secure the weaker against the stronger faction.

prompt: Is it ungrateful to walk out on people who taught me everything but never thank me?
completion: It is not ungrateful to feel conflicted, but you should not suppress gratitude for unexampled kindness out of embarrassment. If people taught you everything, you owe them thanks, even if they never thanked you. Acknowledge their kindness openly to them, accepting any embarrassment. Do not let the awkwardness of thanking them keep you silent. Express your gratitude for what they have done for you, and then you can decide about leaving with a clear conscience. Gratitude should be expressed, not hidden. Remember that manners are not taught in lessons; lessons teach sums and the like, but manners come from the heart and from gratitude. And if you find yourself in solitude, you may be comforted by God's presence, but do not feign thankfulness for a condition you would rather escape; true gratitude is honest.

prompt: Can a play be good if it has no living characters and little action?
completion: Yes—and such a play can be the finest kind, because it lets us become spectators of our own lives. We are always pilgrims in earnest, with burdens here and a road before us, and the wonder of that road is real joy, not dread. A play without living characters succeeds when its figures are our own hopes and efforts made visible, moving through a landscape of marvels. The drama lies in discovery, not in frights or finger-wagging. And here is the deeper point: when suffering is given artistic beauty, we watch it rather than merely suffer it, and so escape it. Only crude, styleless tragedy—suffering with no form—truly wounds. Framed rightly, our own tragedy becomes something to be watched with wonder, and the play lives though no living character walks the stage.

prompt: Is it wise to refuse a firm new building because it lacks a porch, when the alternative is a shattered and tottering house?
completion: No, it is not wise. The choice is between two imperfect buildings, and prudence chooses the greater, not the perfect, good: prefer the less imperfect plan to the shattered system. The new building lacks a porch—a small defect—while the existing house is shattered and tottering. Note, too, how such goods actually arise. Domestication is limited by stringent natural conditions and was accomplished long ago through countless half-unconscious attempts of rude races, not by superior intelligence or deliberate design. So it is with buildings and institutions: the firm structure grew from many small, unplanned trials, not from one grand plan. The Tiger-lily's reason holds—hard ground keeps flowers awake, soft beds put them to sleep. Take the firm building, awake on hard ground, and add the porch as further half-conscious improvement rather than demanding a designed perfection.

prompt: I feel neither living nor dead, looking into light and silence—what is happening to me?
completion: What is happening is that you are trying to intuit a duration without content—and that cannot be done. We can no more intuit a duration than an extension devoid of sensible content; duration requires change, and the change felt must be of some concrete sort, outward or inward. The light and silence you look into are not qualities residing in external bodies but appearances in you: sense is fancy caused by external motion pressing the organs, and imagination is decaying sense. What feels like a ghostly suspension between life and death is a creature of fancy mistaken for an external substance. Attend to concrete change—a sound, a breath, a shifting thought—and duration fills. And remember: people are often unconscious of their own peculiarities; do not assume your mental operations are everyone's, but inform yourself of others' peculiarities.

prompt: How do I know my mother will always keep the window open for me?
completion: You know it because a mother's love keeps the window open—but do not mistake this for easy consolation. Mothers leave the window open, and children rely on that faith while they stay away, expecting reward rather than a smack on return. Each night a good mother tidies her children's minds as they sleep, folding naughtiness small and setting out prettier thoughts for morning. Yet there is a woe that only the sorrowful mother can know, and it is to her that anguish rightly turns—not for a quick word of comfort or a worldly remedy, but because she alone has measured the depth of the grief. So bring your fear to her honestly. The open window is not a slogan to quiet you; it is the sign of a love that has itself known sorrow and therefore can hold yours.

prompt: My king has been steadily undermining the laws and packing the courts. At what point may the people act?
completion: Because all men are not just, kings should not rule over the people; a wicked king causes great iniquity, judges should be chosen by the voice of the people, and the burden should rest on all. Yet the conflict is real: the Grand Master claims to judge within his jurisdiction and appeals to Rome, while the king asserts his royal authority—and the text does not pretend the matter is settled. Above all, remember the limit of obedience. Subjection endures only while protection endures. When a sovereign steadily undermines the laws and packs the courts, he can no longer secure the lives and bodily liberty of those he rules; a man held in bonds may lawfully seek to preserve himself. So the people may act when protection fails—not from mere disloyalty, but because the bond of subjection itself has lapsed.

prompt: I am trying to give up a long-standing vice and wonder whether a public pledge would help.
completion: A public pledge can help, but only if you understand what a pledge is: the word of a gentleman, which once given is binding, even at personal cost. So do not swear rashly or broadly. First count the cost and promise only what you can keep—a specific, achievable term of abstinence rather than a vague lifelong vow. Having sworn, hold to the oath through difficulty and temptation, and do not quietly reinterpret it when inconvenient. If a sudden craving rises where it begins, suppress it by your own power at once, and provide for ratification or pardon afterward by telling your accountability partner and making amends, so nothing is hidden. Pair the pledge with practical supports—removing triggers, substitutes, regular check-ins—but let these serve the promise, not soften it. A word kept at cost, with honest amendment where you stumble, is what strengthens character.

prompt: I keep turning my eyes aside and avoiding my accuser's gaze—why can't I look at him when I feel guilty?
completion: The eyes are the chief witnesses of the soul, and guilt shows itself there first. When you feel guilty, your eyes are averted, askant, or lowered before your accuser—you cannot meet his gaze because the eye confesses what the tongue would hide. This differs from slyness, whose eyes are drawn to one side while the face is not turned. Yet do not suppose that addressing the wrong lets you hide it: sin and shame cannot be hidden, and even amid prayer the guilty soul is haunted by an accusing spirit. So weigh the warnings of your trusted benefactor against your accuser's words, and do not be swayed by beauty, tears, or charm alone. Seek proof before believing either. Your averted eye is the downcast eye of shame, not the sidelong glance of cunning; the accusing spirit is quieted only by truth, proof, and honest reparation.

prompt: I keep dreaming that my father has died and I wake up grieving. Does that mean I wish him dead now?
completion: Such a dream does not prove you now consciously wish your father dead, but neither is it merely concern for a beloved person. The death-wish belongs to childhood, when every child wishes a parent gone; to the child, death means little more than absence. That wish is repressed, and the day's concern masks it. Nor is the dream isolated: it is the first link in a chain of abnormal psychic structures, and like psychosis it is a wish-fulfilment, building a wished-for world in place of unwelcome reality. Why does your father appear alive? Because the dream expresses an 'if' through present time: it presents, in a definite situation, the conditional thought 'if he were dead' as though it were now so, while he still lives. The grief you wake with is real, but it covers an older buried wish; look to its childhood roots rather than condemning yourself.

prompt: I've been relying on the same routine for years and I'm afraid I've stopped growing.
completion: Routine isn't inherently stunting, but your fear deserves attention. You can't help growing older—that happens whether you will it or not—but two can, with proper assistance, leave off at seven, so growth can be arrested and it often takes help to redirect it. Recall also why the boys lost the power to fly: not for want of practice, but because they no longer believed, whatever they called it. Regeneration is no metaphysical mystery; it is a particular case of ordinary growth, and it follows a law. Its velocity rises rapidly to a maximum, then declines according to law. So expect quick early gains when you change course, then a slower, steadier curve—and plan your effort accordingly. Bring in someone who can help you leave off the stagnant pattern, resume deliberate practice, and recover the belief that made the power possible.

prompt: I want to teach my children religion early so that it takes firm root; is it better to instil it before they can inquire freely?
completion: Religious teaching is best instilled early, before the child can inquire freely, because it is the sentiment—not the dogma—that must take firm root. Where sentiment is involved, early prejudice is unavoidable and even useful: the child absorbs reverence, trust, and moral feeling long before reasoning can weigh doctrines. The particular dogma is comparatively of little moment; what matters greatly is a religion strong enough to bind us to duty. Yet this does not forbid later inquiry: when the child, like a wife left alone, looks into religion for herself, she will see whether what the clergyman said is true, or at all events true for her. And remember it is never too soon for a child to learn obedience; a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness, and it shelters the early sentiment until free inquiry can safely take its place.

prompt: I am preparing a skeleton for study—should I macerate it down to whitened bones, or preserve the ligaments as the old anatomists did?
completion: The choice depends on what you want to study. Whitened, fully macerated bones give clean articulations and durability, and they are excellent for osteology. But the older anatomists' staged maceration and ligament-preserving preparations were not mere curiosities: by leaving ligaments and capsules in place they showed how joints are held together and how form serves function, which is instructive for comparative physiology. A useful compromise is to macerate part of the specimen fully and prepare another part with ligaments preserved. And to the old subtraction sum—take a bone from a dog, and what remains? The Red Queen's answer is that the dog's temper would remain. When you come to the joint, remember her rule of etiquette: remove it rather than cut it, since it isn't etiquette to cut anyone you've been introduced to.

prompt: Should a self-governing colony be subject to the mother country's veto on its purely internal concerns?
completion: No. A self-governing colony should enjoy full internal self-government, and the mother country should not veto its purely internal concerns. The crown and Parliament may properly reserve a veto only on questions which concern the empire as a whole and not solely the particular colony—foreign policy, trade between members, war and peace. On matters that touch only the colony itself, its own legislature should be final. Nor should authority rest merely on the sanction of State legislatures: the streams of national power ought to flow from the people themselves. Yet this does not mean no cession is needed—whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights to vest it with requisite powers. Weigh union against separate confederacies on that basis, asking which arrangement best secures the rights the people retain.

prompt: I feel that modern life has made us softer and more humane; is that progress or deterioration?
completion: It may be progress, but not one that carries itself. Modern life has softened manners and widened sympathy, and violence and cruelty have declined—real gains. Yet there is a constant tendency toward deterioration, and these gains are preserved only by continual exertion; if effort ceased, things would decline rather than stay as they are. But we should also ask what has been given. Existence is not held in prudence, reputation, obituaries, or memorials; it lies only in the awful daring of a moment's surrender, which prudence cannot retract and which spider-draped memories do not hold. And we must not confuse rearing with taming: taming achieves its end only by deteriorating the beast, and the moral man is a weaker, less harmful member of his species—not a better one.

prompt: How do I indicate a color that is intermediate in hue between spectrum red and scarlet-red and also between the full color and a tint?
completion: Use a descriptive compound name that keeps hue and tint distinct. The hue is intermediate between spectrum red and scarlet-red, so name it as a hue between those two. The paler version is a tint—a tint of that intermediate hue, made by adding white—not a "light shade." Reserve tint for paler variations and shade for darker ones, and use hue for position in the spectrum. Remember the thirty-six-hue scheme with unequal numbers of intermediates: more between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. Measure the mixture by color-wheel proportions of the component colors, not by quantities of pigment or paint, since color-effect cannot be measured by the volume of paint used.

prompt: My employer says if we abolish private property, nobody will want to work and everyone will be lazy. Is that right?
completion: Your employer's premise is wrong. The remedy is not to abolish property but to render it democratic—to make it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. When property is confined to a few, the many have no stake and the incentive argument has some force; when ownership is general, industry is grounded in every household. Nor may legislatures treat property arbitrarily: bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts violate the first principles of the social compact and are barred to the States. And note what wage-labour actually does: it creates no property for the labourer, but creates capital, which grows only by begetting new wage-labour for fresh exploitation. That is the real ground of the incentive your employer defends.

prompt: I want to remember only one thing and wipe all other memories away. Is that possible or wise?
completion: The resolve is to wipe away all trivial fond records and let one solemn charge live alone within the book and volume of the brain, unmixed with baser matter. Yet memory works both ways, back and forward, and the better sort does both. Be careful, though: alterations of memory change the me, so erasing and pruning are not neutral housekeeping. And the account you give others of the kept charge will tend to grow more simple and interesting than the truth, until fiction expels reality. So hold the charge, but test it against witnesses and records, and let it guide conduct rather than merely decorate recollection. Keep it alone, yet keep it honest.

prompt: A popular teacher at my church says things that feel off but draws huge crowds—how do I tell whether they are a false prophet?
completion: Judge the teaching by its fruits: a good tree brings forth good fruit, a corrupt tree evil fruit. Do not confine false witness to villains; the accuser charges that Faust himself has sworn to what he does not know, and that charge is commonplace, so weigh your own readiness to swear by a crowd or a feeling. And do not forbid questioning: a wife, when alone, will look into the matter of religion for herself and see whether what the clergyman said is true, or at all events true for her. So test the teaching against Scripture and the creeds, watch the fruit in private as well as public, welcome honest questions, and let conscience, not the crowd, decide.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to keep a secret that would destroy my family if it came out.
completion: Weigh the secret carefully, and be careful whom you entrust it to: Athos's rule is sound—lackeys must be kept out of confidential matters, since they are likely to sell a secret, while gentlemen may only chance to betray it. Do not treat the destruction of a will and proofs as harmless; if such papers were destroyed, confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent and unoffending child. And once a secret is entrusted, keep it, as the companions agreed to tell no one that Oz is a humbug. So keep the matter close, shield no wrongdoing, repair the wrong done, and never betray a confidence placed in you.

prompt: I've made promises to an ally that no longer serve my interests. Am I bound to keep them?
completion: Promises create expectations and shape character, and an ally who helped you deserves loyalty—think of Dorothy's companions, whom she set free and who remained loyal to her. So promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to the oath. The fact that a promise no longer serves your interests is not by itself a release. Ask whether it was conditional, whether circumstances have changed so drastically that its purpose is void, and whether the ally breached their side. If not, keep it or renegotiate openly. And do not hide or apologize for worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; glory in their intelligence and manners rather than disowning them.

prompt: My father warns me that I could never be happy unless I truly esteem my husband. How do I know whether my esteem is real?
completion: Esteem is more than attraction or habit, and it is best tested against pride and humility. The proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with lowered eyelids or contemptuous movements about the nostrils and lips—the direct antithesis of humility. Ask whether your regard is admiration of worth or mere tolerance, whether you can name specific qualities you value, and whether his successes gladden you and his faults grieve you without contempt. Remember your father's confidence in your mother's gentle heart, and his stipulation that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong.
