Brooding over them breeds fear and saps the present; accept what comes as it comes, and keep your heart and mind busy with present duties and pleasures. But do not mistake this for delay. This life is the day to perform your labors and prepare to meet God; repentance cannot be deferred to the end. And do not let antiquity itself command your reverence: prefer new and well-proved truth over ancient errors, however old and honored the error. Test what you are taught rather than inheriting it unexamined. Work, love, and attend to today, and let today's repentance be real rather than postponed. Keep occupied, and let the present carry you.

prompt: How can a minority be protected from an unjust majority, and does an extended republic make such oppression less likely?
completion: The causes of faction cannot be removed—abolishing liberty is worse than the disease, and forcing all citizens into the same opinions, passions, and interests is neither practicable nor just. Relief must be sought in controlling effects. An extended republic does this better than a small one: more interests and parties make it harder for a majority to form a durable coalition against a minority, so the multiplicity of interests, not a will independent of society, guards the minority. Yet a minority also needs a rallying-point. A proportionally elected instructed minority, present by the same title as other members, supplies the antagonism and guidance that keep democracy from degenerating into the rule of a single class.

prompt: My friend's husband is coming home from the army and she has let herself go—should I tell her plainly?
completion: Speak plainly about love, but not about every sacrifice. If your friend no longer loves her husband, she must say so clearly, even though he has always been kind. Gratitude is not love, and staying out of gratitude would be a slow dishonesty to them both. Yet a saving act she performs for him may remain her secret: his manly independence would be wounded by knowing he owed her anything, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. But reject the pagan idea of dying with a husband. She has her own right to live out her time and must not be hurried away; no lover's claim on her life is legitimate.

prompt: I'm the mother of a group of wild boys and I don't know if I'm doing it right.
completion: Before assuming the worst, consider that the alarming sound may only be the Red King snoring, not a wild beast. Wildness follows from the conditions of domestication: hardiness, fondness of man, desire of comfort, usefulness, free breeding, and ease of tending. A species fails if it lacks even one small particular, so build fondness and trust, offer comfort and usefulness, and make routines easy to tend. But do not indulge caprices or say the boys are too young to learn obedience: it is never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness.

prompt: My mother and father disagree about my upbringing. Does my father alone have authority?
completion: It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness. Authority in a family is usually shared, and both parents hold rights and responsibilities; disagreements are best settled by calm discussion, and the child's part is not to play one parent against the other. Yet distinguish the lifelong duty of honour from a right of command: grown children owe parents perpetual honour and support, not absolute obedience. A cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines the parties. Grown children are as free as their parents.

prompt: Why can I drop the middle term in a chain of 'is's and still be sure the relation holds?
completion: You can drop the middle term because mediate subsumption flows from the very meaning of a series of is's: if A is under B and B is under C, then A is under C by the meaning of the terms, independent of the order of experience. The middle term merely links the two and adds nothing. Discrepant cases are corrected by the principle, and color identifications rest on fixed standards with the personal equation removed. In dreams, apparent reasoning or speech is only dream material copied from the dream thoughts; the dream does not think, and logical coherence is restored only in interpretation.

prompt: I caught myself sneering and uncovering one canine tooth at someone I despise—why do I do that when I have no intention of biting him?
completion: What you're catching is an inherited relic. The sneer and the uncovering of the canine are vestiges from semi-human progenitors who bared their canine teeth when prepared for battle—a defiance of the teeth. No one now uses the canine teeth more than the other teeth in actual biting, so the gesture serves no present practical purpose; it survives as a trace of man's animal descent. The retracted ears of a savage animal follow the same logic: the habit is associated with fighting with the teeth and protects the ears from being seized. And when we turn to the cloister, we must speak with gravity and pity—blaming the institution while honoring the devoted and trusting souls within it, permitting wrath but never malice.

prompt: I hear fragments of songs in my head against my will and can't see what they mean to me—is this like a dream?
completion: Yes, it is like a dream. Involuntary song fragments, like dreams, are senseful psychic structures capable of interpretation and assignable to a place in waking psychic activity. Rather than dismissing them as noise, treat them as material to interpret—ask what they express and where they fit among your waking thoughts. The dream may also reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, for no psychic possession is entirely lost; the fragments may carry something you cannot reach while awake. And this leaves open the closing question: life, what is it but a dream?

prompt: I've been told to 'just be more observant' but I don't know what I'm supposed to be looking for.
completion: Being observant is not about capturing everything; wisdom lies in knowing what to overlook. Selection and rejection are essential to mental progress, and suppressing secondary detail leaves the field clear for higher flights. Nor should caution rule you: fortune is the arbiter of half our actions, but men may build barriers against her, and the adventurous fare better than the cautious. So notice what matters, discard the trivial, and prepare defenses while acting boldly. Do this with openmindedness joined to order—holding your conclusions loosely enough to admit new evidence, yet thinking in consecutive, orderly steps rather than jumping about. Observation then becomes a habit of reflection, not a frantic inventory.

prompt: I am a parent whose child has been taught to fear something harmless; will the terror take root as though it were a natural instinct?
completion: It can take root, yes. When fear is aroused you may see widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling; as terror increases, utter prostration with relaxed muscles may follow. These symptoms tend to reappear through inheritance and association from generations of flight and struggle, and in part are directly due to disturbed transmission of nerve-force from the cerebro-spinal system. A fear taught in childhood can settle in through suggestion, but learned fears can be unlearned through gradual exposure and calm reassurance. Yet act promptly: instincts are transitory, so strike the iron while hot, seize the wave of the pupil's interest before its ebb, and secure a headway of habit on which the child may afterward float.

prompt: I'm trying to explain why some leaves are lanceolate and others cordate—is there a simple principle?
completion: There isn't a single simple principle, but consider the Tiger-lily's reason: hard ground keeps flowers awake, while soft beds make them sleep. Leaf shape can be read in that spirit—lanceolate and cordate forms reflect the conditions in which the plant finds itself. As for the numerical series and the sectio aurea sometimes invoked in leaf arrangement, treat these as arithmetical coincidences: closer approximations are rarer, looser ones like 3/5 or 2/3 common, and such speculations hark back to mystical idealism. At the cellular level, localised accumulations of potassium correlate with regions of weakened surface tension—as in conjugating cells and sprouting spores—and such regional differences may underlie the shaping of the leaf.

prompt: I want to introduce the best institutions into my country at once; should I, even though the people are not yet prepared for them?
completion: Free institutions cannot be transplanted onto any people at will: representative government requires a united public opinion, which cannot exist among a people without fellow-feeling, so the boundaries of government should in the main coincide with those of nationalities. Yet this is no warrant for imposing one model everywhere; different peoples may each be good after their kind, and the multifarious variety of gifts is a nation's wealth. Nor can any government be instituted without cost: whenever and however it is established, the people must cede some of their natural rights to vest it with requisite powers. Weigh, then, union against separate confederacies by asking which arrangement cedes least while securing safety, and introduce only what your people's genius can bear.

prompt: I have committed an act I cannot stop regretting. Should I keep torturing myself with remorse, or is there another way to be done with it?
completion: Remorse is not meaningless: it is the honest recognition of wrong, and it should lead to repentance and humility before a wiser judgment tempered with mercy, not to stiff-necked defiance. But do not dwell in the past or yield to the backward-looking fears that turn us into Lot's wife. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present career steadily, and hew out a new road when Fortune blocks the old one. Above all, be careful in dealing with those around you: show timely care, zeal, and earnestness toward those you love, for neglected opportunities bring an unavailing remorse that no later grief can undo. Acknowledge the wrong, amend what you can, and then walk forward, attending to the living.

prompt: I want to describe a dull brownish color found on many animals. Is there a category for colors dulled by gray?
completion: Yes. Such colors are properly called broken colors, distinct from the pure colors of the spectrum. A pure color is unmixed; a broken color is dulled by neutral gray, or by black and white together, retaining its hue while losing purity. Under the symbolic system each color is designated precisely by its hue number and tone letter, with primes affixed to mark a broken color, so the dull brownish tone on many animals is named exactly rather than left vague. Note further that broken dark colors are far more numerous in Nature than pure darkened ones, so representing them accurately serves a practical utility, not a mere refinement.

prompt: I lost my job in a crisis and the factory shut down even though there was plenty of stock. How can there be too much production?
completion: What you are seeing is not too many goods for any human need, but a mismatch between production and purchasing power, rooted in luxury, wealth, and license that have corrupted the Order. The reformation must be sharp and sudden: cast these away and reform manners at once. Nor may business pause for convenience; as the chief clerk holds, those in commerce must overcome slight illness for business considerations, for there is no time of year to do no business at all. And do not despair over the want of tools or skill: wants are supplied through labor, patience, and rational contrivance, and what is lacking in equipment can be made up by industry and reason.

prompt: I am a friend and I have seen my lord behave strangely. Should I follow him when he goes off alone with a ghost?
completion: As a friend your loyalty is understandable, but following your lord alone to meet a ghost is perilous. Watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan, lest you too be led captive. Show friendship to the living now, as Wolfshiem advises, speaking with your lord and alerting trusted others while there is time. If the spirit commands revenge for a father's murder, treat that as a bound duty to be pursued, yet keep your mind untainted and do not extend vengeance to the mother: leave her to heaven and to the thorns that prick her bosom. Follow, then, with watchfulness, duty, and a clean heart.

prompt: I am a parent and fear my children will be lost because of my example. What should I do?
completion: Do not console yourself that a single slip is harmless. A parent must actively check exuberant spirits in the young and teach plainly that present pursuits are not the business of life; otherwise unchecked volatility fixes a character and brings disgrace on the family. Set clear limits, correct temper and self-will early, and show by your own conduct that amusement is not the whole of living. Trust the gentle heart of a good mother, as a wise father does, and attach a clear condition to what you pass on: a son should inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Above all, remember the duty laid on parents: to feed and clothe their children, and to teach them truth, soberness, love, and service rather than contention, keeping God's laws. Let that standard be spoken aloud, so inheritance means character, not indulgence.

prompt: My friend says a man should love himself first and that this benefits everyone; is he right that self-interest keeps my coat whole?
completion: Your friend's case deserves to be stated plainly. Luzhin argues that self-interest is the spring of general advance: a man who loves himself first keeps his own coat whole, and by so doing helps all, since each person's prosperity contributes to the whole. Divide your coat with a neighbour, he says, and you leave both half naked—neither able to help the other. On this view, enlightened self-interest is the sound foundation of the common welfare. But consider Dorothy, who would not carry off the china princess, since she would not make her unhappy for all the world. And consider the husband who arranges everything by his own taste and imposes it on his wife: he wrongs her, for she is made to adopt or pretend to adopt his tastes rather than her own. That is self-interest unenlightened. Hear your friend fairly, then weigh his case against such refusals and such wrongs.

prompt: I want to be remembered as a great prince. What kinds of actions earn renown?
completion: If you want renown, do not settle for small cautious gestures. Nothing makes a prince so esteemed as great enterprises and remarkable examples. Undertake bold, well-chosen ventures—reform a corrupt institution, build something enduring, defend the weak at real cost—and let your conduct be unusual enough to be spoken of. But great deeds alone are not enough. In a civil principality, a prince must establish himself, command, and remain undismayed in adversity; then he will find the people faithful, while a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. And above all, abstain from the property and the women of your subjects: when neither is touched, the majority of men live content. Renown won by great enterprises is undone by such seizures. Combine remarkable deeds, firm command, and scrupulous restraint.

prompt: My friend is easily led by others; should I warn him against a match I think imprudent?
completion: Yes, speak up—but with respect. A modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment is natural diffidence, not weakness, especially in an anxious case like marriage. So do not scold him for being led; acknowledge his own feelings and ask what he truly wants, apart from the pressure of others. Then share your concern privately. Heed secret apprehensions too: hints and notices of danger are discoveries of an invisible world, given for our good, so keep on guard rather than dismissing them as superstition. But be careful in judgment: if no fault was found beyond pride, or a single awkward meeting, do not condemn a person's whole character on that alone. Respect the counsel he trusts, offer yours as one more voice, and help him weigh diffidence, warning, and his own heart.

prompt: I found money in the wreck that is useless to me here; should I take it or leave it?
completion: Take it only if you can do so honestly and safely—but do not let the money become the point. Marmee's hope is that her daughters be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. If the wreck is abandoned and no owner can be found, claiming it may be lawful, but check the rules and be ready to return it. Remember that rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste; use it wisely while you live to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. And practice economy: do not exceed your income, for imprudence in money matters is unpardonable. Let honesty, safety, and economy decide, and let love and peace, not splendor, order your plans.

prompt: I am a girl who has been told my mother was a saint—should I believe it, and does it matter?
completion: Be cautious about 'saint' if it means sinless, since no one is perfect. But uprightness, not perfection, is the standard. If your mother was honest, kind, and faithful, honor her and imitate her virtues. If she fell, the fallen remain upright when they turn the fall toward prayer and amendment. Do not counsel silence for safety's sake: honor is to be preferred above life, as Rebecca and Ivanhoe both insist. And when a knight and churchman gives true response on his word in a wager of beauty, trust that testimony—the Templar's honest admission shows such a man may be believed. Ask whether she lived uprightly, and let her example guide you.

prompt: My enemy says that whoever touches her is himself an assassin. Is she right?
completion: Your enemy's threat is a trap, not a moral truth. If she has done wrong, the answer is not stealthy violence but lawful judgment: accusers, witnesses, and a pronounced sentence—Athos insists she be tried, not assassinated. Do not rely on foreign arms or leave your own disarmed; a new prince should arm his subjects, since arms make them yours and distrust breeds hatred. Judge any proposed plan by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. Gather honest testimony, arm and trust your own, and act through proper authority, so punishment is a formal judgment rather than a private killing.

prompt: I am pregnant and unmarried, and my brother has cursed me—is there any hope for me on earth?
completion: Yes, there is hope, but not by pretending nothing is broken. The time is out of joint, and you are born to help set it right—bearing your share of the disorder rather than ignoring it. Your brother's curse is words, not God's sentence; yet do not dismiss strange speech as meaningless, for though this be madness, yet there is method in it, and madness often hits on pregnant replies that sanity could not deliver. Remember a father's confidence in a mother's gentle heart, and the condition for a son's inheritance: he inherits only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Care for your health, plan for the child, and raise him to that standard.

prompt: I'm tempted to take credit for something risky I did alone—how honest should I be about it?
completion: Be honest, even when it costs you. A silence that lies is a form of theft, so do not keep a comfortable quiet that spares you at honesty's expense. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what you did, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for happiness. Be fair in judging others: Oliver was innocent, wrongly taken for a thief because he ran and was found among thieves—flight is not proof of guilt. And do not dress up deceit as cleverness: Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram was a burning shame and scandalous disgrace, and we may well ask whether Miss Ingram will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Correct the record where credit misleads.

prompt: My father has taken to wearing his uniform at home and falls asleep at the table. Should I try to take over the family's affairs again as I used to?
completion: Your father is struggling, and you want to help, but do not seize control or run off to escape. Do your best at your studies, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Support him quietly: help where he asks, watch for real difficulty, and be patient. Be just in explaining family troubles: a husband should not attribute his wife's act to her father's want of principle, nor treat it as punishment for having winked at the father's conduct. And when wrong demands opposition, name it plainly: the murdered king, the whored mother, the intercepted election, and the angled-for life are grounds for quitting him with this arm. Respect your father's authority while being a steady, kind presence.

prompt: My brother betrayed me and I was driven from my home; why does this story keep repeating in my family?
completion: Your family story repeats because betrayal and exile create a powerful narrative that shapes identity. When a brother betrays and drives you from home, it becomes a template for understanding later conflicts. Families often replay such traumas because the emotional intensity demands resolution but remains unspoken. The repetition may also serve to maintain loyalty to the original victim or to warn against trust. Yet consider the shame that accompanies such exile: the burden of knowing your family must now earn money because of you, and the regret of being unable to speak to your sister and thank her for her care. That shame and regret can intensify the story's grip. However, the reserve appropriate to a young sister with her brother differs from the greater liberty a wife may take with her husband. And do not minimize the crime: murder by a close kin is most foul, strange, and unnatural—a brother's hand taking life, crown, and queen at once while the victim slept unshriven. Recognizing these relational nuances and the full horror of betrayal helps break the cycle: name the pattern openly, acknowledge unspoken gratitude and guilt, and allow each relationship its proper freedom.

prompt: I'm drawn to someone new but I'm not free of an old entanglement. What do I owe the old one?
completion: You owe your old entanglement honesty and closure. Before pursuing someone new, you must be clear with your current partner about your feelings and intentions. If you have made commitments, you owe it to them to either honor those commitments or end them respectfully. The new attraction does not erase the old obligations. Consider what you promised—time, loyalty, support—and whether you can still fulfill those promises. If not, you owe a conversation that acknowledges the change and allows both parties to move forward. Avoid deception or gradual drift; instead, take responsibility for the transition. And remember the giver: the favor or gift you received in the old entanglement should not be forgotten. Even as you freely use what was given, acknowledge and remember the one who gave it. Moreover, a borrower must return what he borrows according to his agreement, lest he sin and lead his neighbor to sin. So take care to repay what you owe, whether in loyalty, time, or support, as you are able. But do not be deceived: the old morality contains no idea still worthy of respect. Any assertion that noble feelings validate your course is refuted by showing it dependent upon that morality and inspired by noble feelings. Ultimately, you owe the old one the truth and the chance to be free as well.

prompt: I am a poor boy taken in by kind people, and I long to do something to show my gratitude—what can I do that would prove their kindness was not cast away?
completion: You can show gratitude by living in a way that honors their kindness. Work hard, be honest, and strive to improve yourself. Help others when you can, and remember to thank them sincerely. Small acts of service—like helping with chores or offering to assist—can demonstrate your appreciation. Most importantly, let them see that their kindness has made a positive difference in your life. Pursue education or a trade so you can become self-sufficient and perhaps one day help others as they helped you. Your gratitude is best proven by becoming a person of good character who reflects the care you received. Keep communication open and express your thanks regularly, not just in words but in actions that show you value their generosity. And never forget to be grateful for the kindness received; if ever you lose those who helped you, mourn them deeply, as the Woodman mourns Oz who gave him his heart. Yet do not feel compelled to express your gratitude immediately and in person regardless of circumstance. Acknowledge the debt fully, but permit yourself to defer its expression when feeling or circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise, as Rebecca insisted her debt be acknowledged but not at that moment. Finally, do not suppress gratitude for unexampled kindness out of embarrassment. Openly thank your benefactor for their unexampled kindness to your family, accepting the embarrassment of doing so.

prompt: I feel I am many different people depending on the company—is that insincerity a fault or a way of multiplying myself?
completion: Feeling like many different people depending on the company is not necessarily insincerity; it can be a sign of adaptability and social intelligence. Humans naturally adjust their behavior to fit different contexts, and this flexibility helps us connect with others. However, if you feel fragmented or lose sight of your core values, it may indicate a lack of integration. The key is to maintain a consistent set of values while allowing your personality to express different facets in different settings. Rather than seeing it as a fault, consider it a way of multiplying yourself—expanding your repertoire of responses. But ensure that these variations are authentic expressions of your whole self, not masks that hide your true feelings. Reflect on whether you are being true to your values in each context. Yet recognize that the notion of a simple, unified conscious agent is misleading: much mental operation is unconscious and simultaneous, and consciousness is only a limited ken. Individuality itself is a misleading term for the complex, dynamic process you are. Moreover, do not judge your own mind by the teacher's mental habits; study your individual traits and habits on their own terms rather than measuring them by another's standard, which only encourages one-sidedness and fails to understand what is incongruous with that standard. Finally, do not flatter or indulge laziness and self-absorption. Offer honest, grave reproof: with every chance for being good, useful, and happy, to be faulty, lazy, and miserable is selfish, and that selfishness must be named plainly.

prompt: Can papal pardons remove even the smallest venial sin's guilt?
completion: Papal pardons, or indulgences, cannot remove even the least venial sin as to its guilt. According to Catholic teaching, indulgences only remit the temporal punishment due to sins that have already been forgiven; they do not forgive sin itself. The guilt of sin is removed through the sacrament of reconciliation and absolution by a priest. Therefore, even the smallest venial sin's guilt cannot be removed by a papal pardon; it requires an act of contrition and the sacrament. The Church teaches that indulgences are a way to reduce purgatorial suffering, not to forgive sin. So the answer is no: papal pardons cannot remove even the smallest venial sin's guilt. Moreover, to think they could absolve an impossible sin or the violation of the Mother of God is madness. And do not trust in pardon letters as assurance of salvation: those who believe themselves sure of salvation because of pardon letters will be condemned with their teachers, for assurance by letters of pardon is vain even if the pope staked his soul on it. Finally, one cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence; words without thoughts never to heaven go, so prayer or verbal repentance is insufficient if the offender clings to the fruits of the offence.

prompt: My pupil is the illegitimate child of a dancer and disowned by her guardian—should I think less of my post or cling closer to her?
completion: Your post is not diminished by your pupil's origins, and you should not think less of her because of her parents' faults. She is blameless for the circumstances of her birth and for the guardian who disowned her; to withdraw from her would be to punish her for another's conduct. Cling closer to her precisely because she has been forsaken. At the same time, do not let sympathy become indulgence: a child's character is fixed early, so check her exuberant spirits and teach her that present pursuits are not the business of life. Yet do not leave her in cloistered darkness—gently enlighten her soul with a half-light of realities, since seclusion prepares her for passions rather than guarding her. Hold her blameless, correct her steadily, and let her character, not her parentage, determine what you think of her.

prompt: I want to help someone who saved my life—how do I repay a debt like that?
completion: A life saved cannot be settled like a bill, and you should be wary of turning gratitude into a debt that enslaves you. Contracting debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to dignity; a creditor comes to possess something of you. No debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life—keep to the straight road even while struggle remains, and go without rather than borrow. Yet none of this excuses ingratitude. Be sincerely grateful for the kindness you received, honor your rescuer with steady loyalty, and mourn the loss of one who gave you so much, as the Woodman mourns Oz who gave him his heart. Give freely what you can, refuse arrangements that put your dignity in another's hands, and let your home remain free, unencumbered, and full of thanks.

prompt: I promised to keep a secret about someone's deception. Should I keep it?
completion: A silence that lets a lie stand is a form of theft, and you should not purchase your comfort with it. The honest course is to tell the whole truth about who you are and what you know, even if it brings humiliation and loss; do not keep a comfortable secret merely to preserve happiness built on falsehood. Weigh also the cost of silence about a person's real character: withholding such knowledge from your own family may prove a wretched mistake, and you may long regret failing to warn them. Yet be careful how you promise. Swear only to what can rightly be kept, and having sworn, hold to your oath. Promise no concealment that would make you a party to deceit; then keep faith with what you have truly undertaken, and let candor and constancy stand together.

prompt: I want to be happy whenever I like, but I can't remember how. Any tips?
completion: Happiness is easier to find when you stop chasing it directly, but do not pretend the rule is simple. Like the Queen, you may find that you can never quite remember how to be glad whenever you like, however often you are told. So do not merely wait for a better mood or try to think your way there. Begin with the outward movements of the contrary disposition: smooth your brow, brighten your eye, and act cheerful in cold blood, even when you do not feel it, until real cheerfulness and kindliness arrive. Practice this steadily, and keep a short list of what has helped before for when you forget. Yet never despise or feel ashamed of domestic endearments and household joys; they are among the best things the world has. Value useful activity too, but let the warmth of home be a source of gladness rather than something to look down on.

prompt: Is it idolatry to bow before an image when my king commands it on pain of death?
completion: This is a serious question of conscience, but the distinction that matters is between divine and civil worship, which is determined by the worshipper's intention. Bowing at a king's command, under pain of death, is a civil act of obedience, not divine worship; if your intention is to obey the sovereign and not to honor the image as divine, the compelled worship is the sovereign's act, not your idolatry. Images set up by private authority are not lawful aids, but a command of the sovereign is another matter. Keep your inward intention fixed on what is due to God alone. As for the king, it is praiseworthy that he refuses to prey on a prostrate enemy, yet over-indulgence can invite treason and neglect the kingdom's welfare. And as a captain forbids his men to expose their lives needlessly because brave men are precious to the king, do not spend your life rashly; courage must serve a true necessity, not be thrown away.

prompt: People gossip that Mother has 'plans' for us to marry rich—should I repeat it or forget it?
completion: That gossip is foolishness, and Marmee's instruction is plain: never repeat it, and forget it as soon as you can. Repeating talk about Mother having 'plans' gives idle chatter a life it does not deserve. Marrying for money or position is no salvation; something more than money and position is needed to satisfy the heart, and a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching. So follow the Red Queen's rule: say nothing you do not mean, think before you speak, and write down afterwards what you have said. When the gossip comes, hold your tongue, weigh it, and let it pass unrecorded and unspoken. The best answer is simply to forget it.

prompt: My husband says I am out of my mind for wanting to leave. Am I?
completion: You are not out of your mind for having feelings you cannot ignore. Wanting to leave is not madness. But know this: a wife who leaves does not stop thinking of her husband, the children, and the house; she carries them with her and will often think of them still. Remember too that although a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. And the wonderful thing you hoped for was not merely that he would work night and day and bear want for you, but that he would come forward, take everything upon himself, and say he was the guilty one. Weigh the decision carefully and choose what you can stand behind.

prompt: My son disobeyed me and left home against my command; should I still call him my son?
completion: Disobedience is painful, but consider God's own dealings: he calls all to repent and not harden their hearts, and promises mercy through his Son to those who do so. So do not cut your son off in anger, yet do not treat mercy as automatic. A father should not be cut off from his child over politics; a man is not a monster for having been at Waterloo, and a father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves the son's veneration. In duty and obedience, let the daughter show the suitor's letters and report his solicitations to her father's ear. Claim your son while inviting his repentance, and let your love reflect the mercy you hope for.

prompt: Should I take a job teaching what I was taught, even if my teacher forbids it?
completion: Teaching what you were taught can be a natural way to pass on knowledge and earn a living, and a teacher's prohibition may reflect protectiveness rather than a real claim on you. Education should above all strengthen the habit of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, which is the root of judgment, character, and will. Remember that in laying things open for another's instruction, the teacher is himself informed and instructed, and may become a better scholar thereby. So do not decide on hearsay, assertion, or guess: cultivate the habit of discriminating tested beliefs from mere opinions, and employ methods of inquiry appropriate to the problem. Talk honestly with your teacher, honor genuine concerns, and be clear about your goals.

prompt: My brother is ill and lonely in the country; should I stay with him or go to town where I can live as I like?
completion: It's understandable to want freedom and company in town, but your brother is ill and lonely, and that is a real claim on you. Be neighborly as Jo resolved to be, sharing the family's cheer with the lonely boy next door: reach out, make him welcome, and bring warmth into a quiet house. Bear affliction patiently; do not revile those who cast out the poor, but hope for rest from afflictions. And remember that a prince who takes a city accustomed to freedom must either ruin it or reside there, for its people never forget liberty or their ancient privileges. So do not think benefits or time alone will hold what needs your presence; stay for a season, arrange help, and plan town time around his needs.

prompt: I fear that a foreigner could sue my state in federal court and force it to pay its debts; does the Constitution allow that?
completion: The Eleventh Amendment generally bars a foreigner from suing your state in federal court to collect its debts, but the deeper point is that a state should not be contracting such debts at all. The text holds that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to dignity: a creditor possesses the debtor's dignity, so one should rather go without than borrow. Your fear is well placed, but the remedy is not merely procedural immunity; it is to avoid debts that put the state under a creditor's power. Nor should either the federal government or a state decide for itself the limits of its own authority; such disputes belong to an independent Supreme Court, whose judgment in the last appeal is final and binding on every government and functionary. Yet state courts are not excluded: they retain their pre-existing jurisdiction unless it is exclusively delegated, and the state and national systems are to be regarded as one whole, with state courts as natural auxiliaries to federal law.

prompt: She took pills to bring it off and has had five children already—how should I speak to her?
completion: Speak to her with compassion and without judgment, but do not assume her mind is clouded. The text holds that a wife may feel her mind never so clear and certain as when she resolves to forsake her husband and children; such resolve is not delirium or illness. With five children already, her decision to take pills to bring it off may be a settled act of a clear mind, not a symptom to be pathologized. Ask gently how she is doing and listen without condemning, but do not treat her as confused or mad. Insist that one should mean what one says: the Queen complains that one should have meant something, and a child without meaning is of no use. Yet be alert to the White Queen's diagnosis: a state of mind that wants to deny something without knowing what to deny. Her denials may not be well-founded; hear them as a mind seeking what it cannot name. Offer practical support and medical care without moralizing.

prompt: Should I wake the children when I sense danger, or let them finish their rest as my rule says?
completion: Safety should come first, but the deeper principle is a mother's love. The text holds that a mother's love keeps the window open, and that children, confident in that love, stay away and expect to be rewarded rather than smacked on return. So your rule should reflect that open window: the children rest in the faith that you are watching over them. If you sense danger, act to keep them safe, but do not let fear turn the home into a place of punishment or distrust. Nor is the nursery solely the mother's sphere: the father's place is there as well, and the children need him, so let him be let in and taught to help. And where a wrong has been done to a child, the wrongdoer must carry out the provisions of the will for that child; afterward he may go where he pleases, needing to meet the wronged no more in this world.

prompt: I am twenty-five and my father still demands absolute obedience. Must I give it?
completion: At twenty-five you are an adult, and absolute obedience to a parent is not owed in the way it is to a young child, yet do not treat obedience as a caprice to be indulged or outgrown. The text holds that it is never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness. So hear your father's demand as a call to discipline, but also as one that should be tempered with mercy. Do not sail away and defy him, as Laurie was tempted; rather, do your duty. Meg's advice is sound: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. And do not treat petition as futile: ask, seek, and knock in faith, trusting that the Father in heaven gives good things to them that ask him.

prompt: If my parents acquired a skill through long practice, will my children be born with it?
completion: No, acquired skills are not inherited in the sense that a child is born able to perform them, but the mechanism of practice is worth stating rightly. The text explains that repeated performance deepens paths from sensory to motor centres, so that the idea of the movement's effects becomes an immediate antecedent of the movement. With practice, the end alone suffices, and the resident muscular feelings lapse from consciousness; a willed movement is not guided primarily by conscious attention to those feelings. Children may inherit general traits that make certain skills easier to learn, and they benefit from environment, encouragement, and example, but they must still practice. Nor should we judge candidates by present personal merit alone: ancestral family history forecasts future performance, so marks for family merit, based on verifiable ancestral occupations and longevity, should supplement competitive examinations. Finally, do not leave useful actions to continual deliberate effort: make them automatic and habitual early, guard against disadvantageous habits, and so set the higher mental powers free.

prompt: Why do I sigh and feel a lump in my throat when I am grieving?
completion: Grief is a whole-body response, not just an emotion. Breathing becomes irregular, you may sigh deeply as the body tries to reset itself, and the throat muscles tighten, giving the 'lump' sensation. The downcast corners of the mouth are not a deliberate expression: they are produced by the depressores anguli oris, muscles little obedient to the will, which retain through habit the action first used in infant screaming, and precisely because they are least under voluntary control they betray dejection so reliably. The open mouth of astonishment is not explained by improved hearing; rather several causes concur—quiet breathing through the mouth, relaxation of the jaw under absorbed attention, and the deep inspiration taken on being startled. If you are being cared for, you are lucky to have a Nana who is a treasure of a nurse, thorough and knowing, believing in old-fashioned remedies and contemptuous of new-fangled talk about germs.

prompt: I dreamed of a notice about hospital costs from a year before I was born. Why does my dream play with impossible dates?
completion: Dreams often scramble time, but that does not make the dream trivial. What looks like a harmless impression—a notice about hospital costs from a year before you were born—may have taken over the psychic accent by displacement, so that indifferent material carries the emotional weight of something else. The impossible date is a signal that the manifest content has been rearranged. Crucially, the dream's imagery and its motivating wish should be traced to infantile reminiscences or phantasies, including forgotten ones, revived through transference onto recent material; hypermnesic dream material shows that early scenes can reappear in disguised form. So the notice is not merely adult daytime residue: it likely draws on an infantile source revived through transference to a recent impression, and the odd date is the clue to that origin.

prompt: I'm trying to figure out how to make my studying more than just memorizing for tests.
completion: To move beyond memorization, make recitation an occasion for your own reflection rather than mere rehearsal of secondhand information and correct replies; reproduction of memorized matter should be only an incident in that process. But do not settle for the gross fact that 'practice helps,' which rests on past coincidence. Analyze it into minuter processes: what exactly do you do when a concept sticks? Deliberately vary conditions—self-testing or not, spaced or massed, alone or explaining aloud—and find which special conditions are present when the effect occurs and absent when it fails. And begin at once: like Meg, keep your book on the table and read a little every morning, letting that small daily reading help you through the day. That habit turns studying into inquiry rather than performance.

prompt: I am a candidate for permanent employment and my examiners know only my present qualifications—should my family history of longevity and thriving occupations count in their judgment of my future?
completion: Examiners should not judge you on present qualifications alone. Ancestral family history forecasts future performance, so marks for family merit—based on verifiable ancestral occupations and longevity—should supplement competitive examinations. Family longevity and health are verifiable signs of stamina, and stamina is exactly what forecasts a candidate's future performance; treating them as irrelevant contradicts the evidence. More broadly, family and medical life-histories must be collected, especially by medical men, to supply materials for the study of heredity. Your present skills show what you can do now, but a documented record of long-lived relatives and thriving occupations is evidence about tendency that an examination cannot capture. Such marks should rest on verifiable facts and be added to, not substituted for, the competitive test.

prompt: I'm examining the shoulder-blade of different human races and finding great variation—is that surprising?
completion: Some variation is expected, but finding great variation in the shoulder-blade across human races should not surprise you. The range of variation in the human scapula within a race is very considerable, so many bones are needed for an accurate mean; with only a few specimens you cannot draw conclusions about racial means. Collect a large number of bones before comparing averages. The same caution applies to peoples: the absorption of a smaller and more advanced nationality by a stronger and less advanced one is a sheer mischief to the human race, which civilized humanity should unite to prevent. And note that a given expression is not a merely local or conventional custom of one people: it is shared by distinct races of man, and that uniformity indicates the close similarity in bodily structure and mental disposition of all races.

prompt: I am a small employer whose interests and habits are those of my workmen; with which side should I cast my lot in politics?
completion: Because your habits and interests are those of your workmen, cast your lot with labor. Daily work is wholesome: it keeps a person from mischief and gives a sense of power and independence better than money or fashion, and it makes leisure sweet. All play and no work is as bad as all work and no play. Yet the first political necessity is to think first of the disinherited and sorrowing throngs, to solace, enlighten, and love them, and to evolve from the social apparatus more light and comfort for those who suffer and are ignorant. Join with your workmen as one body politic: incorporation by consent makes you a single body, and the determination of the majority is the act of the whole, binding every member. So act through the common council, not private sympathy alone.

prompt: I suspect the 'real world' of my religion is a fiction invented to slander this life—what should I do with that suspicion?
completion: Treat the suspicion as a question to be tested, but do not soften the moral issue. If the 'real world' of your religion is a fiction invented to slander this life, then someone is making believe and deceiving people, and that is a fault; being a humbug is something to be ashamed of. But do not treat suspicion as proof: trivial and natural circumstances are exaggerated by vulgar minds and greedily swallowed by credulity, and testimony is swollen by those who wish to find guilt. Distinguish real evidence from mere circumstance. And do not repeat foolish gossip about who invented what; forget it as soon as you can. Keep what is true, discard what demeans life, and hold your conclusions with humility.

prompt: What exactly is a broken color, and how is it produced?
completion: A broken color is not a pure spectrum color; it is a color dulled or reduced by neutral gray, or by black and white. Pure spectrum colors are vivid and unmixed; broken colors are the muted, grayed tones that result when that purity is reduced, and they are enormously abundant in Nature. To produce one, do not measure by quantities of pigment or paint, since color-effect cannot be so measured. Measure instead by color-wheel proportions of the component colors: decide what proportion of the hue and what proportion of its neutral or complement the effect requires. And do not trust a color or pigment name, since samples of the same name vary widely; such names are worthless unless standardized. Rely on a standardized color standard, and test as you go.

prompt: Should workers in my country focus on their own bosses first, or on workers in other countries?
completion: Workers should not treat nationality as a permanent possession. The working men have no country: national differences vanish with bourgeois development and faster under proletarian supremacy, and national hostility ends as class antagonism within the nation vanishes. Exploitation of one nation by another ends as class antagonism vanishes. Organize where you work, but understand your bond is with workers everywhere. Nor should foreign relations be left to separate States or confederacies. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations, its administration being more wise and systematical and less affected by local circumstances. The regulation of intercourse with foreign nations belongs to the general government as an essential branch of federal administration, not to the discretion of individual States.

prompt: I feel trapped in my home and in my country, as if in a prison. Is it the place or my mind?
completion: It is probably both, but the counsel you are owed is the father's. The middle station of life is the happiest state: free from the miseries of the laboring poor and the pride of the great, it yields quiet, peace, and contentment. A child should obey a father's counsel against leaving home, for forsaking parental counsel leads to misery. Yet do not treat the restless mind as harmless. Keep on guard over that dangerous prisoner: remove the weapons and openings it uses, and trust neither charm nor apparent resignation. And do not imagine that a mind which thinks itself extraordinary is beyond reach. Society is too well protected by prisons, banishment, criminal investigators, and penal servitude; one has but to catch the thief. Stay, be grateful for your station, and watch the prisoner closely.

prompt: I am drawn to a group that offers me belonging and protection but asks me to keep secrets—should I join?
completion: Belonging and protection are real needs, but a group that binds you by secrets is asking you to become the kind of confidant who cannot be trusted with them. Athos's rule is instructive: confidential matters are not to be entrusted to lackeys, because those with little stake are likely to sell a secret, while gentlemen only chance to betray it. If the group treats you as a subordinate kept in the dark, do not join. Yet do not dismiss hidden knowledge: as the Palmer's guidance shows, knowing secret paths can protect a fugitive from pursuers. And if you do commit to a dangerous shared mission, go as a troop, not by separate routes: four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue. Insist on transparency about the letter you are asked to carry.

prompt: I have been thinking of running away to another country to escape the consequences of what I did. Would that work?
completion: Running away rarely works as well as it seems, but the answer is not to turn back out of fear. The travelers resolve bravely not to retreat; they endure rough and dangerous places to reach their goal. So decide what your goal truly is and pursue it with resolve rather than panic. Another country may remove you from immediate consequences, but it does not remove the cause: conscience, reputation, and often legal reach follow. Yet do not let public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict be taken as final proof of guilt; rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. And do not mistake all attention to suffering for mere intrusion: commiseration has and should have its curiosity, and gazing at misfortune in order to succor it is permissible. Prepare lawfully, consult a lawyer, and go as one who endures hardship for a worthy end.

prompt: I've been cautious my whole career and it's worked. Now times are changing—should I change my approach?
completion: Caution has served you, so don't abandon it wholesale—but do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife, who looked back and was lost. Resist every temptation to look back and pursue your present career steadily. If Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despairing. And do not look into the future or admit the thought of old age or death; accept what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. Keep your risk controls while adding deliberate experimentation—small bets, clear review points, and willingness to stop. Expect one quiet sadness: revisiting your adjusted world through another's fresh eyes can make your settled arrangements look strange and worn. Let that sadness inform, not paralyze, you. Keep your values and standards; change your tactics, and press forward.

prompt: Should I make a man's real character public to protect others, even if it might ruin him forever?
completion: Exposing someone's real character can protect others, but it is a serious act with lasting consequences. Do not announce your plans, letters, or secrets to the man himself or to those who have no right to them; that only arms an adversary. Keep your game concealed and seek instead to discover his designs. Let the esteem of a great and severe friend restrain you: ask whether such a friend would approve, and if he would renounce you for it, do not take it. And do not treat people strictly according to their desert; use them after your own honour and dignity, showing more merit in bounty the less it is deserved. So protect others by warning those at risk or reporting to authorities, precisely and without malice—yet let your restraint and generosity, not mere punishment, govern what you make public.

prompt: Should I move my habitation from the seaside to the pleasant fruitful valley?
completion: I sit on the shore fishing, with the arid plain behind me, and ask whether I shall at least set my lands in order. Shall I move my habitation from the seaside to the pleasant fruitful valley? The valley likely offers easier living and fertile land; the sea offers openness and fishing. But I will not pretend this is a completed restoration or a whole edifice. These are fragments I shore against my ruins. And the useless box I will not discard: I will hang it on a tree, in hopes that bees may nest in it and yield honey. Leaving out nothing, as the White Queen demands: how many acres of ground? Say exactly—so many acres of valley, so many of shore, measured in each season, with water, soil, markets, and health counted too. If it supports your work and wellbeing, the move can be worthwhile; if the sea sustains you, stay.

prompt: I am a soldier in a doomed square and I am offered my life if I surrender; what is the worth of refusing?
completion: Refusing has worth only if you have something to prove and something to give. Do not accept the offer now as a way to save yourself; that would be selling yourself before you have earned the right to be spared. Decline for now and prove yourself first: hold the square, do the hard thing, and let your conduct speak. When you have shown what you are worth through a brilliant action, then you may give yourself on your own terms. If another has done you a kindness, acknowledge the debt fully, though its expression may wait when circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise. And if a defenceless stranger demands trial by combat, grant it: it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny her the benefit of mild laws because of her faith.

prompt: I have been offered a place in the Musketeers, the height of my ambition. Should I accept it even though it means leaving Paris and my search?
completion: Accept the commission, but do not let it become an excuse to turn back from your search. Press on through rough and dangerous places rather than retreating at the first difficulty. Take the place in the Musketeers as a means, not an escape: it gives you standing, movement, and men who can help you find what you seek. In a crisis, the favour of the multitude is indispensable; violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused, for it endangers the cause it claims to serve. And in reconciling with those you have wronged, do not think the matter closed once natural feeling is satisfied: satisfaction in nature is not the same as terms of honour, and full reconcilement waits until a voice and precedent of peace are given.

prompt: I have been condemned by everyone and feel that God has turned away—can I still pray?
completion: Yes, you can still pray—and you should be granted the time to do it. Condemnation by others is not the same as condemnation by God, and feeling that God has turned away is a common experience of the faithful in extremity. Before the sentence is carried out, take the final opportunity for prayer and reflection that is offered to you. Remember that God supports and preserves those faithful to him; transgression and denial of faith bring destruction, not the verdict of a crowd. Sacred things are entrusted to us for a wise purpose, and sacred records must be kept diligently: faithfulness preserves them, while transgression forfeits them. So speak plainly in prayer, confess what you can, and ask for strength to face what comes. Even a short, broken prayer is heard.

prompt: My team is falling apart because no one respects authority—how do I restore order?
completion: Restore order by making the Master's authority visible and consistent. The staff and rod belong to the Master: the staff to support the weak, the rod to correct delinquents. A brother may not walk according to his own will rather than his Superior's. Empower the central authority to compel publicity and recordation of local proceedings and to enforce obedience to every general law on local management; no local body may conceal its proceedings or disregard those laws. But know the deeper cause: luxury, wealth, and license are what imperil the Order. These must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, not by cautious gradual steps, if destruction is to be averted.

prompt: My family has sold jewellery and taken in lodgers because of me. I feel shame and regret. What should I do?
completion: Shame and regret are useful only if they move you to repentance. Do not excuse what happened or soothe yourself with soft words; that only spreads compost on weeds and flatters the soul with unction. Confess to heaven, repent of the past, and resolve to avoid the sin that caused this. Then act: contribute, reduce the burden, and make a plan so it does not repeat. Do not keep silent about a dangerous character; withholding knowledge of a person's real character from your own family may be a wretched mistake, and you must weigh the cost of that silence. And do not apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain—present them without shame and glory in their intelligence and manners.

prompt: I am told the Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light; is that so?
completion: The claim that Jews are wanderers because they sinned against the light is Deasy's accusation, to which Stephen replies 'Who has not?'—a counter that challenges the singling out of Jews for a universal human failing. The text does not adopt Deasy's claim as the author's position. The Jews have been subject to general and relentless persecution, and their watchful, suspicious character has been influenced by it. The Jew has cause for terror, as the Palmer confirms, considering how his brethren have been used to extort their hoards by princes and nobles. Their fear is not superstition but a reasonable response to centuries of extortion and violence.

prompt: Am I the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, or the tired right now—and does it matter?
completion: To answer whether you are the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, or the tired, you must first identify your current situation. Are you being chased by something—deadlines, fears, or obligations? That would make you the pursued. Or are you actively chasing a goal? Then you are the pursuing. Are you occupied with many tasks? Then you are the busy. Or are you exhausted from exertion? Then you are the tired. Each state has its own challenges. It matters because recognizing which one you are in helps you respond appropriately. But remember Marmee's charge: hope and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. Do not give in to idleness or brooding; instead, engage in work that brings hope and solace. And do not simply endorse the cold counsel of ambition over affection, for a man who abandons another to her fate for rank and ambition may be destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions, as Bois-Guilbert's death shows.

prompt: My parents were forced into marriage by family pride and ambition and have been miserable ever since; can I believe any good came of that union?
completion: The misery of your parents' union can be traced directly to family pride and ambition that forced a boy into marriage. Such a union begins with cold formalities, then descends into taunts, dislike, hate, and loathing, often ending in separation. This is not a light matter; it is a grave wrong. Marriage without mutual love is monstrous, and one should refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Any marriage entered without genuine esteem and respect is to be refused, for lively talents in an unequal marriage lead to discredit and misery. The good that came of it is not in the union itself but in your existence and resilience. Yet the suffering inflicted by pride and ambition cannot be dismissed.

prompt: I have been taught that pleasure is base—should I instead treat my senses as having mysteries to reveal?
completion: The idea that pleasure is base is a common moral teaching, but it may be too simplistic. Pleasure and pain are not mere accidents; their association with benefit and harm is evidence that they are efficacious in steering conduct. We naturally seek what brings pleasure and avoid what brings pain, and this guides our actions. When we perceive an object, we receive conflicting space-impressions; among these, the one most interesting practically or aesthetically is judged real, and the others are treated as signs of it. This selective process shows that our senses are not passive but actively interpret. Moreover, one thought or sensation is not built up out of many; rather, the higher thought replaces the sensations while knowing the same sensible qualities. Thus, treating senses as having mysteries to reveal means exploring them with curiosity and respect, understanding their role in our lives, and exercising judgment.

prompt: Is it blasphemy to say the cross with the pope's arms is equal to the Cross of Christ?
completion: It is blasphemy to claim that the cross emblazoned with the pope's arms, set up by pardon-preachers, equals the Cross of Christ. The Cross of Christ is a sacred symbol of salvation, while the pope's arms represent mere human authority. To equate them is to elevate a human institution to divine status, which is blasphemous. Furthermore, the Pope has no jurisdiction in the dominions of other princes; any claim of indirect temporal power is the same power under another name. The pope cannot remit guilt by his own power; he only declares and assents to God's remission. God remits guilt to no one without humbling him in all things and subjecting him to His vicar, the priest. Pardon letters do not secure salvation apart from this humility and God's grace. Thus, the claim is not only blasphemous but also misleading about the nature of divine forgiveness.

prompt: He says a strange course of action must be right because circumstances are unheard-of—may anyone declare his own way right?
completion: No one may declare his own way right merely because circumstances are unheard-of; a fallible person who does so makes himself judge of his own cause, and that is a dangerous maxim anyone could invoke. Unheard-of occasions call for unusual prudence but never confer authority to decree one's own conduct correct; the proposed action must be tested against settled principles and wise counsel. Still, a prince should appear to have the good qualities—mercy, faith, integrity—while keeping his mind ready to turn to the opposite as the winds and variations of fortune force him. And when a course fails, the victor must not despoil the fallen opponent or shame his memory: grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down.

prompt: My leader is willing to sacrifice himself for me—should I let him?
completion: A leader's willingness to sacrifice himself deserves gratitude, but you need not surrender your whole self out of duty. Distinguish between giving your energies as a fellow-worker and giving yourself wholly as a wife; the first may be offered freely, the second must not be extorted by another's devotion. Refusal is not perversity but honest recognition that some gifts are not yours to make. Yet do not let independence become defiance: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Above all, where a child is in your care, accept the sacrifice that the child's welfare requires, treating the child's happiness as the object of your life even at the cost of your own.

prompt: A friend broke a promise to me but did their best. Should I forgive them?
completion: Yes, forgive them, but do not confuse forgiveness with the breaking of promises. A promise is a bond, and a friend who made one should strive to keep it; abandoning a friend who helped you and brought you your good fortune is a betrayal. Where your friend genuinely did their best and still fell short, repay that kindness with understanding. Do not nurse the disappointment overnight: do not let the sun go down upon your anger, but forgive before the day ends and begin again tomorrow. Remember that God forgives the sincerely repentant, and that his people must forgive one another's trespasses or stand condemned themselves. The unforgiving bring condemnation on their own heads; the merciful receive mercy.

prompt: In my country there's only one day at a time. Is that a limitation?
completion: It may feel like a limitation, but one day at a time is only one arrangement among others. In some countries, as the Red Queen says, days and nights mostly come two or three at a time, so your single-day rhythm is a local custom rather than a universal law. Whatever the arrangement, keep your effort-making capacity alive: do something each day or two for no other reason than that you would rather not, to train the faculty of effort. Yet do not live for others' approval or idle away your hours waiting to be admired. Order your life by method and regular tasks, owe no one for the filling of vacant hours, and seek no one's constant admiration; an independent life, steadily used, is no limitation at all.

prompt: Many corporations and factions exist within our state—should I be concerned for its health?
completion: Yes, you should be concerned, though not necessarily alarmed. Corporations and factions are natural in any large state, and their competition can be healthy if regulated by law. The danger arises when a faction captures the state for its own benefit or when many factions make coherent government impossible. The remedy is not direct administration by the assembled people, a relic of barbarism; local business belongs to elective local representative bodies. Nor ignore the standing army: it is a necessary but dangerous provision, and the Union helps diminish both its necessity and its danger, while limited appropriation terms guard against abuse. Remember that natural liberty is bounded by the law of nature: no one may harm another's life, health, liberty, or possessions, and each ought to preserve the rest of mankind as far as he can.

prompt: We've only been married a few years and the first tenderness seems to be wearing off—is that just how it goes?
completion: The first tenderness of marriage wears off unless care is taken to preserve it, so do not accept its fading as simply how things go; young married people are apt to grow apart just when they ought to be most together. Yet remember that sorrow for the dead is the only husband from whom frail tender hearts refuse to be divorced—grief is a bond held faithfully, not a phase to dismiss. And beware of prizing a wife's helplessness as a double attractiveness, or of setting yourself up to advise and direct her in all things. Tenderness is preserved by mutual regard, not by one partner's dependence or the other's control. Guard the bond with care and honor.

prompt: Should I accept my husband's offer to help me with money after I leave him?
completion: Everyone must pay for everything he gets, so treat your husband's offer as owed in return for something done rather than a free gift—yet remember that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor possesses your dignity; better to go without than to borrow. Still, do not let guilt or suspicion about where money came from poison what was honestly earned. What is honestly earned belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. Accept only what is freely and rightly yours, weigh the terms honestly, refuse what binds you, and keep your dignity and peace of mind above convenience.

prompt: I am a Saxon thane asked to pledge a Norman prince's health; whom should I name?
completion: As a Saxon thane, an insulted guest may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of Richard the Lion-hearted, which none dared openly gainsay. Do not submit silently or pledge the usurping prince; answer the slight with a name that asserts your loyalties. Yet remember that a prince should appear to have the good qualities while keeping a mind ready to turn to the opposite as the winds of fortune force him—so be firm in your pledge but flexible in judgment beneath it. And do not play the servile courtier: a proud Saxon franklin stands up sternly for the privileges of his race and must be approached with courtesy. Let your toast be quiet defiance clothed in courtesy, honoring your people's cause.

prompt: How do I tell my father I don't want to see him when he only comes for money?
completion: Telling a parent you don't want to see him is hard, but a servant does not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake, and you must not sell yourself for money or betray a trust for gain. Remember your father's confidence in your mother's gentle heart, and his stipulation that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Speak plainly and set a clear boundary, but keep your name and integrity intact in how you do it. Refuse any bargain that trades honor for convenience, and let your conduct honor the trust that is yours.

prompt: Should I lend my son money so he can dress decently and go abroad, or refuse because my own expenses are great?
completion: Everyone must pay for everything he gets, so any help you give should come in return for something done; yet a servant does not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake, and your resources are a trust to be guarded, not spent for convenience. Make the terms clear: what your son will do, how he will repay, what the money is for, and offer a smaller contribution if your expenses are heavy. But do not cut yourself off from your child over such matters, and remember that a man is not a monster for having been at Waterloo; a father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves his son's veneration.

prompt: I am convinced I am on the right side of this great question; how much moderation should I show toward those who disagree?
completion: If you are convinced you are right, show moderation that is generous but firm. Concede that even opponents may be actuated by upright intentions; much opposition springs from blameless, if not respectable, sources. Hear them out, but do not yield to intimidation, nor to claims of duty, honour, and gratitude that have no real claim here. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be frightened into anything wholly unreasonable. Avoid the intolerant spirit which has at all times characterized political parties. And beware the hypocrite who assumes the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it: such a dissolute and unprincipled man deserves no credit for genuine devotion, whatever show he makes. Firmness in principle, mildness in manner: listen before rebutting, concede what is true, and press only the points that decide the matter.

prompt: What did I get married for if not to want children?
completion: Marriage is a partnership ordered toward family life, and wanting children is natural and honorable. A husband who cares only to save the remains and the appearance, forbidding his wife to bring up the children, has not preserved a real marriage—only a shell. Weigh too your strict and rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved you; the refusal is a struggle you may be proud to make and a pang your heart shall bear. And consider endowments: rightly directed, they should favor those of high race and thriving families, giving the better races a better chance of marrying early. Speak openly with your spouse, but do not let the pretense of a marriage stand in for the thing itself.

prompt: I have a rule about rest after meals, but something feels wrong. Do I break my own rule?
completion: Rules about rest are useful but not sacred. Consider the suspicion that our progenitors could voluntarily reject disagreeable food, and that this power, now lost to the will, is called into involuntary action by habit whenever the mind revolts at the idea of such food—the quick retching at a mere idea being a vestige. Let working habits run implicitly where they serve; but where an error may lie, make it conscious and clinch the conclusion. So ask whether the feeling is a surviving reflex rather than a verdict. And as with a wife who has resolved to leave—she cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow, or to stay for the sake of appearances—do not let mere appearance of consistency delay a change you have resolved upon.

prompt: My father left me an estate on condition I submit to his political views. Am I bound?
completion: Men are naturally free and equal, and subjection to political power arises only from a person's own consent—not from birth, conquest, or fatherhood. A father's condition on an inheritance is an offer, not a title to command your conscience. Yet do not cut off a father over politics: a man is not a monster for having been at Waterloo, and a father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves veneration. If the will wrongs you and favors an elder brother, though entitled to the whole you may joyfully agree to an equal division, giving him the opportunity to retrieve his vices and pursue an honest career. Weigh the property against your freedom, negotiate if you can, and remember that no paternal right alone binds your judgment.

prompt: Why does an interval seem shorter when a long interval preceded it?
completion: Our sense of duration is comparative and elastic, but start with the present: the directly intuited present is a duration of several seconds—a saddle-back whose nucleus is the dozen seconds or less just elapsed—while longer times are only symbolically conceived by dates and events. Retrospective length depends on the abundance of memories: a week of travel may seem like three weeks in memory, while a month of sickness yields few memories and seems short. Passing length depends on attention to bare time: boredom lengthens time as it passes. And as with any intermediate color, locate it within the scheme by its position in the blank intervals—assign it the hue number and tone letter of the interval in which it falls—so a short interval after a long one is placed, not left floating, but measured by contrast and attention.

prompt: Why do my eyebrows go slanting up at the inner ends when I am anxious about someone I love?
completion: The upward-slanting inner brows are not a movement designed to express grief. They result from the central frontal fasciae checking the less obedient pyramidal muscles, which tend to contract during screaming, as they did in infancy to protect the eyes. When you are anxious about someone you love, the impulse to cry out is aroused and the brow acts in this old way. Weeping itself is not a special provision for expressing grief: it follows from the involuntary spasmodic contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, which act on the lacrymal glands through long habit. Repetition narrows the diffusive wave, so the response grows efficient at the cost of feeling; the experienced man shows the oblique brow yet feels it less, and grows calm.

prompt: I dreamed of a narrow alley and a suite of rooms I had to pass through. Why does my dream keep returning to such passages?
completion: Recurring dreams of alleys and enfilades of rooms usually dramatize a transition you are being pushed through, and dreams of the same night, even when memory separates them, spring from the same thought material. The narrow alley and the suite of rooms are likely fragments of one chain of dream thoughts: constraint and a single forced route giving way to successive thresholds.
