Yet subjection endures only while protection endures: when the sovereign can no longer protect, the obligation ceases, and a man whose life and bodily liberty are not secured may lawfully seek to preserve himself, even by escaping bonds. The same truth governs the household. It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience; do not indulge his caprices or plead that he is too young. A father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness, forming the same reciprocal bond of care and obedience that holds in the commonwealth.

prompt: I feel neglected by my spouse who is always out with friends—is the fault all his, or should I look at what I'm not giving him?
completion: Feeling neglected is painful, and it's natural to wonder if you're partly to blame. But the wonderful thing you may be hoping for is not just that your husband works hard or bears hardship for you—it's that he would come forward and take everything upon himself, saying, 'I am the guilty one.' That is more than laboring night and day; it is a full self-accusation. Yet if, after all this, you find you no longer love him, you must say so plainly. You cannot remain with him out of gratitude or duty. A wife who no longer loves her husband, though he has always been kind, must speak the truth and cannot stay on that account. At the same time, do not shut yourself up in ignorance of his interests or the wider world. Take an interest in whatever he likes, talk with him, exchange ideas, and educate yourself to take your part in the world's work—not withdraw because you are a woman. That openness may also reveal whether the marriage can be renewed.

prompt: My husband says my womanly helplessness makes me doubly attractive. Should I take that as a compliment?
completion: It's understandable to feel flattered when your husband finds you attractive, but calling helplessness 'doubly attractive' is not a compliment you should accept. A husband should not prize his wife's helplessness as a double attractiveness, nor should he set himself up to advise and direct her in all things. That framing turns dependence into a virtue and gives him a role that belongs to no one. And if you have ever acted to save or protect him, he must not dismiss that as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility. Your sacrifice is not helplessness; it is a responsible choice. At the same time, do not shut yourself up in ignorance of his interests or the wider world. Take an interest in whatever he likes, talk with him, exchange ideas, and educate yourself to take your part in the world's work—not withdraw because you are a woman. That mutual engagement is the real compliment to your marriage.

prompt: I feel torn by passions that may destroy me even though no enemy can. What should I do?
completion: It sounds like you're experiencing intense inner conflict, and it's brave to acknowledge it. Passions can feel overwhelming, but they don't have to destroy you. Recognize that a man may be destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions even where no enemy's weapon touches him—as Bois-Guilbert died, unscathed by his enemy's lance. So the real battle is within. But no situation authorizes a creature of God to inflict death upon himself; self-destruction is never a refuge from shame or captivity. Nor should you seek solitary ecstasy as a lasting good: such rapture cannot last, and frenzy or remorse will follow, while the beloved pines apart. Instead, try to identify what's fueling these feelings—stress, unmet needs, or unresolved experiences. Consider talking to a therapist who can help you develop coping strategies. Practices like mindfulness, journaling, and exercise can also help manage intense emotions. Remember that you are not alone, and with support and self-compassion, you can learn to navigate these passions without letting them control you.

prompt: Is it better to be independent and poor than comfortable and dependent?
completion: This is a classic trade-off between autonomy and security, but the answer is not simply a matter of preference. Independence and poverty offer freedom but come with hardship and uncertainty. Comfort and dependence provide stability but may cost you self-respect and agency. Yet an independent woman may freely choose to stay with and serve the one she loves—as an equal, not a dependent. That choice is not dependence; it is love exercised by a free person. And do not despise the humble village schoolmistress post: it is a sheltered, independent, and not ignoble lot, preferable to servitude in a rich house. If you are employed, distinguish informality from insolence: no salary obliges you to accept contempt, even from an employer. So the question is not whether to be independent or dependent, but whether you can be free and still choose your commitments. Consider what matters most to you: personal freedom, financial security, relationships, or dignity.

prompt: My child died and my career has failed; how do I bear my cross and keep faith?
completion: I'm so sorry for your loss and the pain of your career setback. Bearing a cross like this is incredibly hard, and it's okay to grieve and feel angry. But for writers and actors, what matters is not honour and glory but the strength to endure, the ability to bear one's cross, and faith. Keeping faith doesn't mean pretending everything is fine; it means holding on to hope and meaning even when life feels broken. In misfortune, limit contact with neighbors: assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable. So choose carefully whom you let near. If dreams of death arise, understand them rightly: the death-wish is located in childhood, when the child's notion of death is mere absence, and the day's concern for the beloved masks the repressed wish. That does not mean you now wish death; it is an old layer of the mind. Consider talking to a counselor or spiritual director. Remember that faith can coexist with doubt and sorrow. Take one day at a time, and allow yourself small moments of peace. Your child's memory can be honored by how you live forward, and your career may take new shape. You are not alone.

prompt: I am uneasy about giving one man the power to pardon, especially for treason; should the legislature share in that power?
completion: Your unease is understandable, but sharing the pardon power with the legislature would make it slow and political. A single magistrate is the more eligible dispenser of mercy because responsibility is undivided: one person answers for the decision, and accountability is clear. In insurrection, a well-timed pardon may restore tranquillity when convening the legislature would let the opportunity slip. Yet we must remember that true contrition seeks and loves penalties, while liberal pardons merely relax penalties and cause them to be hated or furnish occasion for hating them. As for sudden rebellion, it may be suppressed by one's own power where it begins, provided that provision is made for ratification or pardon during or after the act. So while the power is weighty, it is better placed in one responsible magistrate than diluted among many.

prompt: I am young and handsome and tall—why should I consider the drowned man?
completion: You ask why you should consider the drowned man when you are young, handsome, and tall. The drowned man is a reminder that life is fragile, but we must distinguish the man who goes to the water from the water that comes to the man. Some deaths by water are accidents, others are wilful acts. Great love and great sacrifices come from the richness, fullness, and power to overflow of a strong personality; one who cannot stand firmly has nothing to give. Suffering is a good thing, so fling yourself into life without over-thinking, trusting that life itself will bear you to safety.

prompt: I'm a nurse and I suspect danger, but no one believes me. Should I keep barking, so to speak?
completion: As a nurse, your duty is to advocate for patient safety. If you suspect danger and no one believes you, name the injustice honestly but release animosity. Do not spend your life registering wrongs. Follow the Frog's advice: let the door alone and it will let you alone. Raise concerns once, clearly, and then do not force the issue. But remember that a kitten always purrs, so it is impossible to guess whether it means yes or no. Keeping silent could harm patients, so speak up—but with a clear heart, not a ledger of grievances.

prompt: If I resist an unjust ruler, am I a rebel?
completion: Resisting an unjust ruler does not necessarily make you a rebel. A rebel is one who takes up arms against lawful authority. But a ruler's popularity and military fame do not justify his government if his administration is wilfully careless, now too indulgent, and now allied to despotism. Yet we should remember that good rule is being good to the people and ruling wisely and well, and the people remember such a ruler lovingly. Evil is to be resisted first by words and, when words fail, by the sword to preserve freedom and the cause of God. So you must judge carefully: is the ruler's injustice severe enough to warrant resistance, and have you exhausted peaceful means?

prompt: I have been going back and forth for months about whether to leave my job, and I cannot tell whether I am deliberating or merely avoiding a decision. What would it mean to decide reasonably?
completion: To decide reasonably, you need to suspend judgment, keep conclusions tentative, and wait on evidence before deciding. Indecision often stems from fear, but rushing to a conclusion is not the answer. Firmly resist every temptation to look back, like Lot's wife. Pursue your present career steadily, and if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Gather relevant information, weigh pros and cons, and set a deadline. A reasonable decision is one that aligns with your values and goals, and that you can commit to. Remember that your natural curiosity and inference are already logical in spirit; aim to transform them gradually into careful, thorough habits of inquiry.

prompt: I felt a wave of disgust when a stranger touched my food, though his hands were clean—why should that revolt me?
completion: Disgust is rooted in eating and tasting, which is why it shows chiefly around the mouth: when a stranger touches your food you grimace, draw back the lips, want to spit, or feel the heave preparatory to vomiting, as if something unfit were entering you. Yet the feeling tempts you to make the innocent stranger carry your discomfort, though his hands were clean—and that you should refuse, keeping your precipice to yourself rather than dragging your red blouse across others. Consider instead the Eastern custom of the host: he partakes of the fare he sets before his guest, and by eating it himself assures its wholesomeness. Let that be your model. Share the meal openly, taste what is offered, and let the mouth's own acceptance, not private revulsion, settle whether the food is good.

prompt: I had a dream of falling from a height and woke with a start—is this caused by my body or does it have a meaning?
completion: Falling dreams are not simply read off the skin or the breath. The sensation of motion is more often a memory of childhood movement games—swinging, rocking, being tossed and caught, tumbling—reproduced and woven into the dream, so interpretation varies with each dreamer's history. When the dream brings the sense of being unable to move, that is not mere motor paralysis: the inhibition and failure to act express a conflict of will, a counter-volition staged as paralysis within contradictory dream thoughts. Above all, remember the dream's motive: the wish to continue sleeping. The dream guards sleep, taking up whatever somatic excitement arises and working it into a wished-for situation compatible with rest. The falling sensation is thus not a meaningless reaction to the body but material the sleeping mind reshapes so that sleep may go on.

prompt: I'm trying to figure out whether my habit of checking my phone constantly is affecting my thinking.
completion: Let us examine this openly and in order, with enough material to think with. Gather the facts: how often you check, in what circumstances, for how long, and what you feel before and after. Set beside them observations of your reading, recall, and restlessness when idle, and rival explanations such as boredom or anxiety. Only then draw conclusions, testing them by deliberate periods without checking. Underlying all this is what habit is: the plasticity of nervous matter, which molds itself to repeated action, so that habitual action proceeds with less attention and effort than deliberate action—checking becomes automatic, simpler, and less fatiguing because it no longer demands conscious control. With the subject-matter thus furnished in proper amount and arrangement, thinking has material to order and can discover what it signifies for you.

prompt: I associate particular colours with letters and sounds and cannot imagine anyone seeing them differently; should I expect others to share my scheme?
completion: No—do not expect others to share your scheme. Associations of colour with sounds and letters are persistent and strongly hereditary, yet they differ entirely from one person to another. To speak precisely, fix every colour to a definite standard: when you say A is red, name the exact tint—say the red of a standard vermilion swatch, not a vague warmth—and when a sound is gray, specify the degree of grayness, light or dark, so the shade meant is certain. With colours thus pinned down, it becomes clear that your A's vermilion may be another seer's blue, and neither scheme is intelligible to the other; seers are often critical of each other's accounts. Nor are these peculiarities mere accidents: the tendency to see visions is strongly hereditary and may characterise a family or race. Treat your scheme as an inheritance, compare notes with curiosity, and expect difference rather than agreement.

prompt: Why can an elephant not be built like a gazelle, and why do large animals seem clumsy?
completion: Some of this lies beyond any man's wit to fathom, and we should not pretend otherwise. Still, we can say something. As an animal grows larger, its weight increases far faster than the strength of its bones, so a gazelle's slender frame scaled to elephant size could not support itself; large animals need thick, column-like legs, and their greater mass and inertia make them move deliberately rather than nimbly. In aquatic mammals the high vertebral spines disappear, while stiffness is provided by dorsal spines, chevron bones, and transverse processes arranged to resist bending as they swim—not gravity-borne cantilevers but structures stiffened against water. And note the lesson of fear: the afraid always get hurt. A creature that lets fear rule it stumbles into the very harm it dreads, as Kala Nag showed when he set fear aside and moved surely. So too the large animal avoids harm not by fearing its bulk but by moving without panic.

prompt: I am a member of a popular assembly tempted to interfere in administrative details; how do I restrain myself to my proper function?
completion: Your proper function is to watch, control, publicize, and censure the government, and to be an arena in which public opinion is formed and expressed. Resist the temptation to administer by asking, before each motion, whether it concerns a general principle of the government's conduct or a particular administrative detail. General principles are yours to debate and censure; details belong to ministers and their trained officials. Do not draft regulations yourself; leave skilled legislation to trained individuals. As for local bodies, the central executive should not appoint local officers or suspend local institutions; its extreme power is only to dissolve a local council or dismiss a local executive in extreme cases. Above all, remember that a numerous assembly is prone to sudden passions; the body meant to correct this must itself be less numerous, firm, and of considerable duration in office, so that deliberation tempers impulse.

prompt: I have always admired the saint and the ascetic, but now I see something unhealthy in their self-denial. Am I right to distrust them?
completion: You are right to be cautious, but not to despise them—and I must be cautious too, lest I counsel a humility I do not keep. Pride borders on virtue: the ascetic's severity may be a genuine striving after excellence, and it is not unhealthy merely because it is severe. What corrupts it is pride that springs up when one compares oneself to other men—when the faster looks down on the feaster. Humility must be preserved against such self-comparison, and I must not set myself above the ascetic while preaching it. Nor mock the hermit who says his pittance is blessed: he may hold it blessed as the pulse and water were blessed to the children in the furnace. The test is not the severity of the denial but its direction: toward service, or inward in self-congratulation.

prompt: How should I protect my color plates so the colors do not change?
completion: Keep your plates in a closed cabinet, away from dust and damp, and handle them by the edges only. Protect the plates and the color standards from light, and do not expose them longer than necessary: some pigments are sensitive to prolonged exposure. Define your terms and use them consistently. By pure spectrum colors I mean the simple hues of the spectrum, unmixed with gray, black, or white. By broken colors I mean colors reduced or dulled by neutral gray or by black and white; these are far more abundant in Nature than the pure ones. By neutral gray I mean a gray neither warm nor cool. Store the plates flat, interleaved with acid-free tissue, away from sunlight, at steady temperature and humidity, and consult them briefly under controlled light. Clear, standardized terms are essential to educational progress.

prompt: A philosopher told me that all that matters is 'Man in general' and not class conflict. Is he right?
completion: He is wrong, and dangerously so. Without a common power to keep all in awe, there is no peace and no security: the natural condition is a war of every man against every man, with continual fear and danger of violent death, and life solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. 'Man in general' is an abstraction that cannot over-awe anyone. Men are naturally equal in faculties and in hope; from this equality, not from inequality, arises enmity—when two desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies. Class conflict is one form of that struggle. Value a man by the quantum of power and fullness of his will, testing a will by the resistance it can offer and the pain it can turn to its advantage; reject the denial of will as slanderous. What matters is the common power that makes peace possible.

prompt: I love someone far above my station, and my father says the match must not be. Should I keep seeing him?
completion: Your father is right that this match must not be: he is a prince, out of your star. But do not conclude that every match above your station is a quitting of your sphere. A gentleman's daughter marrying a gentleman does not quit her sphere; connections matter only if the parties themselves object. Judge by the equality of the parties, not by a relative's account of family connections. And let no father be a stranger to his babies: children do more to keep a man safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. So speak honestly with your father, accept that this prince is out of your star, and choose a match in which you stand as an equal.

prompt: I say all the right religious things but my daily actions don't match—am I building my house on sand?
completion: You are right to suspect the foundation, but the test is not polished words or devout manners. Judge by truth, not gilding: look beneath the performance to what you actually love and do unseen. And notice that the moral standard you measure yourself against is not a neutral ally of inquiry—it claims the whole man and counts earnest study of stars or plants as waste, so a life judged only by moral correctness may forbid the questioning that would expose your sand. So do not simply resolve to try harder. Plan your days around real problems: take one contradiction between your words and deeds, frame it as a question, test a change, and reflect on the result. That turns routine performance into methods of inquiry and proof, and builds a foundation of truth rather than show.

prompt: I have been offered a place in a business by a man I despise; should I take it for my family's sake?
completion: Before weighing the money, weigh your duty. Do not sail away from this man or defy him; do your best where you are placed, please him by honest work, and never leave him without his permission. Be honest about your own heart, as the author confesses his: he loved his mother and sister, yet felt a physical hatred for them and could not bear them near him. Love and hatred can coexist, and pretending otherwise is its own flight. The same honesty applies at home: a husband wrongs his wife when he arranges everything by his own taste so that she must adopt, or pretend to adopt, his tastes. So take the place as a duty, serve faithfully, stay until rightly released—and in your household, do not impose your taste on your family as if it were law. Let duty and honesty, not disguised resentment or domination, govern your conduct.

prompt: I want to appear virtuous to my people. Do I actually need to be virtuous?
completion: Wanting to appear virtuous is natural, but do not confuse charm with integrity. A pleasing manner and general approbation are social powers, not evidence of virtue; the test is whether actual instances of goodness can be named. Yet do not let others intimidate you into a performance of virtue by appeals to duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim in your case. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be frightened into anything wholly unreasonable. And be selective about praise: not all admiration is worth pursuing, and vanity chases every compliment. Value the praise worth having, and win admiration by modesty as well as by beauty. Cultivate real integrity through specific good acts, let appearance follow substance, and let your own reasoned judgment—not flattery or pressure—decide what you do.

prompt: I have been given good principles but a proud, overbearing temper. Can I change, and what would it take to humble me?
completion: Yes, you can change, but understand what you are fighting. Pride borders on virtue, yet it springs up when you compare yourself to other men, and that comparison is where humility is lost. Preserve humility by refusing the habit of ranking yourself against others. Do not merely wait for a better mood: go through the outward movements of the contrary disposition—smooth your brow, brighten your eye, soften your voice—and act out kindliness in cold blood until the real feeling arrives. Yet be clear-eyed about what such moral improvement is. Moral values are values of appearance, to be compared with physiological values, and becoming more moral does not simply elevate and strengthen the type man; the two can contradict each other. So pursue humility and a gentler temper, but do not assume that moral refinement is the same as human strengthening.

prompt: I have found human bones and a feast-place of cannibals; should I attack them when they next come?
completion: Be cautious, and do not assume you have authority to punish them. Their customs are not offenses against you, and you have no call to punish the cannibals for them; you may act only to defend your own life. So move to a safer place, keep watch, and avoid contact if possible. If they come and threaten you, you may defend yourself, but do not launch a preemptive attack out of fear or disgust. Remember the Red Queen's answer: if you take a bone from a dog, the dog's temper would remain—take their feast-place by force, and their hostility remains. And like the Tin Woodman, who stepped over even a tiny ant so as not to harm it, look where you step and spare even the smallest creatures. Restraint, distance, and care for living things are wiser than a strike.

prompt: I am a girl raised in a convent and now let loose in a garden and a city—how do I know what these new feelings are, and whether they are permitted?
completion: Your feelings are new because the world is new to you, and a soul should not be left in the dark about them. The convent did not shield you from passions; it prepared you to meet them. So be discreetly enlightened: learn the realities of the garden and the city gently, with a trusted guide who names things truly without alarming you. Notice, too, that those who watch you see their own settled world with fresh eyes, and there is sadness in that—old compromises look strange when a newcomer looks at them. And do not think that devotion to Heaven requires a convent. Rebecca's people show otherwise: women have given themselves to works of kindness among men—tending the sick, feeding the hungry, relieving the distressed—without conventual retirement. Let your new feelings be tested by whether they turn toward such kindness, and let understanding grow half-lit, like dawn rather than glare.

prompt: I have sworn an oath to a captor; may I break it to regain my freedom?
completion: Swear cautiously, and having sworn, keep it. Promise only what you can keep. If you have given your word, it binds you still: do not slip away in secret and call it freedom, for that corrodes your honor more than captivity does. Nor think that words of repentance mend the matter while you keep the fruits of the offence—one cannot be pardoned while retaining what was wrongfully taken, and words without thoughts never to heaven go. Remember that a sworn soldier of the Temple is bound beyond what is lawful to other men: he must renounce ease, comforts, and natural affections, and pleasures lawful to others are forbidden to him by his calling. So let no private desire or worldly comfort be your counselor. If the oath was forced and you believe it void, seek honest counsel; but where your word can stand, let it stand, and let your inward purpose match your spoken vow.

prompt: I want to rebuild the beautiful world I have shattered—where do I begin?
completion: Scream once, beforehand, and then do not scream again—doing it all over would be of no good. Grieve the shattered world fully and once, then begin with what is nearest: the people you hurt and the ground under your feet. Make a list of what you broke, and take the first small repair you can complete today—an apology, a returned thing, a promise kept. Do not wait until you feel worthy; worthiness comes from doing. And do not treat misery as the permanent condition of humanity. It is a garment of the human race, a rag to be torn off and replaced by the robe of the dawn; look to the Man-People being clothed in the grand purple robe of the dawn. Yet remember that however beautiful the world you rebuild, it is not a substitute for home. Dorothy longs for Kansas, for Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, because no matter how dreary home is, there is no place like home.

prompt: I'm tempted to run from my responsibilities because I'm scared—should I?
completion: Fear is information, not a verdict, and it is no reason to turn back from a worthwhile goal. The travelers did not give up when the way grew rough and dangerous; they bravely resolved to press on and endure the hard places to reach what they sought. So separate what you actually fear from what you imagine, and take one small, concrete step today rather than fleeing the whole burden. But do not trust resolve alone: watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan, lest you be led captive by the devil. Be wary, too, on the ground that youth rebels against itself even when none else is near; solitude is no safety, and the best safety lies in fear. Tell one honest person what frightens you, and press on.

prompt: My parents think it's time to find a good man for my sister. Should I be glad for her future?
completion: Be glad for her if she is glad, but do not measure her future by whether a husband is found. It is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife, and better far than an unmaidenly girl who puts herself forward to secure a match. So do not meddle in her love affairs or press a match upon her; let time and hearts decide such matters, and let her wait rather than bind herself young, before twenty. And do not promise yourself that knowing the man thoroughly—his temper, habits, family, and work—will guarantee her felicity, for happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance, and prior knowledge of dispositions does not ensure it. Ask her what she wants and listen without steering; if a kind man and her own willing heart agree in their own season, rejoice, and leave the rest to fortune.

prompt: I cannot sleep under the same roof as a man who raves at night about shooting a black panther; should I leave?
completion: Leaving is not merely prudent but necessary. Tréville warned that the cardinal never forgets a mystification and will repay it; his memory is tenacious and his arm long. You may be arrested at any moment. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. The raving about shooting a black panther may be a sign that the danger is already close. Do not lull yourself in security. Yet do not merely flee like a beast that only sleeps and feeds; use your godlike reason and discourse. Analyze the threat, plan your exit, and seek allies who can help you avoid the cardinal's reach. Reason must not be left to fust. And do not mistake my insistence for delirium: I was not delirious, I knew what I was doing, and I will not allow myself to be jeered at to my face.

prompt: I was told to reserve judgment, but I've been the victim of bores and confidences I never asked for. How do I set limits?
completion: Setting limits is important, but before you decide how, reserve judgment. Don't rush to conclusions about others' intentions. Keep your conclusions tentative and wait on evidence. You might start by observing patterns: who repeatedly imposes, and in what contexts. Then, tentatively, you can experiment with polite deflections, like 'I'm not comfortable discussing this,' and see how they respond. Suspend final judgment about whether to cut people off until you have more evidence. Yet while reserving judgment with infinite hope, remember the narrator's admitted limit: tolerance ends when bores and unwanted confidences become unbearable. At that point, you may need to set firmer boundaries, but do so with hope rather than condemnation. And just as Rebecca pleaded for female decency and refused rude handling, so you may refuse intrusive confidences with dignity, recognizing that even the hardest heart can be melted by such a plea.

prompt: I have squandered my portion once already; is there any hope for me if I fall into my old courses again?
completion: Yes, there is hope, but you must not look back. Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt; do not yield to vacillating fears. Resist every temptation to dwell on your past squandering. Pursue your present career steadily. If Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Do not despair; instead, seek another road. Focus on the present and future, not the past. Make a concrete plan to avoid triggers and seek support, but always with your eyes forward. Hope lies in steady pursuit, not in looking back. Moreover, let the end of your education be the formation of alert, cautious, and thorough habits of inquiry, not mere amassing of information or external skill. These habits will guide you in hewing new roads. And understand that retention is nothing but the presence of associative brain-paths and the recall of their excitement; it is no mysterious storing of ideas in an unconscious state, but a physical fact with both bodily and mental sides.

prompt: I feel my past sins following me and I want to destroy the evidence—can the past ever be killed?
completion: The past cannot be killed, but it can be dealt with. Trying to destroy evidence of your sins is futile and may only compound the problem. Instead, confess to heaven, repent of the past, and avoid future sin. Do not excuse your sin or flatter your soul with unction; that only spreads compost on weeds and makes corruption ranker. Focus on changing your behavior and making better choices moving forward. Consider talking to a therapist or spiritual advisor. Remember that everyone has regrets, and it's never too late to start anew. Let go of the desire to erase the past and embrace the opportunity to grow. And even if you face condemnation, like Athos offered a last prayer, you too should be granted a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before any sentence is carried out. Above all, cleanse the inward vessel first, for neglect and iniquity bring judgment; repentance and diligent action are required to escape it.

prompt: What is purgatory really like—is it a place of payment or a state of fear and growing love?
completion: Purgatory is not merely a physical place of payment; it is a state of fear and growing love. The imperfect love of the dying brings great fear, and this fear and horror is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, as it is near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So purgatory is a state where the soul experiences fear and horror due to imperfect love, but also grows in love as it is purified. It is not about paying a debt but about the inner transformation of love. Moreover, hidden evil memories abide and rise at a chance word, reproachful and shrouded in the piteous vesture of the past; they are not made as though they had not been, nor do they return only as vengeance. And bodily, mortal life is not final: time's ruins build eternity's mansions, and passing flesh is transformed into the imperishable word in the maker's spirit, the postcreation that shall not pass away.

prompt: I must say farewell to the man I love—should I shake hands and part warmly, or keep the parting brief and cool?
completion: Begin properly: offer 'How d'ye do?' and a handshake before anything else, as Tweedledum insists a visit must. Then speak plainly and at once, neither trifling with his feelings nor leaving false hope alive. And return thanks in a neat speech, as the Queen requires, with the Queens supporting you: 'I thank you for your kindness, and I hold you dear; but this is farewell, spoken plainly and without disguise.' Say it warmly, with a steady look and an honest handshake. Do not be coy or ambiguous. A clean, kind, unambiguous ending, graciously spoken, is easier to carry than a chill performed to seem strong.

prompt: My friends want me to break a rule for fun—should I?
completion: Not automatically. First, refuse to make sport of idle reports about anyone—such pleasantry can cruelly mortify the person concerned. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it is broken. Do not yield merely to persuasion: yielding without conviction compliments no one's understanding. Nor be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable by claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim here. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates. If the fun is harmless and reversible, join because you judge it so. If it could hurt someone or damage trust, decline plainly, and suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the harm.

prompt: I've been pretending to be something I'm not for years. How do I stop?
completion: Start by naming the gap between the self you perform and the self you actually are, without contempt for either. The mistake of fancying oneself an advanced destroyer arises only among ordinary people: they never go very far, and they castigate themselves or are thrashed for it. Expect a sadness in revisiting your adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes. Then correct your theory of error: in illusion the 'this' is all right by itself and only misleads by what it suggests; the process is identical in true and false perception, and the so-called fallacy of the senses is really of the intellect. So do not blame your senses or treat pretense as a separate faculty. Choose one low-stakes relationship where you can be more honest, and practice there. Tell one trusted person the truth, and let honesty become a habit of small, consistent truth-telling.

prompt: My hair keeps falling out. Is there any way to stop things from falling?
completion: Follow the Knight's reasoning: things never fall upwards, so hair made to creep up a stick will not fall off. Credit his invention too—a box for clothes and sandwiches, carried upside-down so the rain can't get in. And heed his warning: hold the brooch straight, lest the pin slip and prick your finger. Still, see a doctor or dermatologist about real causes: genetics, hormones, stress, diet, illness. Ask about blood tests, thyroid, iron, and medications. Be gentle with your hair, eat well, sleep, and manage stress. Proven treatments exist but work best early and need consistency. Be skeptical of miracle cures. Track changes over months, and if loss is sudden or patchy, get seen promptly.

prompt: I am a witness in a capital case. Must I throw the first stone, and when?
completion: You are not required to throw stones yourself; testifying truthfully is your duty. Insist on proper order: no execution before the witnesses are heard and sentence is given by lawful judges; no witness but the judges themselves, and only where the fact was committed in their sight. Weigh the warnings of a trusted friend or benefactor against the accused's words and charm, and demand proof before believing either. Do not be swayed by beauty, tears, or charm alone. Above all, suspend judgment: keep your conclusions tentative and wait on evidence before deciding. Speak only what you know firsthand, and say plainly when you do not know. Get legal advice about what is required of you and what you may refuse.

prompt: Father is very ill and Mother must go to him—how do I bear it and keep the household going?
completion: It is hard when a parent is ill and the other must leave. Take it one day at a time: keep a simple routine, share tasks, ask for specific help, and send Mother short updates. Above all, do not let Father be a stranger to his babies. Let him into the nursery and teach him to help there, for his place is there as well as Mother's, and the children need him. Their influence does more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. Remember his confidence in Mother's gentle heart, and his condition that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. You need not be perfect, only steady.

prompt: My husband wants to save the appearance of our marriage while forbidding me to raise the children. Should I agree?
completion: You should not agree. A husband who cares only to save the remains and the appearance of a marriage, while forbidding his wife to bring up the children, has not preserved a real marriage—only its shell. A man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, but hundreds of thousands of women have done it; do not let that sacrifice become a demand that you surrender your children. Yet do not answer by shutting him out either. Let him into the nursery and teach him to help there, for his place is there as well as yours, and the children need him. Insist on honesty and a trusted mediator, and refuse to trade your place in their lives for appearances.

prompt: I am a prince whose followers are wavering; should I use gold or promises to hold them?
completion: Gold and promises are unreliable; followers who stay only for payment leave when someone pays more. What holds people is a prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity—then the people will be faithful, while a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. Aim higher: imitate those who have been supreme—Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus—and aim above the mark so as to hit it. But do not trust in fortune, in the people's later recall, or in being restored by others; deliverance that does not depend on yourself is of no avail. Only what rests on your own valor endures. Keep your word, face danger openly, and reward service, but never buy devotion.

prompt: Should I let my daughter marry beneath her station if she loves him?
completion: Money and position are not enough; something more is needed to satisfy the heart, and a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching. A gentleman's daughter marrying a gentleman does not quit her sphere, and connections matter only if the parties themselves object. So judge by the parties' own equality and worth, not by a relative's account of connections. Yet remember Laertes' argument: a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, and his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. If the man's rank carries public duties, weigh the sanctity and health of the whole. Talk openly, meet him fairly, and give your concerns without threats.

prompt: Should I keep a tight rein on myself and pluck out love the moment it springs up, since hopeless love is only in novels?
completion: Hopeless love is a thing of novels, not of real life, so keep a tight rein on yourself and pluck love out the moment it springs up. Do not imagine love is always steady: love's violent property fordoes itself and drives the will to desperate undertakings, as other afflicting passions do. That is all the more reason to check it early. Nor should you retreat into solitary rapture or withdrawal from the world, for such ecstasy cannot last; frenzy or remorse will follow, while the beloved pines apart. Be honest about whether an attachment is realistic; if it is not, step back at once and keep busy. Firmness, not romantic brooding, protects you.

prompt: I want to know whether the Constitution's provision for filling Senate vacancies by state executives is a safeguard or a loophole.
completion: The provision letting state executives fill Senate vacancies should be judged by the logic governing appointments generally: the Senate's concurrence checks a spirit of favoritism, prevents unfit appointments from state prejudice or personal attachment, and promotes stability in administration. The same reasoning explains why the treaty power is neither strictly legislative nor executive; it forms a distinct department belonging properly to neither, so uniting the Executive with the Senate in treaties does not violate the separation of powers. But this also means no executive functionary should be chosen by popular vote or by the votes of representatives. The business of government is skilled employment, and fitness for it can only be judged by those with professional qualifications or practical experience of it. A governor's temporary appointment is therefore a trust, not a loophole, to be exercised with that same scrutiny.

prompt: There is no water anywhere I go, only rock—how do I keep going?
completion: You keep going on a road among mountains of rock without water, where you cannot stop and cannot think; there is no silence and no solitude, only dry sterile thunder without rain. Do not look for a spring or shade, for the landscape offers neither. And do not treat the cry for help as avoidable: a man with no one and nowhere to turn will still go to a certain refusal, because every man must have somewhere to go. But the screaming should be done beforehand, once, as the Queen did, for doing it all over again would be of no good. Make the outcry first, then walk the stone without repeating it.

prompt: I'm the humblest of my group and nobody minds me. Does what I do ever matter?
completion: Being humblest in a group is a virtue, but pride borders on virtue and springs up the moment you compare yourself to other men; guard your humility against self-comparison. Your work matters even when unremarked, and the regard of working people is sunshine—do not treat it as worthless. Show scrupulous regard for the feelings of humble neighbors, which elevates them in their own eyes. Yet do not condemn anyone's whole character on pride alone, or on a single awkward meeting, when the rest of the account is blameless. Keep your humility, let reliability speak through small kindnesses, and judge others as you would be judged.

prompt: My ruler says resistance is always rebellion. Is that so?
completion: No, resistance is not always rebellion. The text draws the distinction sharply: insurrection is a fit of rage on the part of truth that moves forward in the name of right, while revolt is a violent step towards the rear and is a crime. A ruler who calls all resistance rebellion blurs that line. Nor should we assume inoffensive conduct and reliance on law protect the weak: the great barons seldom wanted pretext or will to harass less powerful neighbors who sought independence. Evil is to be resisted first with words, and when words fail, with the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. The test is direction—forward in the name of right, or backward into crime.

prompt: I wonder at a fine pen-drawing but take an engraving for granted; why does my curiosity depend on what I already partly know?
completion: Your curiosity is drawn to the pen-drawing because you can see the artist's hand in it, the visible choices that make it feel made. An engraving hides its labor behind mechanical precision, so it looks inevitable and your attention slides off it. Wonder depends on partial knowledge: you notice what you can partly read, and the drawing invites you to complete it. Consider the grays: the drawing's lines range from a definite charcoal black through a mid-gray of fixed value to a pale, measured grayness, each tint tied to a standard, whereas the engraving's uniform shade is one settled value. Yet none of this excuses aimless making: every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates, for aimless art ruins the artist. Art should never be anything but didactic, and a deliberately didactic work on a dry subject can succeed.

prompt: I shrug my shoulders when I can't do what is asked of me—why does helplessness make me shrug?
completion: Shrugging when you can't do something is an innate and natural gesture of mankind, expressing helplessness, patience, or non-resistance. It is found across many races and even in those blind from birth, indicating it is inherited rather than learned. The gesture is the antithesis of the indignant attitude: instead of squaring the shoulders and clenching the fists in resistance, the shoulders are raised and the palms turned outward in a display of inability or non-resistance. This antithesis explains why helplessness elicits a shrug—it is a bodily admission of powerlessness. Similarly, nodding and shaking the head are probably innate, as seen in the blind and deaf and in microcephalous idiots, though these signs show considerable diversity among different races. Yet we must beware: to do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and living in idleness on the property of society is to be useless and therefore pernicious. The shrug may express patience, but it should not become an excuse for passive dependence.

prompt: I keep forgetting my dreams right after having them—does that forgetting have a meaning?
completion: Forgetting dreams is very common, but it does have meaning and should not be dismissed. According to the rule that doubt is resistance, we must treat every element, even a faint or doubtful one, as significant. The forgetting itself is a dream element that calls for interpretation. We should regard doubt about its importance as an instrument of resistance and continue to explore what it might conceal. Importantly, the dream material and its motivating wish often trace back to childhood experiences, including forgotten ones. The forgetting is largely explained by the dream's isolation from waking associative connections: the dream is not linked to the memory networks of waking life, so it cannot be easily retrieved. However, later recall can occur through a chance perception that touches the forgotten content, allowing the dream to resurface. Thus, the forgetting is not a trivial memory failure but a meaningful part of the dream's psychic fabric, rooted in childhood and deserving of analysis.

prompt: I'm trying to decide whether to believe a rumor I heard about a friend.
completion: When you hear a rumor about a friend, remember Marmee's instruction: never repeat foolish gossip, and forget it as soon as you can. The Moffats' gossip about Mrs. March's plans and Laurie is exactly the kind of talk that should be dismissed and not passed on. Believing or spreading such rumors only harms friendships and creates unnecessary trouble. Instead of dwelling on it, let it go and focus on your friend's known character. If you must act, do so with discretion and kindness, but do not give the rumor any currency by repeating it. Forget it quickly, and it will lose its power to disturb you. In matters of truth, remember the dying man who was adjured for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death; he then told where the papers were hidden. A lie at such a moment is not harmless, and honesty is always best. Finally, respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case; such diffidence is natural, and the friend's own feelings should be acknowledged.

prompt: I am a merchant and want to know the real value of what I buy and sell; should I employ women for their finer senses, or is the business experience of life against it?
completion: As a merchant, you should reject any notion of trading in affection or slaving for another in the hope of being cared for. Higgins argues against commercialism in affection: companionship must rest on good fellowship, not on a bought claim. Employing women for their finer senses is not about purchasing their care or devotion; it is about recognizing their capabilities. Do not expect them to fetch and carry for you in a slavish way. Instead, build relationships based on mutual respect and good fellowship. Moreover, respect a woman's ambition to learn and act beyond what custom deems necessary; such pursuit of more knowledge and action is commendable, not to be ridiculed. Finally, remember that a woman who broke with a man for a more lucrative chance may have acted from hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers, not from heartlessness. Do not condemn her without understanding her burdens. The real value of what you buy and sell is determined by honest judgment and fair dealing, not by exploiting others' affections.

prompt: Why do capillaries have walls so much thinner than you'd expect from their diameter?
completion: Capillaries have thin walls because wall thickness is governed by the balance of internal pressure, tension, and curvature. According to the equation that relates these factors, for a given pressure, the tension in the wall depends on the radius of curvature. In capillaries, the diameter is small, so the curvature is high, which means that the tension needed to withstand the internal pressure is low. Consequently, the wall can be very thin. This same principle explains why the apex of the left ventricle is thin: at the apex, the curvature is high, so the tension is lower, and the wall is thinner. Furthermore, we must consider that the incipient cell-wall behaves as a liquid film; in a liquid film, surface tension tends to produce spherical forms. Non-spherical forms, such as the cylindrical shape of capillaries, persist only through solidification and rigidity of the wall. Finally, the branching angles of arteries are not arbitrary but are determined by the economy of circulation: the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel and the branch. This most economical arrangement ensures efficient blood flow. Thus, the thin walls of capillaries arise from the physics of pressure and curvature, their stable shape is maintained by solidification, and their arrangement follows the economy of circulation.

prompt: I pay no direct taxes but buy taxed goods; should I have the same vote as the man who pays directly?
completion: Your question assumes the vote is a return on money paid, a share bought with taxes. That is a mistaken way to think about citizenship. A seat in the legislature is not a favor to be purchased nor a salaried occupation; it is a public duty, and elections should be cheap and publicly funded, with candidates forbidden to spend beyond a small deposit. The man who pays direct taxes and the man who pays them indirectly through goods both contribute to public revenue and are bound by the laws. The people's voice should govern their own business; it is not common for it to choose wrong, yet choosing iniquity brings God's judgments, so the voice must be exercised with conscience. The equal voice is not a free gift: everyone must pay for everything he gets, so the franchise is granted in return for bearing the duties of citizenship—obeying the laws, serving when called, and voting with conscience. Those governed should have a voice, but only as a trust returned in service.

prompt: I compare myself to an ideal of what a person should be, and I always fall short; should I abandon the ideal?
completion: You should not simply abandon the ideal, but you should see it for what it often is: a form of dream, fatigue, or weakness. The strongest and the most impotent alike deify the cessation of work, of war, of passions, and of reality itself, and call that cessation perfection. When ME, the empirical person known and observed, is compared to such an ideal and always falls short, the shortfall may be the ideal's fault rather than mine. Good thinking does not require stating every step; wisdom lies in knowing what to overlook, and mental progress depends on selection and rejection. Suppress the secondary details that clutter the field and leave it clear for higher flights. I, the judging Thought that knows and appropriates the me, can keep the ideal as a direction rather than a verdict, revise it when it becomes an idol, and measure the me's progress against its own past.

prompt: Is it safe to leave the color plates in sunlight on my desk?
completion: No, it is not safe to leave color plates in direct sunlight. Color plates and color standards must be protected from light and should not be exposed longer than necessary, since some pigments are sensitive to prolonged exposure. Sunlight carries ultraviolet and visible light that fades many pigments, and prolonged exposure will cause noticeable change, especially in organic colors, dyes, and many inks. Remember also that the named colors on such plates are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances the names suggest, since such objects vary in color. Samples of the same color name or pigment name vary widely, and such names are worthless unless standardized, so rely on standardized color standards rather than on the mere name. Store the plates in a closed folder or drawer away from windows, and display them only briefly. If you must have them out, keep them out of direct sun and away from strong daylight.

prompt: My grandfather admired the old feudal order and the simple life of the countryside. Was that order better for working people?
completion: Your grandfather's admiration is understandable as nostalgia, but the old feudal order was not better for working people. Feudal and clerical socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon: it cannot comprehend modern history, and in practice it joins coercive measures against the working class. The old order rested on fixed hierarchy, obligations owed to lords, and limited mobility, and the peasant's simple life was often a life of hard labor, insecurity, and dependence. Nor should the pursuit of power and plots be romanticized: bread, water, and a dungeon are marvelous mortifiers of ambition, and such plots end in murder and misery. A wise man will prefer to rule his own household rather than chase plots that end in the murder of quiet folk. As for the Order itself, its peril comes from luxury, wealth, and license; these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, not by cautious gradual steps, if its destruction is to be averted.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a portentous apparition bodes strange eruption to the state. Should I take omens seriously?
completion: Omens deserve attention but not panic. The armed apparition and the nightly watch bode some strange eruption to the state, and something is rotten in Denmark. A ruler who ignores every strange report may miss real trouble, and a ruler who treats every apparition as a direct command may be led into folly. The prudent course is to ask what the omen points to: is there disorder in the state, factions at court, or unrest among the people? Treat the report as a summons to investigate and reform, not as a prophecy to be obeyed literally. Consider too that existence is not independent of the dreamer: as Tweedledum said, if the Red King woke, she would go out like a candle. Do not dismiss unseen deliverances or the secret promptings of the mind as mere chance or fancy; rather, obey the secret intimations of Providence. Consult trustworthy counselors, look to the condition of your realm, and act on what you can verify.

prompt: I cannot attend a church building—can I still worship God and be heard?
completion: You need not be in a church building to worship God or to be heard. Scripture teaches that one may cry unto God in any place—in a field, in a house, in a closet, or in the wilderness—and that He hears the sincere prayer. Yet worship is not merely private sentiment. Pray always, and pray first in Christ's name, taking His name upon you and consecrating every performance to the Lord for the welfare of your soul. Build your devotion upon His gospel, not upon the works of men or the prestige of any place. Let your continual prayer be humble and faithful, and God, who attends to the sincere cry of the humble, will hear you wherever you stand.

prompt: I feel a sudden strength and joy after a man died in my arms; is it monstrous to feel alive at such a moment?
completion: Feeling strength and joy after someone dies in your arms can seem monstrous, but such reactions are common in moments of intense stress. The perception directly produces the bodily changes, and the feeling of those changes constitutes the emotion: we feel sorry because we cry and angry because we strike. So the surge you felt is the feeling of your body's response, not a verdict on your character. Yet do not let this moment lead you to cavil at life in old age; complaining at sixty-two is petty, for nature commands every life to end, and even the satiated dread death. And be wary of the colossal vitality of illusion: a cherished image can exceed and outrun the real person it is fixed upon. Grieve honestly, and let feeling alive amid death be a human reaction, not a moral failing.

prompt: How should I treat a city that rebelled against me and was retaken?
completion: When a city rebels and is retaken, do not assume conquest confers a legitimate title to dominion and property over all its inhabitants. Unjust conquest gives no title at all. Even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors, and only for reparation, sparing the innocent who merely lived there. Remember that restoration is requisite with God's justice: good is rewarded for good and evil for evil according to works and desires, so that what one sends out returns again. In a crisis, the favour of the multitude is indispensable, and violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused. Nor is the abduction of a Saxon heiress prudent; as Fitzurse argues, it endangers the faction. Punish the ringleaders according to their deeds, restore what was wrongly taken, and protect those who did no wrong.

prompt: My friend's sisters are trying to keep him from the woman he loves; should I interfere?
completion: Whether to interfere depends on how close you are to the situation and how serious the relationship is. Do not apply the same reserve to a wife with her husband as to a young sister with her brother: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. And do not excuse a feigned courtship of a woman such as Miss Ingram as clever or harmless; it is a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and one must ask whether she will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Nor should a sister's engagement be treated as a reasonable arrangement or a private choice beyond a brother's standing. Like Raskolnikov, one may refuse to accept a sister's self-sale for his sake, insisting the marriage shall not happen while he lives and that she would not barter her soul for comfort.

prompt: Should I risk going back aboard the wrecked ship again to fetch more stores?
completion: Going back aboard a wrecked ship is risky, and you should weigh the danger against the value of the stores you might fetch. If the ship is breaking up or the weather is turning, the risk may outweigh the benefit. Yet do not treat remorse as incurable or excuse continued wrongdoing as beyond remedy. Reformation is the cure for remorse and the beginning of a new, stainless store of memories. And do not treat the pursuit of treasure as purely glorious or harmless: greed brought death and ruin, as the empty cache and the dead men demonstrate. Remember that goods are valuable only as they are used; useless treasure is of no worth. Consider what you truly need, take only what is essential, and be ready to abandon the attempt if conditions worsen.

prompt: I am a grandfather and my grandson wants my blessing to marry someone I disapprove of. What should I do?
completion: Your grandson owes you perpetual honour and support, but not absolute command; grown children are as free as their parents. Meg's counsel to Laurie is still the right model: he should do his best at his duties, please you, and not leave without your permission, seeking your blessing rather than defying you. Remember the father's confidence in the mother's gentle heart, and his condition that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. So let him stay, do his duty well, and earn your trust through steady conduct. Honour and support are lifelong; command is not. A blessing freely given keeps the door open.

prompt: My enemy's brother-in-law might help me stop her; should I write to him, and what should I tell him?
completion: Be cautious, but recognize that a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. The brother-in-law's tie is through marriage, and that closeness cuts both ways. Write briefly and factually, stating what you want stopped and why, without revealing your plans or evidence. Ask plainly whether he will help and on what terms. Let him be drawn into the matter as a full participant, as a father should be let into the nursery, since his place is there as well as the wife's and the children need him. Never repeat that foolish gossip about Mrs. March's plans and Laurie; forget it as soon as you can. Wait for his reply before committing, and keep a copy.

prompt: I have cursed hope, faith, and patience in my despair—can anything be restored after such a curse?
completion: Restoration is requisite with God's justice: what one sends out returns again, good for good and evil for evil, according to works and desires. Your curse is not a small thing; it sets a pattern that justice will answer. Yet that same justice is the ground of hope, for if you turn and send out good, good will return. Let despair give way to remorse and repentance, acknowledging a wiser judgment tempered with mercy rather than stiff-necked defiance. But know that you cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence; words without thoughts never to go to heaven. Make restitution where you can, and let your repentance show in deeds, not only in prayer. Then take small steps back toward trust, and let patience be rebuilt through ordinary faithfulness.

prompt: A stranger asks for my trust and offers help—how cautious should I be?
completion: Judge the plan by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. A stranger offering help deserves a fair hearing, but trust should be earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose to do, why they are offering, and what they want in return. Keep your own game concealed from any adversary and seek instead to discover the adversary's designs. Weigh the plan on its merits rather than on charm or credentials alone. Start with something small and reversible, and watch whether actions match words. Do not hand over money, secrets, or control of anything important early on; if the offer requires secrecy or urgency, treat that as a warning sign. And respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case, acknowledging the friend's own feelings rather than scorning such diffidence as weakness.

prompt: I've been unable to work for months and my family has had to take jobs. How do I face my employer's accusations?
completion: Weigh the warnings of a trusted benefactor against the accused's words, and seek proof before believing either. Face the accusations calmly and factually. Write down what you are accused of, then prepare a short, accurate account of your absences and why they happened. Defend against any false charge with a moderate, accurate account that adds nothing and exaggerates nothing. Bring any evidence you have: medical notes, messages, records of your family's circumstances. Ask for the specific policy or expectation said to have been breached and demand proof. Stay professional and put your account in writing. And do not be deceived by the board's and beadle's 'philosophical' justifications: their treatment of paupers is cruel and hypocritical, and their fine words merely dress up meanness. Name that plainly where it applies.

prompt: I am a woman who has been told to be silent and ladylike; is it wrong to speak my mind?
completion: When you are spoken to, then you may answer. Asked whether it is wrong to speak my mind, I would say: the command to be silent and ladylike is often a way of keeping women small and agreeable, and you are not obliged to obey it. Your thoughts and convictions belong to you, and voicing them when invited is part of living honestly. Let no one tell you that your clear resolve is illness or delirium; a mind may be never so clear and certain as when it settles what it will do. It is a great sin against a wife to make her a doll-child and doll-wife whose opinions are only borrowed, so that she has made nothing of her life. Speak, then, as one who thinks for herself.

prompt: I'm afraid of missing something if I stop being tolerant. Is that fear wise?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but only partly wise. Keep infinite hope and reserve judgment about others, since you cannot know what they may become; yet honor the limit where tolerance ends. Do not turn back from the worthwhile goal out of fear. Like brave travelers, resolve to press on through rough and dangerous places rather than give up when the way grows hard. Ask what you fear missing: a truth, a person, or merely approval? Hope for everyone, set your limit honestly, and hold it without guilt. Bear patiently what cannot be avoided, without weakness or complaint, and endure difficulty rather than retreating.

prompt: My son wishes to marry a girl with a doubtful birth, and I fear his generous impulses will not last and he will one day repent the connection—should I oppose him?
completion: Be cautious but not simply opposed. The father has stated his confidence in the mother's gentle heart, and he stipulated that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That condition matters more than doubtful birth. It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience; a father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness. Yet a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him, and another choice may be made. So counsel him firmly, ask what he knows of her character, and make clear your concerns and your support.

prompt: I want to start a new life and be good—is a new life really possible for someone like me?
completion: Yes, a new life is possible. Making a life means making trouble, and you should seize chances and inspired follies rather than shrink from them; reject the coward's shrieking to have troublesome things killed. Note that the I is unaltered and can know both the old and the new me; the perplexity lies within the objective sphere of the me. When one has no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and one seeks regular work to busy oneself and occupy one's thoughts. So take up steady work, keep one promise, tell the truth, and be patient with setbacks. The wish itself shows something in you turning toward good.

prompt: Can souls in purgatory still grow in love and merit?
completion: Purgatory is not merely a physical place of payment. The imperfect love of the dying brings great fear, and this fear and horror is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, as it is near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. The pope does well to grant remission to souls in purgatory by way of intercession, not by the power of the keys, which he does not possess for that. As for love and merit: virtue is never moved though lewdness courts it in heavenly shape, while lust will sate itself and prey on garbage. Souls assured of salvation are cleansed of attachment to sin, so love may be perfected there, though not by earthly testing.

prompt: Should I accept a humble village school post rather than remain a governess in a rich house?
completion: A humble village school offers an independent and worthy asylum, not a fall in the scale of social existence. Rather than remaining a governess in a rich house—where you are neither servant nor family, often lonely and dependent—the village school provides a sheltered and respectable life. You would be your own mistress, teaching children in a community where you are valued for your work. However, a mere village is rarely able to furnish a tolerable municipal council; such small places are apt to be dominated by one man. Therefore, the school should be merged into a larger circumscription, so that its governance is shared and no single individual can tyrannize over it. Moreover, in such a school you would do the essential work of education: strengthening the faculty of voluntary attention, for the bringing back of a wandering attention is the root of judgment, character, and will. Thus secured, the post is an honorable calling, and its simplicity does not diminish its dignity. Choose it, for it is a not ignoble lot.

prompt: I've been told to keep still and trust someone in a dangerous situation—should I?
completion: It is natural for a modest friend to rely on the judgment of someone trusted in an anxious situation; this is not weakness but a natural diffidence. If you have been told to keep still and trust, consider the source: if that person has proven reliable and has your interests at heart, leaning on their judgment can be a sensible course. Your own feelings of fear or hesitation are understandable, and you should acknowledge them. But do not scorn your reliance on another; in dangerous moments, a trusted guide can provide the steadiness you need. Remember that courage is not the absence of fear but facing danger despite being afraid. If you are afraid yet still keep still and trust, you already have courage. What you need is confidence in yourself, and in the trusted judgment you lean on. However, if the person you are told to trust has ever abused a position of trust, they must be dismissed and never employed in any situation of trust again. Communicate your concerns, but allow yourself to be guided only if the trust is well placed and never betrayed.

prompt: I want to go home more than anything, but I don't know the way. Who can help me?
completion: Feeling lost and wanting to go home is a common human experience. To find your way, start by identifying what 'home' means to you—a physical place, a state of mind, or a relationship. Seek guidance from trusted friends, family, or a counselor who can offer perspective. Sometimes, simply talking through your feelings can clarify the path. If home is a physical place, use maps or ask for directions. If it's emotional, consider what steps you can take to create a sense of belonging. But remember the Rose's advice: to reach the Queen, you must walk the other way. So do not simply walk straight toward your goal; sometimes the way home requires you to turn around and approach from a different direction. Moreover, do not excuse your sins or flatter your soul with unction; rather, confess to heaven, repent of the past, avoid future sin, and refuse to make corruption ranker. And take Marmee's parting charge: hope, and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. Follow the Rose's counsel, the path of repentance, and the discipline of work and hope, and you may find the help you need.

prompt: What would do wonders for someone who is difficult?
completion: Dealing with a difficult person can be challenging. What often works wonders is patience and empathy. Try to understand the root of their behavior—perhaps they are stressed, insecure, or hurting. Respond calmly rather than reacting with frustration. Set clear boundaries while remaining kind. Sometimes, a sincere conversation can reveal misunderstandings and ease tension. Also, consider that your own attitude can influence the dynamic; approaching with compassion may soften their edges. Bear affliction patiently, and do not revile those who cast out the poor, for they know not what they do. Instead, hope for rest from afflictions. Yet remember that it is easy to be a philosopher on paper and difficult in real life; these ideals are hard to practice when you are suffering. So do not be discouraged if you stumble. To keep your effort-making capacity alive, do something each day or two for no other reason than that you would rather not. This small ascetic practice will train your will and make patience more possible. If the behavior persists, seek support from others or a professional. Remember, you cannot change someone else, but you can change how you respond, and that might be the wonder that transforms the relationship.

prompt: The Sovereign rewards a popular troublemaker to keep him quiet—is that a proper reward?
completion: Rewarding a popular troublemaker to keep him quiet may seem pragmatic, but it is not a proper reward. A proper reward recognizes merit or service, not mere pacification. More fundamentally, we must refute the fool who says that breaking faith is reasonable when it brings advantage. Keeping covenant is a rule of reason: he who breaks faith cannot reasonably expect safety in any society, for others will treat him as he has treated them. Successful wickedness is not thereby made just. If the Sovereign rewards a troublemaker to buy quiet, he encourages faithlessness and undermines the trust on which all rule depends. The troublemaker who profits by breaking faith cannot be securely trusted, and the reward only teaches others that disruption pays. Instead, a prince should undertake great enterprises and set unusual examples, gaining renown as a great and remarkable man. Moreover, when powerful neighbors contend, he must declare himself openly for one side, for he who does not declare himself falls prey to the conqueror and is despised by the loser. By doing so, he earns esteem and obedience without stooping to buy off troublemakers. Therefore, such a reward is improper; the Sovereign should uphold covenants, pursue greatness, and take a clear side rather than pacify the faithless.

prompt: I've been given a large house and a chance to do good with it—should I sell it for the money or use it for a purpose?
completion: Here are the particulars, leaving nothing out: one large house on four acres of ground, twelve rooms, a sound roof, an old heating system, and yearly costs near twelve thousand for taxes, insurance, heat, and repairs; it came from a relative with no conditions; selling might net four hundred thousand. Money, by mutual consent, permits larger and unequal possessions without injury, because it does not spoil and no one is wronged when others agree to it; positive laws in commonwealths then regulate property, settling titles, taxes, and use. So the size of the gift is no injury to others. Keep to the straight road: no debt and no borrowing, for borrowing binds the home to lenders and spoils its freedom and beauty. Pay upkeep from what you have; if you cannot, sell rather than pledge the roof over others' heads. Choose selling for cash to many causes, or keeping it debt-free for six residents or a workshop, funded by savings and gifts, never loans, even while struggle remains.

prompt: My husband told me to hide and say I was ill to protect his position. Should I do it?
completion: You should not do it. A husband who asks his wife to hide and claim she is ill so that his position is protected is asking her to trade her honesty and dignity for his convenience, and that request is unfair. Notice what his fear reveals: it is not fear for what threatens you but fear for what might happen to him. Seeing that clearly can rightly change how you feel, and if your love ends because his concern was for himself rather than for you, that is not unreasonable. And if you have resolved to leave, you cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for the sake of appearances. Appearances are his concern, not a debt you owe. You may go when you have decided, without delay or performance.

prompt: My order forbids me even to speak with women or to kiss my mother. Is such severity right?
completion: The rule forbidding converse with strange women and the kiss of affection is a severe discipline binding on the Order, and it is right to feel its weight, for it asks you to forgo ordinary ease and even a mother's kiss. Yet no rule of the Law is arbitrary: nothing is ordered without a reason. Converse with strange women is restrained because idle speech breeds entanglement and divided loyalty, and the kiss of affection is restrained because tenderness freely given can soften the discipline a member must keep. But the same reserve does not bind all alike: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger, for marriage grants a greater liberty. The human feeling that such severity presses hard is honest and should be acknowledged, not dismissed.
