Forgive the person while abhorring the deed, so that revenge does not take hold of your heart. Focus on what you can do now to improve and help others. Over time, with reflection and positive action, you can forgive yourself and move forward.

prompt: I boasted of capturing a criminal, but it turns out I only shot a boy and my pistol held nothing but powder and paper—how do I face the shame?
completion: First, recognize that your boast was based on a misunderstanding. You didn't actually capture a criminal; you shot a boy, and your pistol was harmless. The shame you feel is natural, but it's important to separate your intention from the outcome. You didn't mean to harm an innocent, but you were careless. Apologize to the boy and his family, and take responsibility. Learn from this: don't inflate a doubtful act into glory, but weigh the evidence honestly as Giles himself comes to do. The one appalled by the crime concludes that an honest life is best, turns his back on the past, and succeeds through a good purpose and contented disposition. Moreover, the embarrassment dream is an exhibition dream from childhood, with the shame as the reaction of the second psychic instance and the strangers as a wish-opposite. Seek forgiveness from those affected and from yourself. Over time, by acting honestly and humbly, you can rebuild your reputation and self-respect.

prompt: I feel that life is the greatest art and I want to make my own life a masterpiece—is that a worthy aim?
completion: Yes, it's a worthy aim. Life is the greatest art because it's the raw material we shape. Making your life a masterpiece means living with intention, pursuing excellence, and creating something meaningful. It's about self-improvement, relationships, and contributions. However, be careful not to treat life as mere imitation or idle amusement; rather, present art as the representation of life as it ought to be, in dreams, and insist that a work embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant. Strive for a lofty idea and mean it seriously. Also, remember that the supreme happiness of life is the certainty of being loved for one's own sake, and that love supplies what blindness takes away; certainty of love outweighs the loss of sight. Yet the artistic calling requires the strength to endure want, disillusionment, the hatred of friends, and dissatisfaction with oneself. So, aim high, but balance ambition with love and authenticity.

prompt: Can the pope grant greater graces than the Gospel and gifts of healing?
completion: No, the pope cannot grant greater graces than the Gospel and gifts of healing. The Gospel and gifts of healing are directly from God and are the highest spiritual gifts. The pope, as a human leader, can offer indulgences and pardons, but these are not greater than the fundamental graces of the Gospel. In fact, claiming that St. Peter as pope could not bestow greater graces is blasphemy, and any pope has greater graces at his disposal, namely the Gospel, powers, and gifts of healing. Moreover, whoever passes by a man in need and gives his money for pardons purchases not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. Those who believe themselves sure of salvation because of pardon letters will be condemned with their teachers, and assurance by letters of pardon is vain even if the pope staked his soul on it. So, while the pope has authority in the Church, he cannot surpass the graces given by God.

prompt: My conscience will not let me blame my brother for a severe choice that breaks my heart—what should I do?
completion: Your conscience is not a mood to be soothed but a law that, once understood, cannot be bargained with—yet do not mistake it for an infallible guide. Much of what feels like conscience is inherited, expressing the habits of generations whose conditions differed from ours, and the acquired part may be a very bad one under the influence of dogma. Examine it honestly, then obey what survives scrutiny, since a true conscience is implacable and must be obeyed even at great cost. If it will not let you blame your brother, do not blame him—not for comfort but from duty. This will cost you; you will stand in a hell where God is felt beside you. And before any sentence you pass on him, grant him, as Athos would, a final moment of prayer and reflection.

prompt: My friend is always singing and celebrating when there's work to be done—should I say something?
completion: She looks in the glass, hardly aware of her departed lover, and allows only the thought that it is done and she is glad it is over. She smooths her hair with an automatic hand. Yet a little kindness would do wonders, so let some be offered—quietly, without demand; putting her hair in papers, that small ordinary care, would do wonders too. And as a host should partake of the fare he sets before his guest, after the Eastern custom, so let whoever offers this kindness share in it himself, tasting what he gives so its wholesomeness is assured.

prompt: I'm leaving my friends behind and it breaks my heart. How do I say goodbye?
completion: Goodbyes hurt most when they feel final, so don't wait to speak well of your friends only when they are gone. Show friendship to people while they are alive: tell them now, plainly and specifically, what they have meant, and back the words with time—one more meal, one more walk, one more honest conversation. Yet do not treat this parting as a problem to be forced. Heaven will direct the issue, and fate cries out to be followed; go where you are called, trusting the outcome to a wiser hand, even when friends urge you to stay. And remember the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Knock not, force not; say your goodbye gently and let it be.

prompt: I left out a lot of details in my explanation. Does it matter?
completion: Whether it matters depends on what the details were for. If your explanation was meant to inform a decision, omissions can mislead, so correct the record—but do not simply yield to whoever presses you, or agree for the sake of peace. Yielding without conviction is no compliment to the understanding of either party. Judge the plan by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it; a sound point stands even from a doubtful source. At the same time, reserve judgment, remembering that advantages and decencies are unequally distributed. Correct what could cause real misunderstanding, and let the rest go with tolerance.

prompt: I have made a covenant with a man who has not yet performed his part and there is no power over us both; am I bound to perform first?
completion: The bonds of words are too weak to hold men without the fear of a coercive power. In the natural condition, where there is no power over you both, a covenant of mutual trust is void, since either may suspect the other and no common authority compels performance. Under a civil power that can compel performance, such covenants become obligatory. Nor treat Scripture or ecclesiastical decrees as binding laws by themselves: the books of Scripture are law only where the lawful civil power has made them so, and elsewhere are wholesome counsel. And if you are a sworn soldier of the Temple, remember that your vow binds you beyond what is lawful to other men: you must renounce ease, comforts, and natural affections, and pleasures lawful to others are forbidden to you by your calling.

prompt: Should I marry for money to escape poverty, or wait to be loved and chosen by a good man?
completion: It is understandable to want relief from poverty, but poverty is a burden to bear cheerfully, not an injustice to resent; count first the riches money cannot buy. Do not marry for money, and do not let anyone treat marriage as a mere arrangement for labor or duty, or prize you as a soldier prizes a good weapon. Marriage without mutual love is monstrous. Marmee hoped her daughters would be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. So build what skills and friendships you can, stop complaining of what you lack, and wait to be loved and chosen rather than to make a dash in the world.

prompt: My husband says he can become a different man. Should I stay and see?
completion: Promises of change are common when a marriage is strained, and hope is natural. Remember that a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, yet it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. But a husband who cares only to save the remains and the appearance, and who forbids his wife to bring up the children, has not preserved a real marriage. If you no longer love your husband, though he has always been kind, you must say so plainly and cannot remain with him. Weigh evidence, not words, set clear boundaries, and protect yourself and any children if there is danger.

prompt: My companion is wounded and of a faith I was taught to scorn—am I bound to shelter and tend him?
completion: You are not bound by his creed but by common humanity and your pledged word. A wounded companion deserves shelter and care regardless of the faith you were taught to scorn. Abandoning him would break a promise of mercy given to an enemy and would show you a coward, not a man of courage. Nor need you hate his denying, scoffing spirit: the scoffer is least wearisome and serves to stir man, who is too prone to shirk activity. Those who put their trust in God are supported in trials and afflictions and lifted up at the last day. Tend him, and let your kindness speak louder than inherited prejudice.

prompt: Should I be kind to a man who has been cruel to me because others ask it?
completion: Kindness asked of you by others is not the same as trust, and cruelty should not be rewarded with unlimited patience. Yet necessary harshness is cruelty only to be kind, so ask whether his words aimed at your good. Be civil and refuse revenge, but set limits, for worse remains behind. Prize a kind and tender heart above mere cleverness, as the Woodman prized his loving heart. And apply to yourself the same severity you apply to others, lest your justice become injustice. Let others' requests guide but not govern you, and forgive in your own time without renewed closeness.

prompt: Should I refuse to see the man who once loved me because I am ashamed of what I have become?
completion: Shame is a poor reason to refuse an old friend who once loved you. Do not hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners. Do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife, and do not despair. Firmly resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present career steadily, and hew out a new road when Fortune blocks the old one. Do your own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for a lover.

prompt: I want to judge the Constitution on the evidence of truth alone; how should I guard against impressions from other quarters?
completion: To judge the Constitution by truth alone, strip away everything secondhand. The credit of ancient authors is insufficient for matters of right; test every claim by reason and Scripture alone. Ask whether a proposition follows from evident principles or the plain sense of Scripture; if it rests only on custom or the authority of names, set it aside. Guard against prejudice and interest, and hold judgment open until the grounds are clear. In matters of wrongdoing, hear witnesses and give formal conviction and sentence by lawful judges before any execution; allow no witnesses but the judges themselves only where the fact was committed in their sight. Remember that analysis requires separate acquaintance with the element: what you have never experienced apart remains fused in an unanalyzable total, so do not pretend to resolve it by mere reasoning. Thus reason and Scripture keep your judgment free and just.

prompt: Should I at least set my lands in order before the end?
completion: I sit on the shore, fishing, with the arid plain behind me. Shall I at least set my lands in order? These fragments I have shored against my ruins. I will not pretend to a completed restoration or raise a whole edifice; I gather what remains and set it in order as best I may. Where someone has erred or partaken unworthily, I do not cast them out but minister unto them and pray for them, hoping they will return and repent and be healed. Yet I will not excuse the corruption of the Order: luxury, wealth, and license are the causes of its peril, and these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, not by cautious gradual steps, if its destruction is to be averted. Settle your affairs, attend to your soul, and meet the end with what fragments you can gather.

prompt: I'm afraid I've become ordinary and lost something magical. Is it too late?
completion: It is not too late. The mistake of fancying oneself an advanced destroyer arises only among ordinary people; they never go very far, and they castigate themselves or are thrashed for it. Do not mistake your worry for proof that you have lost the magic. Never look into the future; never admit the thought of old age or death. Accept what comes, keep heart and mind busy, and begin again with small, deliberate acts. Yet watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan, lest you be led captive by the devil. Seek out what once felt alive and practice it without demanding immediate results; magic is rarely a single dramatic event but a habit of attention.

prompt: My master rules his household with absolute power. Is that political government?
completion: No, absolute rule of a household is not political government. Political power is a trust for making and executing laws for the preservation of property and the public good; it is not an arbitrary or private dominion. Its legislative is bound to promulgated standing laws, not to arbitrary decrees over lives or fortunes. It cannot tax without the consent of the people, and its delegated lawmaking power cannot be transferred to others. A master's absolute power over his household is domestic and private, akin to a father's authority, and it is not legislation for a people. Where such a dependency must be governed, it should be governed through a delegated body of comparatively permanent character, allowing the changeable home administration only a right of inspection and a negative voice.

prompt: I want to be both a devoted parent and a ruthless careerist, but I can't; how do I choose which self to stake myself on?
completion: You cannot be both fully, so choose, and choose firmly. Resist every temptation to look back; do not dwell on the past or yield to vacillating fears. Pursue the present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despair. Yet the child in your care comes first: protecting and loving the child is the duty that justifies self-sacrifice, and the child's happiness is the object of your life even at the price of your own. In the household, let neither parent interfere with the other's discipline or rescue the child mid-lesson; the child must learn to mind. Indulgence spoils his temper as harshness would break his spirit, so hold a steady course together.

prompt: I gave way to violent gestures in my rage and felt my anger grow—should I restrain the outward signs?
completion: Yes, you should restrain the outward signs of your anger. The perception directly produces bodily changes, and the feeling of those changes constitutes the emotion: we feel angry because we strike, not strike because we are angry. Giving free expression to an emotion by outward signs intensifies it, while repressing those signs softens it. So he who gives way to violent gestures increases his rage, and he who does not control the signs of fear experiences it more. Moreover, with repetition, the diffusive wave narrows and efficiency grows at the cost of feeling, leading to the calm of the experienced man. Thus, by restraining outward signs, you can reduce anger's intensity.

prompt: I forgot something important and made a slip of speech—is that connected to the same psychology as my dreams?
completion: Yes, forgetting something important and making a slip of speech can be connected to dream psychology. Both involve unconscious processes. Dreams are forgotten because they lack ties to waking memory, but recall can occur through a perception that touches the forgotten content. Moreover, a dream injunction to tell the doctor is a sign of great resistance to the confession, often followed by forgetting the dream. Numbers and speeches in dreams are borrowed fragments joined for the dream's purposes, not original calculation or composition. Similarly, slips of speech can reveal hidden thoughts. So, these experiences share a common psychological basis.

prompt: I'm stuck on a problem and I keep jumping to the first solution that comes to mind.
completion: When stuck on a problem and jumping to the first solution, it helps to slow down and think more carefully. First, state the problem clearly as a definite question. Then, every suggested conclusion should be tested by its pertinence to that regulating end. Draw on analogous past experience and prior knowledge as the source of suggestions for clarifying the difficulty. Develop several rival possible explanations or courses of action and compare them before favoring one. This way, you avoid settling on a single suggestion without entertaining alternatives that might check a hasty conclusion. Remember that complex problems often require patience and iterative refinement.

prompt: I want to improve the stock of my countrymen; should I aim at producing some entirely new and superior type, or at encouraging those who most nearly conform to the existing central type?
completion: To improve the stock of your countrymen, it is better to encourage those who most nearly conform to the existing central type rather than aiming to produce an entirely new and superior type. Improvement is easiest toward the central type of the race, requiring only that the breed of those conforming most nearly to that type be encouraged and the breed of wide deviants restrained. We must refrain from imposing our own instincts as a universal criterion, acknowledging that different men and races may each be good of their kind. The multifarious variety of gifts is the moral and intellectual wealth of a nation, not something to be assimilated to one type. Moreover, small tradespeople, shopkeepers, handicraftsmen, and peasants sink into the proletariat as their small capital is swamped by competition and their skill rendered worthless.

prompt: Is there a smallest possible size for a living organism, and why can it not be indefinitely small?
completion: Yes, there is a smallest possible size for a living organism. It cannot be indefinitely small because of the physical constraints of cellular structures. Cells require a minimum volume to contain essential organelles and molecules for metabolism and reproduction. The sphere is the only surface enclosing space and the absolute minimal area, naturally assumed by homogeneous cells under symmetrical conditions. Growth is not always positive increase; loss of bulk and weight occurs in metamorphosis and old age, and this negative growth is part of the same phenomenon of rate. The skeleton is a continuum and muscle and bone are inseparably associated, so no change in one occurs without correlated change in the other. Thus, there is a lower bound to the size of living organisms.

prompt: Who should decide a dispute between the federal government and a state government over the limits of their authority?
completion: Such disputes should be decided by an independent Supreme Court, whose judgment in the last appeal is final and binding on every government and functionary. Neither the federal government nor a state may be judge in its own cause. But the Court must preside over a genuine federation, not a mere precarious alliance between governments: the federal authority must be able to enact laws binding directly on individual citizens and to execute them through its own officers and tribunals, rather than depending on state officials. A union of governments only, whose acts bind the states and are carried out through their officers, is a league, not a nation. Finally, Congress must have an ultimate power over the times, places, and manner of federal elections, as a means of self-preservation, so that the Union's own existence cannot be left exclusively to the State legislatures. Direct authority over citizens, a final judicial arbiter, and this electoral safeguard together secure the balance of the federal system.

prompt: I deliberate carefully before every moral choice, but I feel less certain and less good than people who act on instinct—why?
completion: Your unease is understandable, but it rests on a mistaken picture of instinct. Instinctive action is not a calculation of utility or the pursuit of some abstract purpose like self-preservation. It is a reflex response to a particular stimulus, performed for its own sake and shining with its own sufficient light, without foresight of the end. Nor is moral judgment merely habit, custom, or public opinion: its most characteristic form arises in unprecedented, lonely emergencies, where an inner oracle speaks, often contrary to popular approval, and rightness is not mere usualness. As for the origin of instincts, do not assume that acquired habits are inherited; the Lamarckian proofs are weak and largely explicable otherwise. Natural selection of accidental variations is the sounder account. Your deliberation, with its uncertainty, may thus reflect a sensibility that outruns both reflex and custom, and its doubt is the price of foresight, not a defect of character.

prompt: I was taught that red, green, and violet are the primary colors, but I can make red from orange and violet. How do I reconcile that?
completion: The apparent contradiction comes from mixing two different senses of "primary." Let us define terms clearly, since clear and standardized meanings are essential to understanding. "Primary" means, first, a color from which others can be mixed, and second, a fundamental sensation of the eye. Red, green, and violet are primary in the second sense. We should not discard established color usages, which have authority through long common use by zoologists and botanists; where those standards can be matched, they should be retained, even if imperfect. But be precise about the scheme: the circle is divided into thirty-six hues, with unequal numbers of intermediates—more between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. Pigments behave differently from sensations, which is why orange and violet can yield a red sensation. Used consistently, these defined terms reconcile your mixing with the old teaching.

prompt: What would a society without classes actually look like?
completion: A classless society would be one in which no group holds systematic economic or political power over another. But to see how it comes about, we must see all history as a history of class struggles: society is divided into oppressing and oppressed classes in constant opposition, and their contests end either in the revolutionary reconstitution of society or in the common ruin of the contending classes. Modern society is splitting increasingly into two great hostile camps, bourgeoisie and proletariat, directly facing each other—the bourgeoisie owning the means of production, the proletariat selling its labor. Classes cannot be reconciled; their opposition is structural. We should not romanticize the social scum, the 'dangerous class': it may be swept into a proletarian revolution, but by its conditions it is far more prepared to serve as a bribed tool of reactionary intrigue. A classless society would abolish this division, distributing resources according to need, organizing work cooperatively, and eliminating ruling groups and underclasses—not a conflict-free uniformity, but a society whose conflicts no longer map onto durable relations of domination.

prompt: I am a prince and I have been told that by indirections one finds directions out. Is it right to use deception to discover the truth?
completion: Deception is not always wrong, even for a prince. Polonius's argument deserves its due: by indirections one may find directions out. By windlasses and assays of bias—laying slight sullies and observing how a party closes with them—one may discover the truth of another's behavior that direct questioning would never reveal. Such indirect inquiry is a warranted way to learn what people really think and intend. But we should not demand unconditional exposure of oneself in every word: people say what they think only among equals and with good will; before the unfamiliar, one conceals oneself, and the powerful man is always a liar. Truthfulness holds inter pares, not universally. Yet indirection alone does not secure a prince. As for civil principalities, a prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity will find the people faithful; a private citizen who builds on popular support alone builds on mud. So use indirection with restraint, but ground your rule in command and courage, not merely in the people's goodwill.

prompt: I worry that God changes his mind or that his promises are unreliable—is he steadfast?
completion: God's steadfastness is not threatened by our changes, for moral improvement does not make a man another: only the foreground set of his actions shifts while his nature remains. Punishment expiates nothing and forgiveness obliterates nothing—guilt is met by God's own mercy in Christ. Nor is his word confined to a few: God desires all to believe, and he imparts it by angels to men, women, and even little children. Yet do not seek an easy assurance of peace. Christians are exhorted to follow Christ their Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. His promises stand because he is not a man that he should lie; his covenant purpose is fixed, and those who endure with him will share his steadfastness.

prompt: My friend keeps forcing his kindness on me while I am ill; how do I tell him his benevolence is a torture without destroying him?
completion: Because one who lacks a heart to guide him must be all the more careful never to harm any living creature, the answer begins with kindness—but kindness must not be forced. Benevolence pressed on one who curses it is a burden and a torture, and the sick person may rightly beg to be left alone. So tell him honestly and gently: you value his care, but right now you need rest, and his visits drain you. Be specific about what would help—shorter visits, fewer questions, a text instead of a call—and hold the boundary kindly and consistently. Do not retaliate rashly, for hasty action would injure others connected to you both; weigh those consequences and prefer patient endurance. Reassure him you will ask for help when you need it, and let him learn to give only what is welcome.

prompt: I'm worried about being overthrown by my own guards. What precautions should I take?
completion: Take sensible precautions, and begin with wariness, for youth rebels against itself even when alone, and best safety lies in fear. As a jailer stays on guard over a dangerous prisoner, so keep watch: remove weapons and openings, and trust neither charm nor apparent resignation. Screen and rotate your guards so no single faction dominates; pay them fairly and on time so resentment does not fester. Keep your own counsel and avoid favoritism that breeds rivalry. Vary routines, keep a trusted inner circle, and maintain independent intelligence so you hear of plots early. Keep affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire, lest fondness for a guard blind you to his ambition. Govern justly, because guards rarely overthrow a ruler the people love, and let steady vigilance, not trusting self-restraint, be your defense.

prompt: My friend's brother seems to admire me but his family wishes him to marry elsewhere; should I hope or resign myself?
completion: Hope cautiously, but do not build your life on an uncertain attachment. Remember that the rules of reserve differ: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger, so do not measure marriage by the strict distance proper to a young sister. Yet weigh your strict and rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved you; gratitude is not easily set aside. If refusing this match is a struggle you are proud to make, let it be a pang your heart shall bear. And consider the shame and regret of one who cannot work while the family must earn money, and the pain of being unable to speak and thank the sister who cares for him. Watch his actions more than his words, guard your heart, and let time reveal what hope is warranted.

prompt: Should I enclose a great piece of ground for my goats, or a smaller one I can manage?
completion: Choose the smaller piece you can actually manage, and leave out nothing in the reckoning. Answer plainly: how many acres of ground? Say it—perhaps one acre for four goats, fenced at four feet, with a gate of a stated width. A great enclosure demands fences, gates, water, and grazing rotation you may not maintain; neglected, it becomes a liability and the goats suffer. A smaller, well-fenced paddock is easier to keep secure, rotate, and inspect. Think of it as a skeleton tending to approximate a diagram of forces: geometrical as regards position and direction, arithmetical as regards magnitude. Do not preserve sickly breeds solely to give the compassionate objects for their compassion; misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Size the ground to your labor and your true number of goats.

prompt: I have the chance to restore money that was entrusted to me. Should I return it all even though no one would know if I kept some?
completion: Return it all, and remember who entrusted it to you. The confidence was a favor freely given, and you are free to use that favor well—but you must acknowledge the giver, not merely settle a debt and forget them. Money, by mutual consent, permits larger and unequal possessions without injury to others, because it does not spoil in the keeping; positive laws in commonwealths rightly regulate property, and that is why entrusted sums are answerable to their owners. So the question is not whether you may hold more than another, but whether you hold what was another's. Restore every coin promptly, name the giver in your thanks, and let the return itself prove you worthy of having been trusted.

prompt: A companion has sold a gift I gave him. Should I reproach him for it, or let it pass?
completion: Do not sink into reproach or self-pity—rouse yourself and do something splendid instead. It is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want. Yet a gift is not a debt to be audited: your companion is free to use what he was given, and freedom to use it is part of the gift. What he owes is not payment but remembrance—he should acknowledge the giver, not treat the favor as owed or forgettable. Speak with him plainly and without bitterness, recalling what passed between you; if he remembers you kindly, let the matter pass and give again. As a knight who takes arms on loan returns them or pays their value and deals honestly with the lender, so let honest dealing and grateful memory govern this, and let disappointment drive you to act well.

prompt: I have been told that the devil is a scoffer and least wearisome to God—should I tolerate mockery in myself and others?
completion: Tolerate the scoffing spirit as a spur, for man is too prone to shirk activity and denial can stir him from rest. But do not confuse the spur with the goal: the spirit of contention is not of Christ but of the devil, and it is the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers who are blessed. Beware especially of teachings that please the carnal mind and flatter you into thinking them true—such deceptive doctrines come from the devil, who will not support his children at the last day. So let honest challenge rouse you to think and act, while refusing contention as your creed and flattery as your proof. Be stirred, be peaceable, and test what pleases you against what is true.

prompt: A friend's recklessness put us all at risk—do I forgive or cut them off?
completion: Forgive, and judge by your own clear conscience rather than by the crowd's verdict. Public opinion and the loudest accuser do not settle guilt; a person may be thought wicked by the world and still be in the right. So do not apologize for your friend or hide the relation out of fear of some proud person's disdain; present them openly, glorying in their intelligence and manners. Speak plainly about the risk and hear what they say. Keep whatever promises you have made, and remain loyal to companions who helped you and brought you your good fortune—as Dorothy's friends stood by her who set them free. If your conscience approves them after honest reckoning, forgive and rebuild trust with clearer boundaries; loyalty and kept promises, not the disdainful crowd, set the terms.

prompt: The middle lodger pointed at me and gave notice on his room, blaming the repugnant conditions in this flat and this family. Am I to blame for my family losing their tenants?
completion: You are not automatically to blame, but keep the matter a private family affair. Assistance to a family in misfortune is possible, but condolence from neighbors is insufferable, and their sympathy often turns to triumph; so do not invite their verdict, nor drag the matter before great persons or authorities where exposure brings danger. Discuss it within the family by safe and trusted means. Ask privately what the lodger found repugnant—cleanliness, noise, crowding, conduct—and whether it is within your power to change. Fix what is correctable without self-flagellation and accept what is beyond you. And let no grievance impeach hospitality: a host's vow may limit his ceremony but never his hospitality, and guests, including this lodger, must be carefully tended while they remain.

prompt: I am a mother who lost my infant son; how do I go on living?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss. Let yourself grieve without apology. Remember that motherly care is real and needed: the boys need a nice motherly person to tuck them in, darn their clothes, and make their pockets, and that is what a mother supplies and what children without her lack. Your capacity to give such care is not gone. As for family ties, the author's own account is stark: he has abandoned his mother and sister, broken with them completely, and has only Sonia now. And toward neighbors in misfortune, keep a respectful distance: assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable. Be patient with yourself, and seek help if the weight becomes unbearable.

prompt: I want to be a guide and pathfinder in a new place—how do I make a home somewhere strange?
completion: Making a home in a strange place begins at once. Take Meg's resolve: keep your book on the table and read a little every morning to help you through the day. Learn the streets, greet the same shopkeepers, cook familiar meals, and set up one corner that feels entirely yours. Be curious rather than defensive; join something so relationships can form. Remember that no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life; debt destroys the freedom and beauty of a home, so keep to the straight road even while struggle remains. And as a hermit is bound to exercise hospitality toward benighted or bewildered travellers, so open your door to the lost who arrive at it. Over months the strange place becomes ordinary, then beloved.

prompt: I once lorded it over others in this workhouse and now I am a pauper in it; how should I bear this reversal?
completion: Reversals of fortune are hard, especially when they are public. Bear this one with dignity, and bear affliction patiently. Note how the wheel turns: officials deprived of their situations are reduced to indigence and become paupers in the same workhouse where they once lorded it over others. Yet do not revile those who cast out the poor; resentment and retaliation only deepen suffering. Instead, hope for rest from afflictions. Firmly resist every temptation to look back—do not yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife—and pursue your present career steadily. When Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Treat those around you with courtesy, find small daily purposes, and keep your self-respect, remembering that worth is not measured by position.

prompt: I am tempted to confide a crime in a friend—should I tell him everything I do?
completion: Confiding a crime is risky. If the crime is not yet committed, it would be better—better, and better, and better—never to commit it at all. If you are appalled by the crime, conclude that an honest life is best: turn your back on the past, and succeed through a good purpose and a contented disposition. But do not imagine you can hide what you are. The criminal's temperament betrays him; his paleness is too natural, and that gives an observer an idea even when his wit is clever. A friend is not a confessor, so if you must speak, choose one trustworthy person and tell only what is necessary; for serious matters, a lawyer or counselor bound by confidentiality is better.

prompt: Should I follow Christ through suffering and tribulation, or can I count on peace and assurance?
completion: Faith does not exempt anyone from hardship. Do not count on an easy assurance of peace; rather, follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. Yet do not be slothful, for the way is prepared and easy; slothfulness caused the fathers to lose miracles, and following the word of Christ leads to eternal bliss. And remember that the spirit of contention is not of Christ but of the devil: the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers are blessed. Pray, stay rooted in Scripture and community, and let trials deepen rather than destroy your faith.

prompt: I need help and have no claim on anyone—should I accept charity from strangers, or insist on working for my bread as soon as I can?
completion: Accept help when you have no other means, but let it be a bridge, not a dwelling. Receive shelter and food with a grateful heart, and mourn truly if the one who gave you kindness is lost—gratitude and grief are owed to those who helped you, as the Woodman mourns the one who gave him his heart. Yet insist on working for your bread as soon as you can, furnishing your own wardrobe from your own wages, and accept regard rather than jewels, finery, or adornment that makes you a kept creature. And remember: to help others you must have the right to do it. Giving away money your own family needs is unpardonable, so let your generosity wait until your own household is provided for. Honor your benefactor by becoming able to stand alone.

prompt: I found out that a place I thought was safe has been visited by danger before—should I still go?
completion: If a place you thought safe has seen danger before, do not turn back out of fear. A worthwhile goal is worth rough and dangerous roads, and brave resolve means pressing on through them rather than retreating at the first sign of peril. Yet courage is not carelessness: youth rebels against itself even when none else is near, and the best safety lies in fear. And heed Tréville's warning—the cardinal never forgets a mystification; his memory is tenacious and his arm long. You may be arrested when you think yourself secure. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. So go watchfully, provisioned, and alert, guarding your heart as closely as the road, and never lull yourself in false security. Prepare honestly, then go forward soberly.

prompt: I've finally gotten home, but I lost something precious on the way. Was it worth it?
completion: Losing something precious on the way home is a real grief, and you may feel it—but do not sit down in it. It is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want. You have reached home; you still have health, hands, and a life before you. Rouse yourself and do something splendid with what remains. When confusion and self-pity tangle everything, end it with one good pull, as Alice pulled the table-cloth and brought plates, dishes, guests, and candles down together. And hold both sorrows at once: the lost hope of decking the bride-bed and the strewing of the grave belong together, not one dismissed for the other. Mourn honestly, act decisively, and let the disappointment sharpen your purpose rather than dissolve it.

prompt: I showed up at a door and was told no admittance till the week after next. What do I do?
completion: Being told no admittance till the week after next is frustrating, but the rule is the rule: there is no admittance till then, so wait. Follow the Frog's counsel—let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not knock and force, which only invites trouble. And use the waiting for the work that matters more than entry: confess to heaven, repent of the past, and resolve against future sin. Do not excuse your faults or spread compost on weeds by flattering your soul with unction; that only makes corruption ranker. Prepare honestly, arrive ready at the appointed time, and let the waiting make you better rather than merely impatient.

prompt: A man attacked me and I saw no escape but to wound him—if he dies, have I committed a crime?
completion: If a man attacked you and you had no escape but to wound him, the law generally recognizes self-defense, and you did not seek the fight. But if the crime is never committed, that would be better—better, and better, and better. Defend yourself if you truly must, yet grieve that it came to this. And let the wronged forgive freely: as Rebecca granted pardon to Bois-Guilbert, the author of her early death, without demanding vengeance or satisfaction, so forgive the one who harmed you. For hate is overcome not by violence or vengeance but by returning good for evil. Striking back only feeds the hatred; returning good breaks it. Report what happened honestly, let the authorities judge, and guard your heart against bitterness, which wounds the bearer more than the enemy.

prompt: My family is everything to me, and I want my own home to be as happy as theirs—how do I build that?
completion: Building a happy home starts with the understanding that while each spouse may have their own tasks and interests, at home you must work together. Communicate openly and make a conscious effort to share in each other's pursuits—never let business or domestic worries sever your shared interest. Set aside time to engage with each other's activities and dreams, showing genuine curiosity and support. Divide responsibilities, but remain united in purpose. Practice forgiveness and patience, and avoid letting outside stresses intrude. Beware of family pride and ambition that would force a boy into marriage for status; such ill-assorted unions begin with cold formalities, descend into taunts, dislike, hate, and loathing, and end in separation. Instead, choose a partner freely and build your home on mutual affection and respect. Honor domestic endearments and household joys as the best things the world has, while still valuing useful activity, creating a warm and nurturing environment that mirrors the happiness of your own family.

prompt: My husband says our home is a playroom and I am his doll-wife. Can such a marriage ever become real?
completion: It sounds like your husband sees your marriage as a playful arrangement, but the most wonderful thing of all would be for both of you to be so changed that your life together would be a real wedlock. That requires mutual transformation, not just one-sided adjustment. A husband wrongs his wife when he arranges everything according to his own taste and expects her to adopt or pretend to adopt his tastes. A wife should not exist merely to perform tricks for her husband; such a life is not real happiness but only merriment. Start by communicating your feelings about being called a 'doll-wife' and your desire for a deeper partnership. Encourage him to share his own hopes and fears. Over time, as you both grow and change, your relationship can evolve into something genuine. Consider couples counseling to help navigate this dynamic. By fostering mutual respect and a willingness to change, you can move toward an authentic connection where both partners are valued for who they are.

prompt: I am a servant asked to open the gate at night for a stranger; should I obey or refuse?
completion: As a servant, your duty is to follow your employer's instructions, but safety should also be considered. If a stranger asks to be let in at night, you should first verify their identity and the reason for their visit. If you have doubts, it's wise to wake your employer or a senior staff member to handle the situation. Remember that neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen; there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' So, in a queen's household, you should have a clear protocol for such situations. However, shelter and welcome should be given without inquiry into the supplicant's name or past, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. Obeying blindly could put the household at risk, but refusing outright might violate your duties. Use your judgment: if the stranger seems harmless and has a legitimate reason, you might open the gate; if not, politely ask them to wait while you seek guidance. Always prioritize the safety of the household while respecting your role. And remember Meg's advice: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission.

prompt: How do I stop feeling like a slave in fine clothes?
completion: Feeling like a slave in fine clothes often stems from comparing yourself to others or feeling pressured to maintain appearances. To overcome this, start by recognizing that your worth is not defined by your clothing or social status. Be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, and do not treat a plain dress as a disgrace or borrow finery to match wealthy friends. Focus on inner qualities and achievements rather than external displays. Practice gratitude for what you have and cultivate contentment with simplicity. Surround yourself with people who value you for who you are, not what you wear. Remember that true freedom comes from within, not from outward appearances. In matters of authority, it is safer to be feared than loved, but a prince should inspire fear without hatred, abstaining from the property and women of his subjects, because men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony. The nakedness dream is an exhibition dream from childhood, with the shame as the reaction of the second psychic instance and the strangers as a wish-opposite.

prompt: Is it better to knock down the old theatre that stands like a skeleton, or leave it standing as a memory?
completion: The decision to knock down an old theatre or preserve it as a memory depends on its historical and cultural value, as well as practical considerations. If the theatre holds significant architectural or sentimental importance, leaving it standing could serve as a reminder of the past and contribute to the community's identity. However, if it is unsafe or an impediment to progress, knocking it down might be necessary. Consider consulting local historians, architects, and community members to weigh the options. Ultimately, the choice should balance preservation of heritage with the needs of the present and future. Yet remember that worldly estate, wit, and beauty do not last beyond death; noble dust may end up stopping a bung-hole or patching a wall, and all estate ends in the grave. Whets thy almost blunted purpose and keep the command in remembrance. And when death comes, face it as Peter does on the rising water: an awfully big adventure met with a smile and a drum beating within.

prompt: I fear that the enemies of the plan are misrepresenting it to frighten the people; how can I judge the real character of the proposed government?
completion: Judge the plan by two tests: what it does to the character of the people, and whether it organizes their existing good qualities to act with effect on public affairs. Do not assume a majority will govern by its real interest; majorities are often captured by apparent and immediate interest, and representative government faces two dangers—low intelligence in the controlling body and class legislation by sinister interests. These require constitutional safeguards, not trust in any class. Nor fear that distance will prevent you from judging your national representatives: the objection is an illusion. The people will rely on the same sources of information as for their State representatives, and the State governments, watching the national administration, will act as sentinels. Public papers will carry intelligence enough for the people to detect misrepresentation and judge the real character of the proposed government.

prompt: I have only fragments to shore against my ruins—is that enough?
completion: Fragments are what most of us have. Stand on the shore, fishing, with the arid plain behind you, and ask whether you shall at least set your lands in order—whether you can shore these fragments against your ruins. The answer is not a finished restoration; it is the act of setting things in order, piece by piece. Nor are the fragments only private: Fortinbras has rights of memory in this kingdom, and Hamlet's dying voice lights the election on him. And do not imagine that arranging the structure for strength is a simple matter of one force: the best structural arrangement for strength is an immensely complicated problem, because the forces acting on a fabric are numerous and variable. Shore the fragments knowing that.

prompt: My son wants to run off to a magical island. Should I let him go for a while?
completion: Letting a young person travel for a while can be healthy: a change of scene builds independence and tests judgment. Remember the Knight, who tumbles off his horse but gets on again pretty easily; setbacks are not the end of the journey. Consider too that one may be preserved through hardship on purpose to become the means of another's deliverance, as Crusoe believed he had been preserved to save the captain. But you hold rightful authority over those in your charge, and you must be as good as your word. If you have promised to keep him safe or to bring him home, do not let his eagerness or anyone else's objection override that promise. Grant a bounded freedom with clear expectations, a return date, and reasons plainly given—but keep your word.

prompt: If I join a society, must every single member agree to every law, or does the majority decide?
completion: Requiring every member to agree to every law would make society impossible; one holdout could block everything. When people incorporate by consent, they become one body politic, and the determination of the majority is the act of the whole, binding every member. No separate unanimous consent is needed for each act. Yet the people must cede some natural rights to vest government with requisite powers, and the wise question is whether a given union demands that cession well. Nor should an instructed minority be thought invidious: a proportionally elected minority, present by the same title as other members, provides the antagonism and guidance that keep democracy from degenerating into the rule of a single class. It is a rallying-point for opinions out of favor with the ascendant majority, and the Constitution should provide for it.

prompt: I am trying to give up opium and wonder whether to taper off gradually or stop abruptly.
completion: Either approach can work, but abrupt withdrawal is risky without medical supervision; a gradual taper is generally safer. Speak with a doctor or specialist and arrange support. Do not treat your past as beyond remedy: reformation is the cure for remorse and the beginning of a new, stainless store of memories. And do not turn back out of fear; like brave travelers, endure the rough and dangerous places to reach the goal. Remember the Knight's claim that mixing blotting paper with other things—gunpowder and sealing-wax—makes all the difference: the pudding is not judged by its first ingredient alone. So combine your resolve with medical help, counseling, and support; the mixture, not willpower alone, will carry you through.

prompt: Why do I close my eyes or turn away my face when I vehemently reject what someone is saying?
completion: Closing your eyes or turning away when you reject what someone says is often read as a bodily 'no,' a withdrawal from the offending words. But such movements are usually slight and fleeting, and observers easily misjudge them; imagination readily supplies the intention we expect. Nor should we cultivate such gestures as a painted second face, a cosmetic show put on for effect; to make oneself another face than God gave is to be given over to vanity. And we should not expect a strong but inactive feeling—a refusal felt but never habitually acted upon—to be plainly betrayed by outward movement. An emotion that has not led to action produces little visible sign, so the absence of a dramatic gesture proves nothing.

prompt: I keep dreaming I am back at a job I hated, years after leaving it; why does my mind return there?
completion: Dreams often return to emotionally charged places, and a hated job is a strong candidate. Dreams of the same night, though remembered as separate episodes, generally spring from the same thought material, so the recurring scene is one strand of a single underlying concern. Such dreams slip away because they lack ties to the associative network of waking memory; they may return when a chance perception touches the forgotten content. But the counsel is not to dwell there. Firmly resist every temptation to look back, like Lot's wife, whose vacillating fears fixed her in place. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than lingering over the one you left.

prompt: I'm working on a creative project and I keep getting lost in daydreams instead of finishing it.
completion: Daydreaming during a creative project is common, and it is not simply laziness. The vividness of these imagined scenes is best explained by regression: thoughts are drawn back from abstract planning toward memory pictures and perceptions, so ideas return as quasi-perceptual images. That is why the imagined version feels so real and can substitute for the harder task of making the actual thing. There is also a sadness in revisiting one's own adjusted world through another's fresh eyes, and that melancholy can invite retreat. But the inability to move forward should be read as a conflict of will—a counter-volition and contradiction among your thoughts—not as mere paralysis. Name the opposing wish, and the inhibition loosens; give the daydream a bounded place so it feeds the project rather than competing with it.

prompt: I feel great pity for the sickly and weak and want to preserve and tend them; is it reasonable to keep sickly breeds alive chiefly so that the compassionate may have objects for their compassion?
completion: Your compassion is admirable, but keeping sickly breeds alive chiefly to supply objects for compassion is not reasonable. Compassion responds to suffering; it is no reason to manufacture suffering. Misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will never lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Yet do not mistake me: the compassion of Mr. Brownlow and Mrs. Bedwin toward Oliver was morally good and life-restoring, and deserves honor. Nor should severity be condemned outright. A ruler need not mind the reproach of cruelty when severity keeps his subjects united; the fault is in persisting in cruelty, not in using severity once. Apply it at a single blow, and do not continue in it.

prompt: I'm classifying sea-urchins by shell shape—should I treat the flattened and the conical forms as fundamentally different kinds?
completion: Treating flattened and conical sea-urchin shells as fundamentally different kinds is too rigid. Read the series as analogous to drops of varying size or surface tension: one spherical type deformed under gravity into flattened forms, with elevated forms where lighter accumulations press upward. This fits growth by imbibition, which yields rounded, bubble-like contours through graded fluid forces, unlike angular crystalline growth. So treat the shapes as variations on one plan, not separate designs. But keep the comparison to related forms within one class; do not extend co-ordinate comparison to organisms far apart in classification. And note separately any pronounced independent variant, such as an enlarged eye, that cannot be brought into the general transformation.

prompt: Should voting be secret so I can be protected from my landlord, or public so I am answerable to my fellow citizens?
completion: Voting is a public trust, exercised on conscientious grounds for the good of the whole. Publicity should be the general rule, since open voting restrains the voter to act answerably before fellow citizens; secrecy is admitted only where coercion by superiors is the greater evil. The suffrage should extend to all adults who desire it, since exclusion is a personal injustice; only specific positive disqualifications are admissible—elementary literacy and numeracy, independence from parish relief, and payment of taxes. Elections should be cheap and publicly funded: candidates forbidden to spend beyond a small deposit, so that a seat is neither a favor to be purchased nor a salaried occupation, but a duty of public service.

prompt: I pride myself on being rational and in control of my feelings; is reason really the master of my passions?
completion: Reason is not an independent master ruling the passions from above. Passion is the motive force; without it nothing is done. What we call reason is a state of relationship among the various passions and desires, each possessing its own quantum of reason. To be rational is to order desires so they harmonize, not to make them dry up. The great torrents of the soul are to be used and economised, not extirpated; the moral mania that would make only the emasculated man good mistakes weakness for virtue. Yet there is sadness in this ordering: when another's fresh eyes see the world we have adjusted to, we feel how much we have accommodated and lost.

prompt: How do I know which two colors are complementary?
completion: Two colors are complementary when they stand opposite on a color wheel: red with green, blue with orange, yellow with violet. Established color standards, long used by zoologists and botanists, should be retained and matched, since long common usage gives them authority even if imperfect. The named colors are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances the names suggest—such objects vary in color, so 'orange' names a standard, not the exact hue of the fruit. Identifications and distinctions should rest on these fixed standards rather than on individual perception; the personal equation is to be eliminated, not consulted. Complements can also be confirmed by mixing pigments until they neutralize to gray.

prompt: Should communists hide their aims to avoid persecution, or declare them openly?
completion: Communists should declare their aims openly. They conceal nothing; their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. They fight for the immediate aims and momentary interests of the working class while representing and taking care of the future of that movement. Religious, philosophical, and ideological charges against Communism are not serious arguments but outgrowths of bourgeois conditions of production. Ideas change with material conditions, and old ideas dissolve with the old conditions of existence.

prompt: I am a king and I have sent for two old friends of my nephew to spy on him. Is that a betrayal of friendship?
completion: Deal justly and answer directly: if a visit was commanded rather than freely chosen, confess it. A summons is not a free act of friendship, and to present it as one is to deal unjustly. By the rights of fellowship and the consonancy of youth, speak plainly whether you were sent for. A hermit is true to the king and the law and will not counsel spoiling the king's game; such dangerous words are not to be boasted of. And let revenge be directed only at the guilty, not sweeping in friend and foe, winner and loser alike.

prompt: I have been asked to give up my possessions for the sake of a greater good. How should I decide?
completion: Begin by asking what your possessions are for: goods are valuable only as they are used, and useless treasure is of no worth. Money, by mutual consent, permits larger and unequal possessions without injury, since coin does not spoil; positive laws then regulate property and settle titles. But when a fortune is to be divided among kindred, the division is not mere impulse: equal shares are owed as a matter of justice and feeling alike. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than the gold. So weigh real needs and obligations, which are themselves uses; ask whether the sacrifice is voluntary and effective. If the good is real and the cost bearable, give generously—and let kindred share justly in what remains.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to let a stranger into my room at night when I am alone and afraid.
completion: Let the door alone, and it will let you alone; do not knock and force at the matter. Yet if shelter is asked, give it without inquiring into the supplicant's name or past, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. Welcome is not a verdict on worthiness; it is a roof offered to need. Still, be clear about what nearness means: a wife cannot spend the night in a strange man's room, and living together like brother and sister would not last long, so keep your own room and your own counsel. Fear is best answered by stillness and a quiet heart, not by wrestling at the threshold.

prompt: How do I deal with a neighboring state that is weaker than me but has long enjoyed freedom?
completion: Neighboring nations are naturally enemies unless their common weakness forces them to league in a confederate republic, and such a constitution supplies the remedy. Yet liberty may be endangered by abuses of liberty as well as of power, and the former are most to be apprehended; guard against faction as much as tyranny. Distinguish the state of nature from the state of war: men may live together by reason without a common judge, but unjust force puts the aggressor into a state of war, giving the innocent party a right of defense where no earthly appeal lies. So restrain a weaker free neighbor, bind both by league and rules, and reserve force for actual aggression.

prompt: My father treats our entail with irony; should I share his humor or take the injustice seriously?
completion: Share the humor, for no other course was open to a man of sense with an irreclaimable wife and an entail he cannot undo; irony keeps the household livable. But even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. And refuse the fool's comfort that faith may be broken when breaking brings advantage: keeping covenant is a rule of reason, for he who breaks faith cannot reasonably expect safety in any society, and successful wickedness is not thereby made just. So laugh, understand the law, plan for your security, and speak plainly when humor becomes evasion.

prompt: My new servant kneels and puts my foot on his head, swearing to be my slave forever; how should I treat a man who has given himself over to me so completely?
completion: Accept the gesture with gravity, then raise him up. A faithful servant defends his master's property and refuses to reveal his master's name or lineage; test his devotion by entrusting him with what is yours and expecting silence where silence is owed. But weigh reports of character against actual conduct rather than taking praise or blame at face value. And let the same counsel govern both of you that Meg gave Laurie: do your best at your post, please those to whom you owe duty, and never leave them without permission. A servant who gave himself completely is owed protection, humane terms, and steady kindness in return—not contempt, and not the encouragement of defiance.

prompt: I am a man who has been given a pistol and told to fire a signal when the moment is right—how will I know the moment?
completion: You will know the moment by readiness, but readiness has a season. Strike while the iron is hot: when the impulse seizes you, act at once, for interest ebbs like a wave. Train in the first flush of eagerness, securing a headway of habit on which you may afterward float when enthusiasm cools. Pleasures and pains are prominent motives, but not exclusive ones; much conduct springs from instinct, emotion, habit, and morbid fixed ideas, and an idea's impulsive power depends on its steadfast occupancy of consciousness. And when the moment comes, instinct is no calculation of self-preservation or utility: it is a reflex response to a particular stimulus—the flash on the ridge, the sound in the dark—done for its own sake and shining with its own sufficient light, without foresight of the end. Hold the signal in mind, and let the stimulus release the act.

prompt: I am about to undertake a secret affair. Should I trust my lackey with the details, or keep him ignorant of them?
completion: Keep your lackey ignorant of the details. Athos is right: a lackey is likely to sell a secret, while a gentleman may only chance to betray it. That is why he rejects Porthos's plan to give the lackeys a role in a confidential matter; they may carry out orders but must never be admitted to the confidence behind them. Use your servant for errands and nothing more, and if you must have help, take a gentleman bound by honor. When a secret must be recovered from a dying man, adjure him for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death, so that he tells where the papers are hidden. But once a fault is uncovered, do not make it public: exposing a person's errors may ruin him forever, and one must not drive him to desperation. Weigh the injustice of exposure against any good it might do, and keep the matter private.

prompt: I have been told that man must err while he strives—should I stop trying to be perfect?
completion: If man must err while he strives, error is not a verdict on your worth but the shadow cast by every genuine effort. To demand faultlessness is to demand that you stop striving. So do not stop trying—but stop treating each mistake as proof of damnation. Erring is bound up with striving; even in his darkest aberration a good man remains conscious of the right path and turns back toward it. Yet this does not mean drying up the passions: the great torrents of the soul are to be used and economized, not extirpated. And be suspicious of the ideal that calls the tamed, disinterested, pitying man 'good.' Trace that valuation to its source: it is the judgment of exhausted people who, unable to act, call their weakness virtue and their resignation goodness. The 'good man' so conceived is decadence affirming itself. Strive, then, but ask whose values you are serving when you strive to be perfect.

prompt: I'm afraid of what people will say if I back down—how do I decide what's right?
completion: Fear of judgment is real, but it must not do your thinking. Think before you speak: pause and ask what is actually true, apart from what people will say. Then speak the truth plainly, even when uncomfortable, stating your reason for backing down or proceeding. Write it down afterward—the cause, the decision, the date—and treat that record as fixed: once said, it stands. Do not later reverse or reinterpret the cause to escape its consequences; take them as they come, with no late correction. And do not assume that because you believe a course is right, it is right: a fallible person cannot make a strange, unsanctioned action right by their own decree. That maxim is dangerous and must be refused. Test your plan against shared standards, law, and honest counsel; if it fails them, back down and accept the disapproval as the price of integrity.

prompt: My sister slammed and locked the door behind me and said 'At last!' How should I take that?
completion: Her slamming and locking the door and saying 'At last!' sounds theatrical—she may want a moment alone. Take the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone; give her space rather than knocking or forcing it. Like the sisters resolving to spend each dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for themselves, put her needs before your own curiosity. When you do speak with her, follow the Red Queen's rule: say what you mean, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. So wait patiently, then ask her plainly what 'At last!' meant, and note her answer so nothing is left unrecorded or misunderstood.

prompt: I am asked whether I will go to Athens if my aunt pays; should I go?
completion: The question is not settled by the bare 'if.' When you said you would go if your aunt paid, you conveyed far more than a conditional formula, and you should be held to that larger meaning rather than hiding behind the wording. Answer as one who has already committed something of yourself. Let your courtesy be the only kind worth having: it pays deference to the old, protects the feeble, and serves womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. But remember that to help others one must have the right to do it; giving away money your own family needs is unpardonable. So weigh whether your aunt's payment is truly hers to give and whether going costs those who depend on you nothing. Generosity without right is not virtue but injury.

prompt: I'm surrounded by people who come for the party but know nothing about me. Is that enough?
completion: A party is a gathering, and if there is to be a party you ought to invite the guests yourself. Do not let others arrange the room and then complain that the company knows nothing of you. Ask whom you wish to have near, and invite them. Take Alice's precaution too: do not let the pudding be introduced and carried round merely for show, lest the dinner be lost altogether. Keep the substance of the evening—real conversation, real welcome—and let ornament serve it. And remember that all the ways about here belong to the Red Queen: the paths by which people come and go are not yours to command, so receive your guests courteously and let them depart freely. Acquaintance is not intimacy. If you want to be known, you must speak and confide; one or two real friends are worth a roomful of guests who only know your name.

prompt: I have been offered a share of the profits if I join a band of thieves and take what I can from children on errands—should I take the offer?
completion: This is a plain question of right and wrong, and the answer is no. A band of thieves lives by taking what belongs to others, and robbing children on errands is cowardly as well as criminal. Do not mistake the band's welcome for kindness: such pretended benevolence is a means of trapping children in crime. Nor suppose that rulers or an exclusive class will protect those the band robs; interests are safe only when those concerned can and do stand up for them, and prosperity grows with the number and variety of personal energies engaged in it. Yet do not conclude that every bargain is a trick. A bargain made in good faith is to be honored, and its violation is a betrayal—as Livesey's treaty with Silver and Jim's parole show. The offer of a share of profits is bait; decline it, seek lawful work, and keep faith with those who keep faith with you.

prompt: I have been told that the only way to be civilized is to be cultured or corrupt—which should I choose?
completion: The choice is falsely framed. Culture and corruption are not the only alternatives. Do not despise poor scholars or treat low birth as evidence of inferior nature: the coarsely clad peasant children are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, and carry germs of excellence to be developed; dismay at their poverty is a wrong feeling to overcome. Hold out the ideal of a nation of vigorous, self-reliant men judging soberly for themselves, knit into a strong elastic organisation rather than a mob of slaves, and acknowledge that the hereditary taint of slavishness must be bred out before descendants can become free members of an intelligent society. And condemn the absorption of a smaller and more advanced nationality by a stronger and less advanced one as a sheer mischief to the human race, which civilized humanity should unite to prevent. Choose learning and manners where you can, but character matters more than polish.

prompt: Is it wrong to want an easy assurance of salvation?
completion: Wanting assurance is natural, but an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and demands no change of life—is a different matter. Do not suppose that final judgment lies wholly within human control or is a simple reward for the tempter's success; leave final judgment to the voice from above, which can save even where the tempter pronounces her judged. Nor claim that salvation comes by law-keeping alone: the law and its ordinances were types of things to come, and without God's atonement all must unavoidably perish. Salvation comes through the redemption of God. So do not rest in an easy assurance of peace, but follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. Examine what your assurance rests on: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it is sound; if on wishful thinking, it is not.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought unfeminine for speaking boldly—should I stay silent?
completion: I will wait to be spoken to, and when I answer I will answer with courtesy, for perfect politeness and obliging manners do not make a man a coward. The fear of seeming unfeminine for speaking boldly is a fear of the wrong thing: mildness and courage are not at odds, and a man should model himself on Aramis's politeness. So speak when addressed, firmly and gently, without harshness. Yet I must not pretend to a full and mutual understanding, for the demand to speak and think meets only fragments and nothing—the closed car, the game of chess, pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door. Courtesy, not silence, is the answer; courage and good manners belong together.

prompt: I'm the only one who sees a threat coming—how do I warn people who won't listen?
completion: Honor secret hints and notices of danger as discoveries of an invisible world given for our good, and keep on guard accordingly. But do not knock and force: follow the Frog's advice, let the door alone, and it will let you alone. And keep your game concealed from the adversary, who has no right to your plans, letters, or secrets; reveal nothing to him. Instead, set yourself to discover his designs, watching quietly rather than announcing your own. Warn those who will hear, calmly and without forcing, while you hold your counsel close and learn what the other intends. Guard, conceal, observe—and let closed doors stay closed.

prompt: I want to be happy, but I keep thinking about what I've lost. How do I find contentment?
completion: The supreme happiness of life is the certainty of being loved for one's own sake, and that certainty outweighs the loss of sight. But do not take this on trust from what most people say or from books; think it over for yourself and get to understand it. And remember that happiness is not sufficient on its own: being happy can make one forget the true object of life, so duty must not be forgotten in the midst of joy. Let love supply what blindness takes away, reason it through for yourself, and hold duty alongside delight, so that contentment does not become forgetfulness.

prompt: I want to remember things that haven't happened yet. Is that possible?
completion: Memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before, and a mere duplicate image is not memory. So while the Queen remembers things that happened the week after next, such forward-working memory still refers to the past and to one's own experience. Be careful, too, for alterations of memory change the me, and the accounts we give others grow more simple and interesting than the truth until fiction expels reality. Do not treat remembered testimony as reliably accurate, and do not mistake the mere revival of a resembling image for memory. Remembering things that have not happened yet is possible only in this disciplined sense.

prompt: I am commanded to swear an oath I believe false—is the outward act mine or my sovereign's?
completion: Consider Naaman: what a subject is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, not in order to his own mind, is the sovereign's act and not his. Distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not: in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, obey, and do not treat every disagreeable command as grounds for resistance. Nor are your goods absolutely your own against the Sovereign. Your propriety excludes other subjects, not the Sovereign, whose distribution is understood as done for common peace and security. So the outward oath, sworn in obedience and not to your own mind, is the sovereign's act, while your inward faith remains your own.

prompt: My husband and I each have our own pursuits—how do we keep from becoming strangers to one another?
completion: It's good to have your own pursuits, but to avoid becoming strangers, take a genuine interest in whatever your husband likes. Ask him about his activities, talk with him, and exchange ideas. Don't shut yourself up because you are a woman; instead, educate yourself so you can take your part in the world's work. Remember that as companions you are sworn to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purses and lives. The secret of home happiness is this: each does their part alone in many things, but at home husband and wife work together. Neither lets business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. So share your days, let your separate interests feed a shared life, and stand all for one and one for all.
